Eck Robertson recorded 'Sallie Gooden' for Victor in New York on July 1, 1922. His solo recording is an early example of Texas-style variations on a short fiddle melody. The Discography of American Historical Recordings lists Robertson as the arranger, not the composer.

Henry Reed also recorded the tune for the Library of Congress in 1966. These are separate versions, not credits for every recording on this page.

Sources: UC Santa Barbara, Discography of American Historical Recordings, Victor matrix B-26664; American Folklife Center, Library of Congress.

title: Old Joe Clark
alternative_titles: Joe Clark
description:
'Old Joe Clark' circulated as both a song and a fiddle tune, with many comic verses. The Traditional Tune Archive discusses its use as a play-party tune and notes Alan Jabbour's observation that he had found no nineteenth-century printed examples. That is not evidence that the melody was composed in the twentieth century.

Stories identifying Joe Clark with a particular Kentucky resident are not a secure origin for the tune. Ira Ford included it in Traditional Music in America (1940).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz.

title: John Henry
description:
'John Henry' tells of a Black steel-driver who competes against a steam drill. The story circulated in work songs and ballads before appearing in many instrumental versions. Guy Johnson examined the legend in his 1929 book John Henry: Tracking Down a Negro Legend.

The historical person and the location of the contest remain disputed; the tune does not settle those questions.

title: Angeline the Baker
alternative_titles: Angelina Baker
description:
'Angeline the Baker' is related to Stephen Foster's 1850 song 'Angelina Baker,' whose lyrics describe an enslaved woman separated from her lover by sale. An early fiddle version was recorded by Uncle Eck Dunford for Victor in 1928. The tune appears in David Brody's Fiddler's Fakebook (1982).

The recording here is by Tom Joad, preserved by the Internet Archive, not a recording of Foster or Dunford.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org).

title: St. Anne's Reel
description:
One of the most widely-played reels in North America, 'St. Anne's Reel' is a point of convergence between Old-Time, Celtic, and Quebec fiddle traditions. Its exact origins are disputed — claimed by both Irish and French-Canadian traditions. It was recorded in the early 20th century by Canadian fiddlers and adopted into Old-Time through the shared dance hall culture of the 19th century.

The recording heard here is a 78rpm disc by Bob Hill and his Canadian Country Boys, digitized by the Internet Archive.

Included in Pat McNulty's *Dance Music of Ireland* (1965). AB (Reiner & Anick, Silberberg): AABB (Begin, Brody, Cranford/Holland, Jarman, Mallinson, Martin & Hughes, Miller & Perron, O'Neill, Perlman, Sweet, Taylor): AA'BB' (Phillips).

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: Waterbound
description:
In pre-bridge Appalachia, being 'waterbound' — stranded by a flooded creek or river — was a frequent and sometimes dangerous predicament that could last days. Mountain roads followed creek beds and crossed streams repeatedly, making heavy rains an instant barrier. The tune captures the patient waiting of someone stuck on the far bank, watching the water rise and fall. It was widely collected across the Blue Ridge and Smokies.

The recording heard here is by Derek Piotr, Guy Wolff, preserved by the Internet Archive.

Included in Andrew Kuntz's *Ragged but Right* (1987). AB (Silberberg): AABB (Kuntz). "Waterbound" was originally recorded in March, 1929, by the Grayson/Carroll County, southwestern Virginia, group Fields Ward's (1911-1987) Buck Mountain Band consisting of Fields Ward (gtr., vocals), Ernest V.

title: June Apple
alternative_titles: The June Apple, June Apples, The June Apples
description:
Named for a variety of apple that ripens in early summer in the Southern Appalachians, 'June Apple' is a Mixolydian reel with roots in the mountain fiddle tradition. The Mixolydian mode — associated with Scots-Irish modal music — gives it a slightly archaic quality that distinguishes it from major-key dance tunes. It has been collected in multiple versions across Virginia, North Carolina, and Kentucky.

The recording heard here is by Derek Piotr, Guy Wolff, preserved by the Internet Archive.

Included in Miles Krassen's *Appalachian Fiddle* (1973). Standard or AEae (Tommy Jarrell) tunings (fiddle). AB (Silberberg): AABB (most versions). A June apple is an early ripening variety of apple, maturing in the spring in the southern United States. It tends to be smaller and more tart then later-ripening apples. Most versions of the tune are in the mixolydian mode, although Benton Flippen (b. 1920, Surry Country, N.C.) plays it in A major. The late Mt.

title: Leather Britches
description:
'Leather Britches' has one of the most appetizing titles in the old-time repertoire. 'Leather britches' are string beans dried in their pods — a preservation technique widespread across the Appalachian mountains before refrigeration, where the beans were strung on thread and hung to dry in kitchens and porches through late summer, then cooked with fatback through winter. The drying process turns them leathery and chewy, intensifying their flavor. It was a ballroom and court dance tune in its earlier life; in the mountains it became a driving reel. Flatpicker Doc Watson recorded an version, and it remains one of the most commonly played tunes at Appalachian jams.

Included in E.F. Adam's *Old Time Fiddlers Favorite Barn Dance Tunes* (1928). See " Lord MacDonald (4) " which is thought to be the origin of the American version.

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)
tags: ancient, appalachian, G major, folk history

title: New Ground
description: A tune named for agricultural clearing practices, reflecting the centrality of farming in Appalachian life.

title: Hickory Jack
description:
Hickory (Carya spp.) was one of the most valued trees in the Appalachian forest — hard, shock-resistant, and used for tool handles, wagon wheels, axles, and furniture. The name 'Jack' was a generic working-class name in American folk culture (see also 'Cracker Jack,' 'Flapjack,' 'Steeplejack'). Hickory Jack as a character represents the competent, self-reliant Appalachian worker — the backbone of the mountain economy. The tune has a similar character: reliable, sturdy, unpretentious.

The recording heard here is by Boyd Asher, preserved by the Internet Archive.

Included in Jeff Titon's *Old Time Kentucky Fiddle Tunes* (2001). Recorded in 1937 for the Library of Congress by Alan and Elizabeth Lomax from the playing of Luther Strong. Titon (2001) says the tune's provenance was the southeastern Kentucky coal fields, and is closely related to a central Appalachian tune called " Route (The) ."

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: Ducks on the Millpond
description:
'Ducks on the Millpond' evokes one of the most pastoral images in Appalachian folk life: the millpond, built to power a grist mill, where the community's grain was ground and where, inevitably, a few ducks would settle on the still water. The millpond was a social hub in mountain communities — a place where neighbors met while waiting for their corn to be ground — and naming a tune for it situates the music in a specific, deeply local world. The tune itself has a gentle, unhurried quality in A major that differs from the driving breakdowns more typical of old-time music, giving it a slightly contemplative character. It was played both as a dance tune and as a piece of pure musical pleasure. The two-part AABB structure is symmetrical and singable.

Included in Anthony Spadaro's *10 Cents a Dance* (1980). Airy, N.C. D Major. ADae tuning (fiddle). AB (Silberberg): AABB (Brody, Krassen, Phillips/Lundy, Spadaro): AA'BB' (Phillips/Sutphin, Hollow Rock String Band). Most modern versions are derived from the playing of Grayson County, southwest Virginia, fiddler Emmett Lundy (1864-1953).

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: Midnight on the Water
description:
'Midnight on the Water' is widely attributed to Luke Thomasson and/or Charles Cunningham of Bosque County, Texas, and is one of the most hauntingly beautiful tunes in the American fiddle tradition. The D minor waltz has a quality of still, dark water — which is precisely what the title evokes — and in the right hands can stop a crowded dance hall. Texas fiddler Benny Thomasson (Luke's son) made it a centerpiece of his contest performances, and the tune spread through the contest circuit into wider circulation. It belongs to a category of Texas fiddle waltzes — along with 'Over the Waterfall' and 'Over the Waves' — that function more as slow, expressive performance pieces than as functional dance accompaniment. The three-part structure (AABBCC) gives it more room to develop than a standard two-part tune.

The recording heard here is by Jack Saturday, preserved by the Internet Archive.

Included in Will Welling's *The Hartford Tune Book* (1974). DDad tuning (fiddle). AABB (Spadaro): AA'BB' (Brody, Matthiesen, Reiner & Anick).

This popular composition is usually credited to Texas fiddler Luke Thomasson, although it has been published that Luke's son Benny (a famous Texas-style fiddler who popularized the melody) long remembered the night he heard both his father and uncle composing the tune on the family porch (c. 1900?).

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: Peacock Rag
description:
The ragtime influence on Old-Time fiddling was substantial in the 1920s — Scott Joplin's rags (1899–1917) had permeated popular culture, and fiddle players absorbed the syncopated rhythms into their repertoire. 'Peacock Rag' belongs to a category of rag-influenced dance tunes that appeared in Southern and Midwestern fiddle contests of the 1920s, reflecting the era's appetite for modern, syncopated music. The peacock's flamboyant display suggested the showmanship required.

Included in R.P. Christeson's *Old Time Fiddler's Repertory vol. 1* (1973). One part (Lowinger): AABB (Brody, Christeson, Phillips): AA’BB’ (Beisswenger & McCann, Silberberg). Popularized by, and often attributed to, Arthur Smith (Tenn.) {1929-30}.

title: Money Musk
description:
'Money Musk' is one of the oldest and most historically documented reels in the New England and American fiddle tradition. It appears in print as early as 1788 in William Vickers's Scottish dance book, under the name 'My Lord Musk's Reel' — Lord Musk being a Scottish nobleman whose estate name lent the tune its label before American corruption turned it into 'Money Musk.' The tune crossed the Atlantic with Scots-Irish and English immigrants and became foundational in New England contradance music; it appears in virtually every early American dance manual and fiddle collection, including Ryan's Mammoth Collection (1883). It was played at community dances for over two centuries in the same communities, making it a living thread connecting the colonial era to the present. The straightforward D major reel structure — clear 8-bar strains, symmetrical phrasing — is ideal for contradancing with large numbers of couples.

The recording heard here is a 78rpm disc by John Baltzell, digitized by the Internet Archive.

Included in Daniel Dow's *Thirty Seven New Reels and Strathspeys* (c. 1780).

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: Fisher's Hornpipe
description:
Composed by Johann Fischer (c.1733–1800), a German-born musician who settled in London, 'Fisher's Hornpipe' was published around 1780. It crossed the Atlantic and was embraced in New England contradance and Southern fiddle traditions alike. The hornpipe style — originally a sailor's dance — features characteristic dotted rhythms that distinguish it from reels. Thompson's 'Compleat Collection of 200 Favourite Country Dances' preserves early versions.

The recording heard here is a 78rpm disc by WM. B. Houchens, digitized by the Internet Archive.

Included in Alexander McGlashan's *A Collection of Scots Measures* (1781). FISHER'S HORNPIPE (Crannciuil {Ui} Fishuir).

title: Temperance Reel
description:
The American temperance movement of the 19th century was one of the most powerful social reform campaigns in US history, culminating in Prohibition (1920–1933). Temperance groups often used popular fiddle tunes at their meetings to draw crowds, renaming them with morally improving titles. 'Temperance Reel' is one of several tunes that acquired teetotaling associations while remaining stubbornly associated with dancing and festivity.

Included in William Bradbury Ryan's *Ryan's Mammoth Collection* (1883).

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: Bile Them Cabbage Down
alternative_titles: Boil Them Cabbage Down
description:
'Bile Them Cabbage Down' has been teaching new fiddlers to hold a bow for well over a century. The title refers to boiling (or 'biling' in Appalachian dialect) cabbage — a dietary staple of mountain households through autumn and winter. The tune appears in Southern collections from the 19th century and was played at community gatherings as both dance music and an informal teaching tool, since the two-part pentatonic structure in D major is almost entirely playable in first position with no complex string crossings. Its famous lyrics — 'Bile them cabbage down, boys / Bake them hoe-cakes brown / The only song that I can sing is bile them cabbage down' — exemplify the functional simplicity of mountain social song, where the text exists to give the room something to sing while the fiddler drives the dance.

Included in Viola "Mom" Ruth's *Pioneer Western Folk Tunes* (1948). Standard or AEae (McMichen) tunings (fiddle).

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

Known in Ireland as 'The Little Beggarman,' this Mixolydian reel was carried to America by Irish immigrants in the 18th century and embedded itself deeply in Appalachian and Southern fiddle traditions. The lowered 7th gives it a modal quality that distinguishes it from major-key reels. It appears in O'Neill's 'Music of Ireland' (1903) and has been collected across Appalachia under dozens of names.

The recording heard here is by Ian Jacks and Tom Joad, preserved by the Internet Archive.

Included in Francis O'Neill's *Music of Ireland: 1850 Melodies* (1903). RED HAIRED BOY, THE (An Giolla Ruad).

description:

title: If I Hadn't Been A Fool
description:
The most documented recording of this tune comes from Vee V. Latty, a Missouri old-time fiddler. Vee V. Latty was born near Fulton, Callaway County, Missouri, in 1910 and began playing fiddle at the age of ten. "If I Hadn't Been a Fool, I Might Have Been a Lady" appears on his recorded repertoire, suggesting it was part of the Missouri old-time fiddle tradition in the early-to-mid 20th century.

He won the 1927/28 Missouri state fiddling championship, broadcast on WOS radio station out of Jefferson City, competing first on October 28, 1927, against 52 fiddlers from north of the Missouri River. Another 53 fiddlers from south of the river competed on November 25th, with the contest culminating in a championship on December 30 that pitted five winners from each side of the river against each other.

Latty was invariably accompanied by his wife Marie, playing an electric Hawaiian guitar, and they were sometimes joined by their son Wayne on guitar. He openly acknowledged his wife's contribution, stating after winning the 1927 championship: "I want to give my wife a great deal of credit for my success." Vee Latty died in 1956.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Makin' Hay
description: Makin' Hay is a reel in the key of C from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Hop Scotch Polka
description:
Based on the composition 'Scotch Hot' by Billy Whitlock, this tune became known as 'Hop-Scotch Polka' after a 1949 revival featuring new lyrics by Gene Rayburn and Carl Sigman.

Whitlock made an acetate recording in 1924, and it went virtually unnoticed for decades.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Uncle Dink
description:
Documented from the playing of Gene Goforth (1921-2002) of Eminence, Missouri, this tune is named for his father, Richard 'Dink' Goforth.

"Uncle Dink" comes from the playing of fiddler Gene Goforth (1921–2002), of Eminence, Missouri, documented from a recording made by Mark Wilson in 1997.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Hold Old Bald While I Dance With Josie
description:
Sourced from the playing of Missouri fiddler Jim Herd (1919-2002). The title contains folk-etymology variants related to 'Josie.'

It was recorded on Rounder 0437, the album Jim Herd – Traditional Fiddle Music of the Ozarks, Vol. 3 (released 2000), and has been transcribed and notated in the Traditional Tune Archive by Andrew Kuntz.

title: Pat The Budgie
description:
Composed by Graham Townsend (1942-1998) around 1960. It is a reel in C major.

"Pat the Budgie" was composed by Graham Townsend (1942–1998), a fiddler from Barrie, Ontario, around 1960–1961.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Moccasin Reel
description:
"Moccasin Reel" was composed by Andy DeJarlis, born in Woodridge, Manitoba in 1916, who came from a long line of fiddlers on both sides of his family.

His great-grandfather was an early settler in the Red River Valley, where settlers acquired their fiddles by trading pelts with fur traders, many of whom came from Scotland — and thus was born the Red River Jig and the distinctive Red River Style of fiddling.

Steeped in this tradition, it is only natural that Andy's "Caribou Reel," "Moccasin Reel," "Whiskey Before Breakfast," "Woodridge Breakdown", and many other tunes would bear the stamp of his forefathers.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Mississippi Snag
description:
"Mississippi Snag Boat" is attributed to Bert Payne, a Kansas fiddler. It has been passed along in the old-time community through fiddlers like Spencer and Rains. The shorter title "Mississippi Snag" appears to be a variant name for the same tune or a closely related piece, and is associated with the Missouri old-time fiddling tradition — appearing on the album "Nile Wilson – Tiehacker Hoe-Down" (MSOTFA 202D), recorded by the Missouri State Old Time Fiddlers Association, which works to promote and preserve the traditional fiddle music of Missouri and the surrounding region.

The tune title draws on vivid Mississippi River navigation vocabulary. A "Mississippi sawyer" was a river pilot's term for an uprooted tree in the water which sways back and forth with the current (like a sawing motion), with the tree breaking the surface suddenly in front of a boat. River pilots had names for different types of snags, including sawyers, preachers, and planters, depending on how they moved. A snag generically referred to any submerged obstruction — a serious hazard for 19th-century river traffic. On the Mississippi, the problem was of such proportions that special government "snag boats" patrolled the river to clear these dangers. This real-world river culture was a rich source of imagery for folk tune naming in the 19th century.

"Mississippi Snag" belongs to a broader cluster of old-time tunes named after Mississippi River life and lore.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Idlewood
description:
1. Lynn "Chirps" Smith — The tune is widely credited as a fiddle tune by Lynn "Chirps" Smith. It is described as a great tune composed by Chirps Smith, and he recorded it on his album "Down in Little Egypt." He also has a version recorded at a dance included in his "home recordings," and goes by the username MidwestFiddler on the Fiddle Hangout forum.

2. Ed Haley — According to the Fiddler's Companion, the tune comes from Ed Haley, the blind Kentucky fiddler known for his vast repertoire of unusual and complex tunes. At least one player's version is based on the one from Billy Mathews' collection of tunes. On the Tater Joe's Old-Time Fiddle resource, "Idlewood" is listed and attributed to Chirps Smith, dated January 30, 2016. Players in the community feel that "Idlewood" should become well known — it's considered "much fun to play." Some players note that Chirps' recording reveals a nuanced B part that is easy to simplify, though simplified versions work fine in ensemble/dance settings.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Maple Sugar
description:
Canadian (originally), American; Two-Step or Reel. AA'B (Perlman): ABB' (Bayard): AA'BB' (Bain, Beisswenger & McCann): ABAC (Bohrer/Kibler): AA'BB'CC'BB' (Phillips): AA'BB'AA'CC' (Silberberg). Composed in 1956 by Ontario fiddler Ward Allen (1924-1965), a professional fiddler who won contest after contest in Canada the 1950's and had a successful career playing on the radio. Allen played with Montana Slim, Wilf Carter ("the father of Canadian country music"), appeared on the Grand Ole Opry, and had a radio show on Frank Ryan's station CFRA in Ottawa, Canada. "Maple Sugar" was released by Sparton Records in 1956 as the 'B' side to the Canadian "Back Up and Push (2)", which was expected to be the stronger tune. However, "Maple Sugar" was to become a hit in Canada, and received some airplay in the United States as well.

It is also a tune which has varied considerably in the vicissitudes of the 'folk process' and has even acquired a set of words. In addition to being a staple of 'down east' Canadian fiddling, it has been popular in northern New York and northern New England; as Vic Kibler (Hamilton County, New York) said, "At every fiddle contest they all played it." It was in repertory of Buffalo Valley, Pa., region dance fiddler Harry Daddario. Shetland fiddler Aly Bain's version (which he calls "traditional Canadian") is much superior to that collected by Bayard (which is really one strain which is modulated to another key), who thought it a strain of a song air transformed into a dance tune.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Uncle Jim's Waltz
description: Uncle Jim's Waltz is a reel in the key of G from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Trip To Durrow
description:
"Trip to Durrow" has been attributed to Irish fiddler Dan Cleary (1918–2004), of Ballinamere, County Offaly. Cleary was a multi-instrumentalist who played the uilleann pipes, piano, and tin whistle, and was a member of a number of céili bands in the mid-20th century — notably the Ballinamere Céili Band, which won All-Ireland titles in the mid-1950s.

This reel is named for the Irish village of Durrow. The village of Durrow is in County Laois, in the southeast part of Ireland. One way to get to Durrow is to travel from the Celtic Sea, up the River Nore, and then to the River Erkina — Durrow is located close to the confluence of those two rivers.

The tune's name may stem from Cleary's days as a young man with the Colmcille Céili Band, of Durrow, Co. Offaly, who played regularly in the Forresters Hall in Tullamore. This connection — a young musician making regular trips to Durrow to play céilí dances — is likely what inspired the tune's title.

The tune was recorded by The Johnstons in 1969 — with Mick Moloney on banjo — making it the earliest known recording. Many in the Irish traditional scene first heard the tune played by Paddy Moloney on the first Drones and Chanters LP, released in the 1970s. The oldest documented source, considering both recordings and transcriptions, dates to 1960.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Everybody Two Step
description: Everybody Two Step is a reel in the key of C from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: The Shaskeen Reel
description:
"The Shaskeen Reel" is one of the most celebrated pieces in the entire Irish traditional music canon — a tune with deep geographic roots, linguistic archaeology, a chain of performers, and a name that has sparked debate for over a century.

The word shaskeen is derived from the Irish seisgeann, meaning either a marshy country or fen, a truss of corn, or gleaned land. The precise geographic source of the name is debated: The title is also thought to have come from the name of a river in County Longford, a tributary of the Inny near Ballymahon. To speculate on its earlier origin, there existed an old, now-deserted village of Seascainn, part of the larger townland of Gabhlán near Doocastle in East Mayo, where apparently Michael Coleman travelled to a spraoi at 'Scanlon's house.' Séamus Ennis, with his characteristic wit, once offered a more colorful definition: Seamus Ennis once introduced the tune in the Tradition Club by saying the word meant 'a red piece of flannel that was tied to the tail of a cow that had mastitis', according to Finbar Doyle, who points out Seamus sometimes had a "delicate conjunction with veracity."

The tune is also known as "Ballinakill Shaskeen," "Butcher's Brussels Reel," "Hag Behind the Fire," "Miss S. Treby's Hornpipe," and "Shaskeen Clog," and is associated with south County Leitrim, Ireland.

Supposedly, the tune was played by a piper from the area, but instead of being named for the musician (as is often the case), the melody was called by the place the piper lived.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Snowbird In The Ashbank
description:
This tune title, referencing the dark-eyed junco bird and rural ash piles, is applied to multiple unrelated tunes in the Upland South and Midwest. Documented in 1954 and 1934 collections.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Down Home Waltz
description:
American waltz in D Major, AABB' form. A similar melody appears in Samuel Bayard’s 'Dance to the Fiddle' (1982).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: My Cape Breton Home
description:
Composed in 1988 by Jerry Holland (1955–2009) to commemorate his and his father's shared love for Cape Breton, Nova Scotia. Holland was born in Brockton, Massachusetts, to Canadian parents and was active in the Cape Breton expatriate musical community before moving permanently to the island in 1975.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Black Hawthorne
description: Black Hawthorne is a reel in the key of G from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Abe's Retreat
description:
Reel in A Mixolydian, AABB form. Known also as 'Battle of Bull Run' and 'Manassas Junction.' Associated with Abraham Lincoln. Recorded in West Virginia and the Upland South. Standard, AEae, or GDgd tunings. Included in A.P. Spadaro’s '10 Cents a Dance' (1980).

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: Adrian's Hornpipe
description:
Hornpipe/reel in G Major, AABB form. Originally named for Boone, Iowa fiddler Fred Adreon (1871–1949), later misheard as 'Adrian.' Popularized by Nebraska fiddler Bob Walters and Missouri fiddler Cyril Stinnett. Noted by R.P. Christeson in 1949 and 1968. Printed in Christeson (1973), Milliner & Koken (2011), and Phillips (1995). Recorded by Vesta Johnson and Dwight Lamb.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: All Young
description:
Reel in A Mixolydian, standard tuning. From the repertoire of Melvin Wine, who learned it via his great-grandfather David S. 'Smithy' Wine (1829–1909) and his father Bill Wine. Printed in Milliner & Koken (2011) and Phillips (1994). Recorded on Marimac Recordings (1989).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Altamont
description:
Reel associated with the Galax, Virginia fiddle tradition. Circulated in Old-Time and bluegrass contests since at least the mid-20th century.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: (And) The Cat Came Back
description:
Composed in 1893 by Harry S. Miller, originally a comic novelty song. The tune migrated from minstrel stages to children's music and old-time fiddle repertoires.

Fred Penner's 1979 children's recording introduced it to multiple new generations.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Antelope Gap
description:
Reel in A Major. Attributed to Texas fiddler J.W. Whatley. Preserved by Howard Rains and Trish Spencer on 'Old Texas Fiddle.'

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))
notes: Howard Rains and Trish Spencer recorded this tune on Old Texas Fiddle.

title: Apple Blossom
description:
Apple orchards were a cornerstone of Appalachian farm economies — apple butter, cider, dried apples, and apple brandy ('apple jack') were essential preserved foods and trade goods. The brief apple blossom period in late spring, when hillside orchards turned white and pink, was one of the most celebrated moments of the Appalachian seasonal calendar. Old-Time waltzes often carry the names of natural phenomena that marked the agricultural year.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Apple Jack
description:
'Apple Jack' belongs to the large family of Appalachian breakdown tunes named for foods, drinks, and rural materials — a tradition that includes 'Cornbread and Buttermilk,' 'Sugar in the Gourd,' and dozens of others. Applejack — a fermented and distilled apple beverage that was the primary liquor of many mountain communities before commercial whiskey became widely available — was produced across the Appalachian region from the 17th century onward, especially in Virginia, New Jersey, and the Carolinas. The drink appears in numerous folk songs and references as a symbol of frontier self-sufficiency and social gathering. The tune itself is a rhythmic breakdown in the standard old-time AABB form, passed down through the oral tradition of Appalachian musicians whose names and specific origins are no longer traceable.

Included in Clare Milliner & Walt Koken's *The Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes* (2011). The tune is sourced to fiddle and banjo player Samuel Jackson "Sammy/Sammie" Walker (1910-1987) of Barren County, south-central Kentucky, on the Upper Cumberland. Wallace was at one time a blacksmith and farmer. In the 1940's Walker had a band that, after 1946 included his daughter Nell playing mandolin and guitar.

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: Arrington's Breakdown
description:
Breakdown associated with Charlie Arrington, a professional fiddler of the 1920s–30s. Documented by modern fiddlers including Chirps Smith and the Volo Bogtrotters.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))
notes: Chirps Smith recorded a version of this tune.

title: Art Wooten's Hornpipe
description:
Reel in G Major, standard tuning. Notated from Bob Walters (1889–1960). Printed in Christeson (1973) and Phillips (1995).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Auger In The Ditch
description: Auger In The Ditch is a reel in the key of G from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Aunt Mary's Hornpipe
description:
Breakdown in D Major, AABB form. From the playing of Missouri fiddler Vee Latty (Little Dixie area). Listed on Charlie Walden's '100 essential Missouri fiddle tunes.' Printed in R.P. Christeson (1973).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Baby Ben
description:
From the repertoire of Alabama fiddler James Bryan.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Backstep Cindy
description:
Crooked three-part tune (A, B, C) in high-bass tuning (ADAE). A cornerstone of the Round Peak tradition, Surry County, North Carolina. Associated with Tommy Jarrell and Fred Cockerham. Included in Miles Krassen's 'Appalachian Fiddle' (1973).

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: The Baltimore
description:
"The Baltimore" is a tune title that appears in several old-time and related folk traditions. Like many old-time fiddle tunes named after places, it likely took its name from Baltimore, Maryland — a major port city and, historically, a significant crossroads for American folk music traditions.

Baltimore has long been a hub for bluegrass and old-time music. As the coal industry declined in the mid-20th century, Southern migrants traveled the "Hillbilly Highway" north, bringing their string instruments to working-class neighborhoods in Baltimore. This migration embedded Appalachian fiddle traditions firmly into the city's culture.

Old-time music as a genre lays ancient African and Celtic folk narratives over different forms of the same four or five strings. Tunes named after cities — like "The Baltimore" — were a common naming convention, often honoring a place where a tune was popularized, first played at a dance, or composed by a local fiddler.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: (On The) Banks Of The Ohio
description:
One of the most recorded murder ballads in American folk music, 'Banks of the Ohio' tells the story of a young man who drowns a woman when she refuses to marry him. The earliest known recording was by Red Patterson's Piedmont Log Rollers in 1927; the ballad itself is anonymous and likely dates from the mid-to-late 19th century, circulating through oral tradition for decades before anyone pressed it to wax. Like many Appalachian murder ballads, it presents the killer's perspective without moral judgment, leaving the listener to supply the outrage. 'I asked my love to take a walk / to take a walk just a little walk / Down beside where the waters flow / Down by the banks of the Ohio' — the language is pastoral, almost tender, which makes the murder more disturbing. Bill Monroe, Olivia Newton-John, Emmylou Harris, Doc Watson, and dozens of others have recorded it. The Ohio River, which forms the boundary between Kentucky and Ohio, was a real and symbolically powerful geographic feature in the 19th-century American imagination — the line between slave and free states.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Banjo Tramp
description:
Breakdown in D Major, standard tuning, AA'BB' form. Traced to Ohio fiddler Ward Jarvis, who learned it from Kentucky fiddler Ed Haley.

Jarvis was born in West Virginia in 1894 and was deeply influenced by Ed Haley.

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: Barndance Polka
description:
The tune "Barndance Polka" is attributed to Art Stamper, appearing in major old-time fiddle references including the Gettysburg Collection of Old-Time Fiddle Tunes (compiled by John S. Lamancusa) and the Tater Joe's Old-Time Fiddle repertoire list.

Art Stamper (1926–2005) was a master traditional fiddler from Floyd County, Kentucky, rooted deeply in the eastern Kentucky old-time and country music tradition. He was closely associated with the musical heritage of the Appalachian region and was known for playing tunes with a distinctively rhythmic, dance-ready style — making him a natural source for a polka-inflected barndance piece. He recorded and performed with a number of traditional musicians throughout his career and is regarded as one of the key carriers of Kentucky mountain fiddle tradition. Feel: Upbeat, 2/4 or cut-time pulse, ideal for square dancing or social dancing contexts.

The tune appears among 522 traditional old-time tunes transcribed from jams, source recordings, festivals (such as Clifftop and Rock Bridge), and workshops (Rocky Mountain Fiddle Camp, Swannanoa, Augusta, Fiddle Hell).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Battle of Cedar Creek
description:
Named for the Battle of Cedar Creek (October 19, 1864) in the Shenandoah Valley, Virginia.

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: Bean Walker's Mile
description:
Reel/polka in C Major, AA'AA'BB form. Notated from Lynn 'Chirps' Smith. Phillips notes the 'A' part matches 'Dominion Reel.' Printed in Phillips (1995).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Beaux Of Albany
description:
Reel in D major. Traces roots to 18th-century Scottish music, appearing as 'The Braes of Auchtertyre.' Popular in the New England contra dance tradition.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Beaver's Hall
description: Beaver's Hall is a reel in the key of C from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Bell Cow
description:
Reference to rural livestock culture. Published in Ethel Park Richardson's 'American Mountain Songs' (1927). Recorded by the Dixie Crackers in 1928, later popularized by the New Lost City Ramblers.

It was set in the key of G Major/Mixolydian in the Old-Time String Band Songbook (Oak Publications, 1964) by the New Lost City Ramblers (John Cohen, Mike Seegar, Tracy Schwartz, Tom Paley), who obtained their version from the 1928 recording by the Dixie Crackers.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Belle of Lexington
description:
Associated with southwestern Virginia, specifically Grayson and Carroll Counties. Definitive recording by Emmett Lundy (1864–1953). Belongs to the 'Smith's Reel' family. Included in Miles Krassen's 'Masters of Old Time Fiddling' (1983).

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)
notes: Emmett Lundy recorded a version of this tune.

title: Betty Baker
description:
Reel in D Major, AB form. Known as a West Virginia standard, but played by Kentucky fiddlers including Manon Campbell, Clyde Davenport, Ed Haley, and Hiram Stamper. Printed in Titon (2001). Recorded by Ernie Carpenter.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Betty Baker (Over the Hill to Betty Baker)
description:
Named for a stock folk character. Documented versions include: American reel in D Major, from Eastern Kentucky and West Virginia; Air and breakdown in G Major, printed in Ira Ford's 'Traditional Music in America' (1940).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Bibb County Hoedown
description:
Seven Foot Dilly and His Dill Pickles recorded 'Bibb County Hoedown' in Atlanta in November 1930, with A. A. Gray on fiddle. The group belonged to the north Georgia string-band scene. The tune also appears in Gene Silberberg's Tunes I Learned at Tractor Tavern (2002).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org).

title: Big Eyed Rabbit
description:
Animal-themed tunes were among the most popular in the Old-Time repertoire — 'Big Eyed Rabbit,' 'Rabbit in the Pea Patch,' 'Rabbit Where'd You Get Them Long Ears' — reflecting the rabbit's prominent place in both Appalachian hunting culture and African American trickster tales (Br'er Rabbit). The rabbit was a dietary staple and a figure of folk wisdom: always watchful, always ready to run, surviving through cleverness rather than strength.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Big John McNeil
description:
BIG JOHN McNEIL(L)/McNEAL. Standard (or infrequently AEae) tuning (fiddle). AABB (Gibbons, Messer, Sweet): AABB' (Miller & Perron): AA'BB' (Bégin, Perlman, Phillips). Though now known as a Canadian standard it originally was a reel composed (as "John McNeil") by the brilliant Scottish fiddler Peter Milne (1824-1908), one of J. Scott Skinner's teachers and early playing partners, who earned his living playing in theaters until his opium addiction (he abused laudanum, originally prescribed for rheumatism) reduced him to busking on ferry-boats crossing the Firth of Forth. He died in unpleasant circumstances in a mental institution. John McNeil was a famous Highland dancer of the mid-to-later 19th century (see note for "John McNeil's Reel" for more). The melody was in the repertoire of Cyrill Stinnett, a fiddler who epitomised the 'North Missouri Hornpipe Style' of playing, who apparently learned it and other tunes from listening to Canadian fiddlers broadcasting on the radio from Canada. Indeed, an recording of the tune was made 'Down-East' Canadian fiddler Don Messer with his group the Islanders, early in the 1940's-among the first of the sides the group waxed. A very similar melody, or a version, is "Lord Ramsay's Reel." Perlman (1996) notes the tune is a popular tune on Prince Edward Island, and a favorite vehicle for stepdancing in Prince County, PEI, on the western part of the island. Irish fiddler Sean Maguire recorded the melody in the 1960's under the title "Betty's Fancy (2).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Big Sandy
description:
There are actually two distinct fiddle tunes commonly associated with the "Big Sandy" name in American traditional music.

"Big Sandy River" is credited to Kenny Baker and Bill Monroe, composed in 1963. It is primarily a bluegrass tune, written in the key of G.

Kenny Baker was Monroe's longtime fiddler with the Blue Grass Boys, and the tune reflects that virtuosic bluegrass fiddle style. It is considered an essential bluegrass fiddle piece, frequently appearing at jams alongside tunes like Lonesome Moonlight Waltz and Monroe's Hornpipe.

The tune takes its name from the Big Sandy River, which forms the border between eastern Kentucky and West Virginia — deep in the heart of Appalachian old-time and bluegrass country.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Bill Brown
description:
Reel in A Major, AEac# tuning. Irregular form (A-part 8 measures, B-part 4 measures). From the playing of John Salyer, recorded in 1941/42. Printed in Titon (2001). Recorded by Bruce Molsky.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Bill Driver's Tune
description:
William 'Bill' Driver was born in Eldridge, Missouri, and spent much of his fiddling career in Miller County, near Iberia. His father, also William Driver, was born in 1859, adopted by the Driver family, and later worked as a Free Will Baptist circuit preacher. He died in 1934.

Driver's repertory is documented as part of the African American fiddle tradition of central Missouri.

Source: John Lamancusa collection, oldtimefiddletunes.net.

title: Billy in the Lowland
description:
"Billy in the Lowground" is one of the most enduring and widespread of American traditional dance tunes in the key of C, known throughout the South, Midwest, and West and even into the northern part of the United States. As with most such long-lived and widely disseminated reels, there is a tremendous variation of the core melody due to both regional style, musical style (e.g., bluegrass, western swing), and individual fiddlers' idiosyncratic renderings.

The American tune borrows motifs from British and Irish sources. Scholar Samuel Bayard traced its genealogy carefully. The tune originated in Britain as a slow 3/4 time song tune from c. 1710 or earlier, called "O Dear Mother (Minnie) What Shall I Do?" He sees the development of the tune as having then split into two branches, and during the 1740s a 6/8 "giga" or jig form was composed called variously "All the Blue Bonnets Are Over the Border." Later in the century the second branch was fashioned from the original 3/4 tune into a fast duple time (4/4) dancing air which went by several titles including "The Braes of Auchtertyre/Auchentyre," "Belles of Tipperary," and "Beaus of Albany." These latter tunes are the immediate ancestor of the "Billy in the Lowground" group of tunes in America.

William of Orange: The tune is said to be Scottish in origin, and the title refers to William of Orange at the Battle of the Boyne in 1690, where a "deep swampy ravine" figured in the tactics of the battle.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Bitter Creek
description:
Reel in G Major, AABB form. Recorded in 1929 by Oscar Harper. Included in R.P. Christeson's 'Old Time Fiddler's Repertory vol. 1' (1973).

The tune was recorded in Dallas, Texas, for OKeh Records at the end of November, 1929, by Texas fiddler Oscar Harper (1888-1952), accompanied by guitar player Doc Harper.

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: Black-Eyed Susie
description:
Old-time tune appearing in multiple collections across the Appalachian region.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Black-Eyed Suzy-Anna
description:
The tune's lineage is remarkably deep. Musicologist Samuel Bayard traces the history of the tune back to the British Isles, beginning with a melody called "Rosasolis," set by Giles Farnaby (c. 1560–c. 1600), which appears in the Fitzwilliam Virginal Book.

Another version of the melody is called "Morris Off" and appears in Jehan Tabourot's Orchesographie (1588); it is still used for English morris dances and has been called the earliest recorded morris tune. Still another version appears as an old Welsh harp tune in Alawon Fy Ngwlad / Lays of My Land.

Later developments of the tune were popular in England and Scotland from the early 17th century through the 18th, under the title "Three Jolly Sheep Skins"; while in Ireland a variation became known as "Aillilliu mo Mhailin" (Alas my little bag) — a humorous lament for a stolen bag of sundries.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Black Jack Grove
description:
Black Jack Grove is an American reel from Kentucky. It is typically played in A Mixolydian, with some versions using A Dorian or A Major in the 'B' part. It is performed in standard or AEae tuning. Jeff Titon (2001) notes its presence in 1915 and 1919 Berea College fiddle lists. Kentucky fiddler Walter McNew (1912-1998) learned the tune from his father, John McNew, who reportedly played it while working as a depot agent for the L & N Railroad. Walter also noted the influence of Madison County fiddler Doc Roberts.

McNew learned "Black Jack Grove" from his father John McNew (b. 1888), a telegraph operator and depot agent for the L & N Railroad, who would play his fiddle between dispatches during the graveyard shift at his train depot.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Black Sally Goodin
description:
Black Sally Goodin is a Missouri breakdown (cut or 2/4 time) played in G or D Major, often in standard or GDad tuning. It is included in Charlie Walden's '100 essential Missouri fiddle tunes' list. The tune was sourced from African-American fiddler Bill Caton (or Katon) via Vee Latty of Callaway County, Missouri, who was recorded in the 1950s.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Black Satin
description:
Black Satin is an American reel in G Major, performed in GDad tuning. It was in the repertoire of the Perry County (Tenn.) Music Makers, consisting of Nonnie Presson and Bulow Smith, who recorded the tune for Vocalion Records in 1930. Nonnie learned it from local banjo player Will Warren. Fiddler George Mert Reves (1884-1992) of Arkansas also performed a version in DDad tuning.

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: Black Widow Romp
description:
Black Widow Romp is a modern composition in the old-time style written by Chris Romain (also spelled Romaine) from the Washington, D.C. area. It is credited to Romain in Dan Levenson's 'Buzzard Banjo' tab book, with some sources also including Levenson as a co-contributor.

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: Blake's March
description:
Blake's March is a fiddle tune in the key of G composed by musician Norman Blake. It was recorded on the compilation 'Original Underground Music from the Mysterious South' (reissued on 'Natasha's Waltz') by the Rising Fawn String Ensemble.

Blake (born March 10, 1938) is a traditional American stringed instrument artist and songwriter, born in Chattanooga, Tennessee, and raised in Sulphur Springs, Alabama.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Blue Eagle
description:
Blue Eagle is an American reel from Texas, played in D Major in standard tuning. The tune is attributed to Oklahoma-born fiddler Orville Burns, who settled in Texas. The title references the National Industrial Recovery Act's symbol.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Blue Goose
description:
Blue Goose is an American fiddle tune named for the blue-gray color phase of the snow goose.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Blue Mule
description:
Blue Mule is an American reel from the Ozarks, recorded for the Library of Congress by Vance Randolph in the early 1940s. It is also known as 'Old Blue Mule' or 'Austin Breakdown.' Early 78RPM recordings include Bob Miller's Hinky Dinkers (1930) and Jess Hillard & His West Virginia Hillbillies (1933). Missouri fiddler Art Galbraith (1909-1993) noted learning the tune from family members.

"Blue Mule" was recorded for the Library of Congress by musicologist/folklorist Vance Randolph in the early 1940's from Ozarks Mountains fiddlers, where it is a regionally popular tune formerly seldom heard in other parts of the country. It was in the repertoire of Missouri fiddlers Art Galbraith (1909-1993, who said it was learned from older members of his family) and Bob Holt (1930-2004), and by Bill (Willie) Bilyeau for the Library of Congress.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Boating Up The Sandy
description:
Boating Up The Sandy is an American fiddle tune named after the Big Sandy River, a 19th-century transport route between West Virginia and Kentucky.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Boatman
description:
Boatman (or Boate Man) is an English country dance tune. It was first published by John Playford in the first edition of 'The English Dancing Master' (1651) and appeared in subsequent editions through 1698. A song adaptation, 'The Bonny Scot,' was published by Allan Ramsay in 1724.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Boatman Tune
description:
The Boatman Tune is an old-time fiddle tune in D Major documented in the Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes. It was recorded in 1989 by fiddler Lauchlin Shaw at the Festival of American Fiddle Tunes.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Bob Tailed Mule
description:
Bob Tailed Mule is associated with Arizona fiddler Kenner 'KC' Kartchner (1886-1956). Kartchner played the tune in AEae tuning, which he referred to as 'The Italian.' It was documented in Stacy Phillips's 'Traditional American Fiddle Tunes' (1994).

The primary recorded source is a Jim & Kim Lansford recording on Vigortone Records — "Call Your Dogs" (2003) — learned from a 1943 field recording of Snowflake, Arizona fiddler Kenner Kartchner.

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: Bob Walters' Hornpipe
description:
Bob Walters' Hornpipe is a reel in D Major from Nebraska fiddler Robert E. 'Uncle Bob' Walters (1889-1960). The tune was captured in a 1954 field recording by Dwight Lamb and later included in the Milliner-Koken Collection. The name was given posthumously.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Bob Walters Tune 113
description:
Christeson's The Old-Time Fiddler's Repertory**, not a name Walters himself gave the tune. The 245 fiddle tunes in Christeson's book are indexed by tune number, and those numbers on reference sites correspond directly to the tune numbers in the Old-Time Fiddler's Repertory book. Many of Walters' tunes had no formal name. Walters had an extensive repertoire of tunes learned from many different sources — at one time he had written down over three hundred tunes for which he knew the names, and he played many others for which there were no titles. Untitled tunes were often cataloged simply as "Tune [#]" or attributed generically to their source fiddler — hence "Bob Walters Tune 113."

Transcriptions of Walters' music outnumber all others in R. P. Christeson's two volumes of The Old-Time Fiddler's Repertory*.

Robert E. "Uncle Bob" Walters was born on June 16, 1889, in Decatur, Burt County, east Nebraska. His grandfather, Ike Walters, and his father William Wilson "Wilse" Walters were both noted fiddlers.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Bone Yard
description:
Bone Yard is a modal old-time fiddle tune attributed to Garry Harrison.

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: Booth Shot Lincoln
description:
Booth Shot Lincoln is an American fiddle tune referring to the assassination of President Abraham Lincoln in 1865.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Boston Boy
description:
Boston Boy is an American breakdown in D Major, standard tuning. It was a favorite of fiddler 'Uncle Pen' Vanderver.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Bound to Have a Little Fun
description:
Bound to Have a Little Fun is an American reel in G Major attributed to Adison Wallace. Kentucky fiddler Bruce Green popularized the tune, learning it from Adison's son, Gusty Wallace.

Gustace "Gusty" Wallace was born in Hart County, Kentucky, on November 24, 1890, but lived in Metcalf County, Kentucky, when Bruce Green visited him in the 1970's.

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: Box the Fox
description:
Box the Fox is an American reel from Pennsylvania, played in D Major, standard tuning. It was transcribed by Samuel Bayard from the playing of Isaac Morris.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Boy In The Gap
description:
Boy In The Gap is an Irish reel in D Major. Irish accordionist Paddy O'Brien describes the title as referencing a goalkeeper in the game of hurling, or generally a person guarding a gap in a fence.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Boys Around The World
description: Boys Around The World is a reel in the key of C from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Boys My Money's All Gone
description:
Boys, My Money's All Gone is an American reel, typically in A Dorian or Mixolydian. It was recorded in 1929 by Tennessee fiddler Charlie Bowman (1889-1962) and His Brothers as part of a musical skit.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Brandywine
description:
Brandywine is an American reel in G Major. It is associated with both old-time and bluegrass musicians, including Kenny Baker.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Brasstown
description:
Brasstown is an old-time reel composed by Donna (of Fiddling Demystified) and named for Brasstown, North Carolina, home of the John C. Campbell Folk School.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Breaking Up Christmas
description:
Breaking Up Christmas is an Appalachian fiddle tune. The title refers to the final community dance marking the end of the twelve-day holiday season from December 25 through January 6.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Breezy Point
description:
Breezy Point is an original composition by fiddler Jane Rothfield, appearing on her album 'In the Moment.'

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Briar Picker Brown
description:
"Briarpicker Brown" comes from the fiddle playing of Kentucky fiddler Buddy Thomas, who died in 1974 at the young age of 39 and was from Emerson, Kentucky (Lewis County).

He played some bluegrass and country music but favored old-time fiddle tunes. He died unexpectedly in 1974 at the age of 39, and Kitty Puss is his only commercial recording.

The melody is known as a Kentucky tune in modern times, largely due to an recording by Buddy Thomas. However, Thomas had learned the tune from an elderly Portsmouth, Ohio, fiddler named Morris Allen. The tune structurally resembles West Virginia fiddler Clark Kessinger's "Everyone to the Puncheon," and Allen was in fact a friend of Kessinger.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: British Field March
description:
British Field March is a fiddle tune sourced to Quince Dillon, a fifer in the Mexican War. Dillon stated the tune was a British field march used during the retreat at the Battle of New Orleans.

The tune is sourced to the repertoire of fifer Quince Dillon, who said it was a British field march from the War of 1812.

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: Brown Button Shoes
description:
Brown Button Shoes is an American reel from northeastern Kentucky. It was played by fiddler Joe Stamper and Portsmouth, Ohio, fiddler Jimmy Wheeler.

The tune was also in the repertoire of Portsmouth, Ohio, fiddler and instrument repairer Jimmy Wheeler (1917-1987), who learned it either from his father or Acey "Aaa" Neal.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Brownie's Reel
description: Brownie's Reel is a reel in the key of C from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Buck Mountain
description:
Buck Mountain is an American reel in D Major, associated with Albemarle County, Virginia. It is attributed to Napoleon Bonaparte 'Uncle Nip' Chisholm, active in the 1930s. The tune was popularized by the Virginia Vagabonds.

The tune was popularized regionally by a group called the Virginia Vagabonds, formed in 1932, whose guitar player, Earl Smith, was related to Chisholm and learned the melody from him (the elderly fiddler was perhaps his great uncle). Fiddler Armin Barnet, the source for the tune in The Portland Collection and who is credited with popularizing it among 'revival' fiddlers, went to graduate school in Charlottesville, N.C., in the early 1970's and picked up the tune from regional players.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Buckskin Reel
description:
Buckskin Reel is an American fiddle tune. The title references buckskin, the frontier clothing material of the American frontier.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Buckwheat Batter
description:
Buckwheat Batter is an American jig (6/8 time) in A Major. It was recorded by the West Virginia Tweedy Brothers in 1928.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Bug In The Taters
description:
Bug in the Taters was recorded on May 14, 1927, in New York City by Al Hopkins and His Buckle Busters, with fiddler Charlie Bowman credited on the label.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Bull at the Wagon
description:
Standard or AEae (Lewis Brothers) tunings (fiddle). Recorded in El Paso, Texas, by the Lewis Brothers (Dempson, b. 1891, on fiddle and Denmon on guitar ) for Victor in July, 1929, who are the source for the reel. Oklahoma fiddler Earl Collins learned his version from the Lewis Brothers (or, as some say, from Tom Sauber), but altered it somewhat, especially in the 'A' part. See also the related tunes "Karo" and "Red Bird."

The Lewis Brothers were originally from San Antonio, Texas, although the family relocated to Crow Flat, New Mexico, in 1902, when they were still boys. Denmon Lewis (1894-1977) played the guitar but also played the fiddle. In 1969, when interviewed by Charles Faurot for liner notes to County Records 517 ("Texas Farewell: Texas Fiddlers 1922-1930") at the age of 75, he still worked daily on his cattle ranch in Otero County, New Mexico. Isaac Dempson "Demp" Lewis (1890-1960) was the duo's primary fiddler on recordings but they both played the instrument for local dances and organized dances at Liberty Hall, El Paso. It was through an entrepreneurial woman who ran some of these dances that they were introduced to the Victor A & R representative, who had the duo record four sides on July, 11th, 1929 (all of which were released), including their most famous tune, "Bull at the Wagon."

Notation sources: Dempson Lewis (Texas) [Brody]; Earl Collins (Oklahoma) [Milliner & Koken, Phillips]; Hank Bradley (Seattle) [Silberberg].

Published in Brody (Fiddler's Fakebook), 1983; p. 58. Fiddler Magazine, vol. 21, No. 3, Fall 2014; p. 27. Clare Milliner & Walk Koken (The Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes), 2011; p. 86.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Bull of the Woods
description:
Bull of the Woods is an American reel in G Major. It is sourced to Limestone County, Alabama, fiddler Paisley Hagood (1905-1977). The title refers to a logging camp foreman.

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: Bummer's Reel
description:
The tune was printed by S.S. Stewart (Phila., Pa.) in a piano/banjo arrangement (by Thomas J. Armstrong) in 1884. Stewart was a music publisher as well as a banjo manufacturer. Bayard (1981) finds no particular antecedents from the British Isles or Europe, and believes it may be an American composition that perhaps derived from Irish tradition; at any rate he says it was a great favorite with Pennslvania fiddlers. He did find an Irish tune, "Bean an Tighe ar Lar" (Woman of the House), with an 'A' part that was similar to the 'A' part of "Bummer's Reel," but with a different 'B' part. O'Neill maintains the piece is similar to "Cows Are a-Milking (The)," while Bayard finds another Irish tune with similarities under the title "Maighstreas an Ti" (Lady of the House). Some versions of "Bummer's Reel," keeping in mind that many American variants have considerable differences, are similar to the American tune "Peaches and Cream." R.P. Christeson (1973, p. 109) gives a tune, "Breakdown No. 155" from Bob Walters (Burt County) [Nebraska], and identifries the parent tune as "Bummer's Reel." A version also appears in Howe's collection, c. 1860.

Notation sources: Harvey Thompson (Pa.) [Christeson]; Harry Daddario (Union County, Pa.) [Guntharp]; Bayard (1981) gives 10 versions from 10 different southwestern Pa. fiddling and fifing sources; Elmer Barton (Vt.) [Phillips].

Published in Bayard (Hill Country Tunes), 1944; No. 49 (appears as an untitled reel). Bayard (Dance to the Fiddle), 1981; No. 247A-J, pp. 206-209. A.S.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: A Bunch Of Chickens
description:
A Bunch Of Chickens is an old-time breakdown in G Major from Indiana, sourced from fiddler John W. Summers.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Burt Anderson's Tune
description:
Burt Anderson's Tune is a reel in C Major from Cumberland Plateau fiddler Clyde Davenport (b. 1921) of Monticello, Kentucky.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Bye Bye My Honey I'm Gone
description:
Bye Bye My Honey I'm Gone is a song written c. 1885 by Monroe H. Rosenfeld. It was composed as a schottische and later adapted into other formats, including a 1918 patriotic version.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: By The Waterfall
description:
A meditative Appalachian tune. Waterfalls were significant landmarks in the region, serving as sites for water power, recreation, and aesthetic contemplation. In the 19th-century Romantic tradition, they symbolized the sublime power of nature.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: C&A Breakdown
description: C&A Breakdown is a reel in the key of C from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Cacklin Hen
description:
'Cacklin Hen' and 'Cluck Old Hen' are easily confused titles, but they can refer to different tunes. Fiddlin' John Carson's 1923 'Old Hen Cackled and the Rooster's Going to Crow' should not be used to date this melody without comparing the versions.

Source: John Lamancusa collection, oldtimefiddletunes.net.

title: Caliche Creek
description:
Caliche, a hard calcium carbonate layer in arid Southwestern soils, was a significant obstacle to ranchers and farmers. This tune is associated with the Texas fiddle tradition.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Calico
description:
Jim Bowles (1903-1993) of south-central Kentucky learned it from Thomas Page. Stephen B. Tucker recorded it for the Library of Congress in 1939. It is distinct from the tune 'Citaco' or the 'Calico' tuning (AEac#).

Jim Nelson maintains that Bowles learned the tune from Thomas Page (Titon, 2001).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Calico Corn
description:
A breakdown named for the multi-colored 'calico' or Indian corn common in American agriculture. Recorded by The Indian Creek Delta Boys (2015) and Lynn 'Chirps' Smith (1994).

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: California Cotillion
description:
A G Major cotillion or march documented from Galax, Virginia fiddler Eck Dunford, who learned it from Hicks Ring around 1941. Ring reportedly learned it from German musicians.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Camp Chase
description:
Named for the Union prisoner-of-war camp in Columbus, Ohio, which held Confederate prisoners from 1861 to 1865. The name reflects the impact of the Civil War on regional communities.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Camp Meeting on the Fourth of July
description:
A D Major march. James Bryan stated the tune was used for evening processional services at 19th-century Arkansas camp meetings. His source was Tom Jackson, who learned it from Coleman Barwick of Blountsville, Alabama.

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: Carroll County Blues
description:
AAB (Brody, Reiner & Anick): AA'B (Beisswenger & McCann, Phillips). "Carroll County Blues" was the Mississippi fiddle and guitar duo Narmour and Smith's biggest hit recording. The original melody is said to have been composed by fiddler Will Narmour (1889-1961) and was named for his home county, Carroll County, north-central Mississippi, but whether Narmour actually composed it is in dispute. Narmour, however, did record the tune with a man named Shell (Sherril) Smith, whose wife, it has been written, recalled that Narmour may have heard the tune either being whistled by a black farmer (according to David Freeman), or hummed by a black field hand (remembers Henry Young). This farmer claimed authorship and called the tune "Carroll County Blues." Narmour and Smith then "worked the tune out," presumably meaning that they arranged it for fiddle and guitar. Narmour is known to have been friendly with black bluesman Mississippi John Hurt, who lived in nearby Avalon. It has also been maintained, ostensibly by older community members in Avalon, that Narmour's mentor, Gene Clardy, an older local fiddler, was the one who composed "Carroll County Blues." However, the story about the black farmer is also disputed, and, further, it may be that Gene Clardy neither wrote nor played the tune.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Catlettsburg
description:
A C Major reel named for the town in Boyd County, Kentucky, at the confluence of the Ohio and Big Sandy rivers. It was a signature tune of fiddler Ed Haley (1885-1951).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Cauliflower
description:
A G Major reel unique to the repertoire of Portsmouth, Ohio fiddler Jimmy Wheeler (1917-1987).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Cello
description:
The title is pronounced with a soft 'C', as in "celebrity." Al Smitley collected the tune from an elderly fiddler by the name of Ray Shepard whom (in May, 2000) was still playing in his 80th decade. Smitley says: "Shepard grew up in southern Ohio and it was there that he learned the tune. He moved to Michigan (south of Saline) when he was a young man." Origins are obscure, but it may have been a minstrel tune or a part of a quadrille.

Notation sources: fiddler Al Smitley of Michigan's Ruffwater Stringband [Johnson].

Published in Johnson (The Kitchen Musician's No. 7: Michigan Tunes), vol. 7, 1986-87; p. 12.

Retrieved from "https://tunearch.org/w/index.php?title=Annotation:Cello&oldid=325047"

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Centennial Foxtrot
description: Centennial Foxtrot is a reel in the key of G from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: (Old) Chattanooga
description:
A traditional fiddle tune from the Walden's Ridge and Sequatchie Valley area near Chattanooga, Tennessee. Blaine Smith (1915–1997) learned the tune from Bob Douglas and his father in the 1920s.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Charlestown Gals
description:
A tune circulating under variants like 'Charleston Gals', appearing in mid-1840s minstrel sheet music.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Chase The Banshee
description:
Classified as an Irish Polka, though its character is influenced by American old-time traditions. Linked to the Flanagan Brothers and recorded by Kevin McHugh for the Coleman Archive (2005).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Chase the Squirrel
description:
A D Major reel collected from George Strosnider of Greene County, Pennsylvania. It is considered a composite tune, with parts reminiscent of 'Shepherd's Hey'.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: (Old) Cheat Mountain
description:
Named for Cheat Mountain in West Virginia, site of Civil War skirmishes in 1861. The name refers to the river's treacherous nature.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Cherry River Rag
description:
A C Major rag associated with Ashland, Kentucky fiddler Ed Haley. It is named for the Cherry River in West Virginia.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Chickadee's Polka
description:
A G Major polka composed by Bob McQuillen of Peterborough, New Hampshire, in 1975.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Chicken Polka
description:
A Swedish novelty polka in the repertoire of Pennsylvania fiddler Jehile Kirkhuff.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Chicken Reel
description:
Standard or ADae tunings (fiddle). AABB (Brody, Ford, Phillips, Ruth, Spadaro, Sweet, Thede): AABBC (Bayard {Ireland}): AABBAACC (Krassen {Higgins}): AABBCDDAABBC'C' (Krassen {Summers}). "Chicken Reel" was composed by nineteen-year-old Joseph M. Daly (1891-1968) as a piano composition, and published in Boston in 1910. It translated well to the fiddle (once moved to the key of 'D' from Daly's original key of 'C') and became a popular fiddler's piece. The long glissando followed by quick eight notes is imitative of the jerky movements of the fowl. Daly may have either adopted an existing folk melody or "composed" it from folk strains (Fuld, 1966, 1971). It was characterized as a "Performer's Buck" (i.e. buck dance). Regarding those folk strains, Bayard (1981) vaguely states that the tune may have been of Scottish or Irish in origin, and makes general reference to tunes in O'Neill without citing them. Though the tune is usually played in two parts several fiddlers have added variations. Miles Krassen states Indiana fiddler John Summers, whose roots were in the northern (US) tradition, had B and C parts which were probably composed by him and identifies the latter as a strain commonly found in hornpipes. Bayard collected another 'C' part from southwestern Pa. fiddler Walter Ireland and generally found the versions from that area of the country had little of the pronounced sliding that accompany the tune in the South. The melody was in the repertoire of Arizona fiddler Kenner C. Kartchner since the early 20th century and Bronner (1987) notes it was commonly played for dances in New York state at that time (often in combination with the tune "Black Cat").

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Chicken Under the Washtub
description:
A tune composed by Pacific Northwest fiddler Vivian Williams. It is a modern piece written in an old-time style, later recorded by Jason Carter.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Chief Logan
description:
Named for the Mingo leader Chief Logan (c. 1725–1780), whose story was prominent in the Ohio Valley and Appalachian frontier consciousness. The tune is typically played in A or D.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Chiggers In The Bedsheets
