title: Cincinnati Breakdown
description:
A tune with fluid nomenclature, often called 'Cincinnati Hornpipe' or 'Cincinnati Rag'. Documentation is sparse, though it has been associated with fiddler Chirps Smith.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Cindy
description:
AB (Brody): AABB (Phillips/1989 {the 'B' part is 'crooked' in Phillip's version}): AA'BB (Phillips, 1994). A known frolic tune, appearing in many folk music collections and even old elementary school songbooks. The title appears in a list of traditional Ozarks Mountains fiddle tunes compiled by musicologist/folklorist Vance Randolph, published in 1954, and was recorded for the Library of Congress in 1939 by Mississippi fiddler John A. Brown. A very popular Cajun version of the tune, probably borrowed from the American song, is "J'etais au Bal" (I Went to the Dance Last Night).

Cindy in the summertime,

Can't have Cindy all the time,

Don't want Cindy at all.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Cleveland's March to the Whitehouse
description:
Believed to date from Grover Cleveland's election campaigns in the 1880s or 1890s. The tune was passed down orally in the Blue Ridge mountain region.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Climb the Golden Stairs
description:
A G Major breakdown distinct from the minstrel tune 'Climbing Up the Golden Stair'.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Clyde Durst's Tune
description:
A Missouri reel in C Major, documented from fiddler Cyril Stinnett and included on Charlie Walden's list of essential tunes.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: The Coast Is Clear
description: The Coast Is Clear is a reel in the key of D from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Colonel Crockett
description:
The title refers to two different tunes. One appeared in George P. Knauff's 'Virginia Reels' (1839). The other, a version of 'The Route' in A Dorian, is attributed to Kentucky fiddler Bruce Greene.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Coming Down From Denver
description:
An A Major reel rooted in Missouri and Nebraska traditions. While linked to Denver by name, the melody circulated earlier under titles like 'Lardner's Reel' and 'Old Gray Mare'. Missouri fiddler Cleo Pursinger was instrumental in its 20th-century transmission.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Coming Up The Pike
description:
An Ozark reel in C Major. It was recorded by Vance Randolph in the 1940s from fiddlers including William Bilyeu and Delbert McGrath. Art Galbraith is the source for the notated version.

It was recorded for the Library of Congress in the early 1940s by musicologist/folklorist Vance Randolph, from Ozarks fiddlers — among them William Bilyeu (1943) and Delbert McGrath (1942). Art Galbraith (1909–1993): Galbraith, who lived near Springfield, Missouri, learned the tune from one of several fiddlers in the Bilyeu family of Ozark, Missouri.

title: Coon Dog 1
description:
An Appalachian breakdown in standard tuning, deeply rooted in northeastern Kentucky hill country traditions. It is also known as 'Old Coon Dog'.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Coon Dog 2
description:
'Coon Dog' refers to a family of related breakdown tunes. 'Coon Dog ' has roots in Oklahoma and was documented from fiddler Bill Grant.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Cora Dye
description:
An Illinois reel in G Major, named for Cora Dye, who reportedly played the tune on guitar. A 1972 recording was made of fiddler Jim Reed.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Cornhusker Frolic
description: Cornhusker Frolic is a reel in the key of C from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Corn In The Crib
description:
Corn in the Crib is a reel in G attributed to fiddler Blaine Smith. It appears in the Gettysburg Collection of Old-Time Fiddle Tunes and the Tater Joe's resource collection. Precise origins are undocumented, consistent with much of the public domain old-time fiddle repertoire.

It also appears in the Tater Joe's Old-Time Fiddle resource collection, listed as "Corn In The Crib" and credited to Blaine Smith, dated November 23, 2017.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Cotton Picker's Drag
description:
Also known as Cotton Picker's Rag, this tune in B Major is possibly a composition by Missouri fiddler Ben Tinnon (1891–1975). Tinnon led the band Grinnell Giggers, named for the regional practice of gigging the grinnell fish in Mississippi River backwaters.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Cowboy's Dream
description:
This D Major American reel is associated with southeastern Ohio. John McCutcheon identified it as an Ohio tune, with the lineage tracing back to John W. Hutchison (1915–1979).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Cowhide Boots
description:
Cowhide Boots is an old-time breakdown in G Major. It is associated with Missouri fiddler Lyman Enloe (1906–1998), who was in the Ozarks. Printed sources include Phillips (1994), Shull, and Silberberg (2002). Recorded versions include Enloe (1976) and Carthy Sisco (Voyager CD 362).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Cranberry Rock
description:
Cranberry Rock is a C Major reel from West Virginia. It is noted for similarities to Billy in the Lowground. Source for notated versions include Burl Hammons (1908–1993). Published in Milliner & Koken (2011), Phillips (1994), and The Portland Collection vol. 3 (2015). Recorded by the Reed Island Rounders (2002).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Crapshooter's Rag
description:
Crapshooter's Rag is a Texas-style old-time rag in standard tuning. The tune is often linked to Hugh Farr (1903–1980) and Karl Farr, though attribution remains a point of debate among researchers, with some credit also given to Larken Williams. It was Included in R.P. Christeson's Old Time Fiddler's Repertory vol. 1 (1973).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Creal Springs Breakdown
description:
Creal Springs Breakdown is an old-time tune named for the town of Creal Springs, Illinois. The town, founded by Edward G. Creal (1835–1891), was a prominent Midwest resort destination featuring a seminary with a music conservatory (1884–1916), providing a context for local musical activity.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Creighton's Hornpipe
description:
Creighton's Hornpipe is a D Major hornpipe. Lotus Dickey learned it from A.S. Bowman's The Young Violinist's Favorite No. 1 (1891). Bowman was a Philadelphia-based composer and bandleader. Notated version: Lotus Dickey. Recorded by Dickey (1992).

Albert Bowman, born around 1844, was a journeyman violinist, bandleader and composer in Philadelphia and southeastern Pennsylvania.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Crockett's Honeymoon
description:
Crockett's Honeymoon, also known as George Ainley's Tune, is a G Major breakdown. The title originated in the 1970s, potentially assigned by George Ainley to an untitled medley from a 1920s recording by Crockett's Kentucky Mountaineers. It shares lineage with the Maid Who Left the Mountains and various Irish honeymoon reels documented in Ryan's Mammoth Collection (1883).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Crook Brothers Breakdown
description:
The Crook Brothers were a Grand Ole Opry act active for over 63 years, known for harmonica-driven music until Herman Crook added a fiddle in 1931. Fiddlers included Kirk McGee and Floyd Ethridge. Although the band recorded for RCA-Victor in 1928, the specific tune Crook Brothers Breakdown is not part of their recorded output.

The brothers recorded four instrumentals for RCA-Victor in 1928, which sold well, but those were surprisingly the only recordings by the Crook Brothers until 1962. Eventually, the deaths of so many old-time musicians resulted in the remaining members of the Possum Hunters and the Crook Brothers combining into one band, which continued to play on the Opry until Herman Crook died in 1988.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Crow Creek
description:
Crow Creek is an Illinois hoedown, often attributed to fiddler Stelle Elam. The tune is included in the collection Dear Old Illinois, notated in D. It is played in various keys including A, D, and cross E (EBEB), reflecting ongoing performance practices.

The tune has circulated in more than one key, which has caused ongoing debate in the old-time community: The tune has been published in A, but many players have always played it in D—some tracing this preference back to at least 1981.

title: Crow Little Rooster
description:
Crow Little Rooster is an A Major reel sourced to Oklahoma fiddlers Max (1916–2001) and Earl (1911–1975) Collins, originally from Missouri. Published in Silberberg (2002).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Cuckoo's Nest
description:
Cuckoo's Nest is a long-standing folk tune documented since the early 18th century. It appears in English Morris dance traditions, Scottish collections, and American old-time breakdown repertory. The title refers to both the bird and 18th-century bawdy euphemism.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Cuffy
description:
Cuffy is a G Major reel associated with southwestern Virginia and Surry County, North Carolina. It was in the repertoire of N.H. 'Nicky' Mills, whose playing influenced later revival fiddlers. The name reflects 19th-century minstrel stage traditions involving blackface performance.

Armin was the source for the tune for the Highwoods String Band, who recorded an version on their album "No. 3 Special," after which it was in the common repertoire of "revival" fiddlers of the 1970's and 1980's.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Curmudgeon's Fancy
description: Curmudgeon's Fancy is a reel in the key of A from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Cut Knife Hill
description:
Cut Knife Hill is an E Major reel composed by Métis fiddler John Arcand (b. 1942). The title refers to an 1885 battle during the North-West Rebellion near Battleford, Saskatchewan.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Cutting At The Point
description:
Cutting At The Point is an obscure old-time fiddle tune with no widely published historical origin. As with much of the genre, the composer is unknown.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Damon's Winder
description:
Damon's Winder, also known as Damon or Rocky Mountain Goat, is a D Major reel. It is a version of Marmaduke's Hornpipe. Fiddler J.W. Day recorded it in 1934 under the pseudonym Jilson Setters. A 'winder' refers to a dance figure.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Dance All Night
description:
Dance All Night is a widespread American reel or song, notably recorded by Gid Tanner and the Skillet Lickers. Guthrie Meade suggested a relation to Buffalo Gals. Its lyrics sometimes reflect Unionist sympathies in Appalachia.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Dance Around Molly
description:
Standard or AEae (Art Stamper) tunings (fiddle). AABB (Phillips, Silberberg): AA'BB' (Beisswenger & McCann). A traditional dance tune collected in Missouri and North Carolina. "Well-known tune among Missouri fiddlers" (Frank Maloy), and indeed, it has been recorded by (and is associated with) several fiddlers from that state. It is on Charlie Walden's list of '100 essential Missouri fiddle tunes'. Howard Marshall says the reel is associated with fiddlers from the north and central part of Missouri, such as Jake Hockemeyer, Johnny Bruce, Cleo Persinger, Taylor McBaine, Pete McMahan, and Charlie Walden. Howard says: "All the fiddlers I've known credit Jake Hockemeyer with the best version anywhere and it was one of Jake's fiddle contest "money tunes." I played backup guitar for Hockemeyer in several contests in the 80s when he played the tune to good effect even though by that time his arthritis problems were getting him down. The tune is what I'd call a hornpipe." The melody has lost some currency in modern times among contest players in the state.

Tommy Magness (1916-1972) with Bill Monroe (mand.) Bill Wesbrooks (bass) and Clyde Moody (gtr.), early 1940's. Photo courtesy of James Monroe."Dance around Molly" was played by Tommy Magness over WSM in the 1940's and the composition is often credited to him--certainly he popularizing it, as his 1951 recording was highly influential. According to one story in circulation, Magness composed the tune one night after a gig when eating in a restaurant with his band. A waitress named Molly started bantering with the band and got them to play a tune so she could dance to it.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Dandy Lusk
description:
Dandy Lusk is a crooked reel from Letcher County, Kentucky, played by Fernando 'Dandy Lusk' (b. 1890s), who learned from his mother, fiddler Elvina 'Viney' Campbell Lusk. It was recorded in 1952.

Elvina and Fernando were aunt and cousin of fiddler Manon Campbell (1890-1987) who was recorded by folklorists, and who also learned some of his repertoire from the Lusks.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Darling Nellie Gray
description:
Darling Nellie Gray is an abolitionist song composed by Benjamin Russell Hanby in 1856, inspired by the story of runaway slave Joseph Selby. It entered the American dance repertoire as an air and dance tune.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Davey Come Back and Act Like You Oughta
description:
This A-modal Appalachian tune is arranged by fiddler Erynn Marshall and appears on her 2012 album, Calico.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Dean Reed's Favorite (Oh How She Lied)
description: Dean Reed's Favorite (Oh How She Lied) is a reel in the key of A from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Devil Eat The Groundhog
description:
Devil Eat The Groundhog originates from Kentucky fiddler Owen 'Snake' Chapman (1919–2002), who learned it from his father, Doc Chapman (b. 1850).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Dickey's Discovery
description:
Dickey's Discovery is a D Major breakdown named for Indiana fiddler Lotus Dickey (1911–1989), who documented it in 1985. It is related to King's Lament and Brisk Young Soldier.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Dick Sand's Hornpipe
description:
Dick Sands was a 19th-century stage performer and clog dancer associated with P.T. Barnum's shows. A 1879/1880 dance book by J.F. Finn bears his name.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Dill Pickle Rag
description:
Dill Pickle Rag is a novelty rag composed in 1907 by Charles L. Johnson (1876–1950). The title was inspired by a carton of pickles a bookkeeper was carrying at the music company where Johnson worked. It was widely recorded and became part of the old-time repertoire.

"Dill Pickle" was learned by itinerant West Virginia fiddler John Johnson (1916-1996), originally from Clay County, from fiddler Dorvel Hill who lived in a coal-mining town called Pigtown, not far from the town of Clay, W.Va.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Dinah
description:
Dinah is an A Major reel related to a large family of tunes including Seneca Square Dance and Coon Dog. Samuel Bayard collected a vocal version in Pennsylvania.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Dirty Sheets
description: Dirty Sheets is a reel in the key of D from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Dixie Banner
description: Dixie Banner is a reel in the key of C from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Dixie Blossoms
description:
The tune was remembered by fiddler Art Galbraith as dating to around 1916, and was "a perennial favorite of his mother" (Reiner & Anick). Beisswenger & McCann add that it was played by a cousin for Galbraith's who fought in World War 1. Galbraith also recalled "Byron Kelly, an old bass player, the only black man left in Christian County, used to be a professional, he liked this one a lot"1. "Dixie Blossoms" is a composition by ragtime and song composer Percy Wenrich (1887-1952) who composed it in 1906 as "Dixie Blossoms March-Two-Step." He was also the composer the music of "Put on Your Old Grey Bonnet" (1909) and the ragtime melody "Peaches and Cream" (1905), among many others, and was known for incorporating "folk" elements in his tunes2. Wenrich was born in Joplin, Missouri (he was known as "The Joplin Kid"), but moved to Chicago in 1901, and in 1909 removed to New York where he had a long and successful career in Tin-Pan-Alley. However, his early influences were from his mother, an accomplished amateur pianist, and from the booming club and music scene in Joplin, home to several important ragtime composers and performers, black and white. A similar tune is "Chicken Pie," collected in Reynolds County, Missouri, however, it is not the "Chicken Pie" in Marion Thede's book, which is an unrelated tune.

Notation sources: Art Galbraith (1909-1993, near Springfield, Missouri) [Beisswenger & McCann, Phillips, Reiner & Anick].

Published in Beisswenger & McCann (Ozarks Fiddle Music), 2008; p. 38. Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 2), 1995; p. 41. Reiner & Ancik (Old Time Fiddling Across America), 1989; p. 122.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Dixie Hoedown
description:
Recordings include Rounder 11661-0133-2, "Art Galbraith, James River Fiddler: Dixie Blossoms" (2007, extended reissue of 1981 LP).

Back to Dixie Hoedown

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Doc Corn's Tune
description:
Doc Corn's Tune is attributed to Illinois fiddler John Ray 'Doc' Corn (1893–1984), documented in 1976.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Dogs in the Dishes
description:
Dogs in the Dishes is a D Major breakdown from southwestern Pennsylvania, documented from Irvin Yaugher in 1944. It shares a strain with Blockhouse Dutchman.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Dog Treed A Possum Up A White Oak Tree
description:
Dog Treed a Possum Up a White Oak Tree is a D Major reel from Illinois, attributed to fiddler Howard Sims (1896–1977). It was preserved through fieldwork by Chirps Smith and Garry Harrison in the 1970s.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Doney
description: Doney was recorded in 1939 by Charles Long (Mississippi) for the Library of Congress. It shares structural elements with Goodbye Liza Jane. The term 'doney' is a 19th-century slang term for a woman, derived from Italian or Spanish origins and circulated in traveling-show communities.

title: Don Tremaine's Reel
description:
Don Tremaine's Reel is a D Major reel composed in 1961 by Canadian fiddler Graham Townsend. It was named for the announcer of Don Messer's Jubilee.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Dora Dean
description:
Dora Dean is a country rag composed in 1896 by Bert Williams (1874–1922). It was named for vaudeville entertainer Dora Babbage Dean, who popularized the Cakewalk with her partner Charles Johnson.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Down in Little Egypt
description:
American reel in G Major. The tune was in the repertory of fiddler Noah Beavers (1897-1990) of southern Illinois, and named by collector Lynn "Chirps" Smith after the nickname for that region.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Down The River
description:
"Going Down the River" is classified as an Old-Time Breakdown in AABB form. It is associated with Kentucky, North Carolina, and Missouri.

"Going Down the River" was recorded for Victor Records in Memphis, Tennessee, in September 1928 by the Arkansas group Dr. Smith's Champion Hoss Hair Pullers, although it was not released by Victor until 1929. It featured the twin fiddling of Brian Lackey and Clark Duncan on the cut.

However, a very similar version had been recorded a year earlier by The Hill Billies (Tony Alderman & Charlie Bowman, fiddles) as "Boating Up Sandy", one of many different tunes by that title.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Dr. Brown
description: Dr. Brown is a reel in the key of A from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Drunken Hiccoughs
description:
Old-time and Texas-style air, waltz, and song tune in 3/4 time. Scholar Samuel Bayard associated the melody with the Scottish "Todlin Hame" family and identified numerous vocal variants across the British Isles and America. It is documented across many U.S. states.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Drunken Hiccups
description:
Old-time and Texas-style air, waltz, and song tune in 3/4 time, documented across several U.S. states. Paul Clayton categorized the tune as old and of English origin, while Samuel Bayard linked it to the Scottish "Todlin Hame" tune family and identified several vocal variants.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Duck River
description:
Standard or ADae tunings (fiddle). Jeff Titon (2001) says the specific "Duck River" tune seems to be particular to the Salyer family, although it is part of a fairly common tune family. West Virginia fiddler Israel Welch played a version of this tune he called Forks of Cheat. Titon says the tune family to which "Duck River" belongs also includes "Ma Ferguson," "Nancy Dawson (2)," "Nancy Dalton," and "Hell Up Coal Holler (2)." See also "Mabel," "Possum Up a Gum Stump," and "Drum Tune."

Notation sources: John Morgan Salyer (1882-1952, Salyersville, Magoffin County, Ky., 1941) [Milliner & Koken, Phillips, Titon]; Alan Garren (Portland, Oregon) who learned it from the Bruce Greene recording [Songer].

Published in S. Johnson (The Kitchen Musician No. 2: Occasional Collection of Old-Timey Fiddle Tunes for Hammer Dulcimer, Fiddle, etc.), 1982 (revised 1988, 2003); p. 8. Milliner * Koken (Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes), 2011; p. 173. Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes vol. 2), 1995; p. 45. Songer (Portland Collection), 1997; p. 67. Titon (Old-Time Kentucky Fiddle Tunes), 2001; No. 35, p. 68. Samuel P. Bayard (Dance to the Fiddle March to the Fife), 1981: No. 235, p. 195.

Recordings include Bruce Greene - "Vintage Fiddle Tunes." Berea College Appalachian Center AC003, John M. Salyer - "Home Recordings 1941-42, vol. 1" (1993). Oak Records OOK CD 001, "Brittany Haas" (2004).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Duck's Eyeball
description:
American reel of uncertain origin, linked to "Richmond" by Kerry Blech. It was in the repertoire of western Virginia fiddler Luther Davis. Recordings include a 1948 home disc by Tommy Magness. John Hartford noted similarities to versions by Ed Hayley, Frazier Moss, and Charlie Acuff.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Dull Chisel
description:
Modern old-time tune composed by the Illinois fiddler Garry Harrison (ca. 2000). Played in A in AEAE tuning, it became widely adopted in fiddle jams. Jack Burgess and the Stanly County Boys recorded it in 2003.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Dunbar
description:
American reel in C Major associated with the Kentucky fiddler Ed Haley (1885-1951). Mark Wilson and Guthrie Meade suggested it may be related to "Billy in the Lowground" and named for the town of Dunbar, West Virginia.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: The Dusty Miller
description:
A family of eight distinct melodies sharing this name, with the oldest documented versions appearing in 18th-century Scottish collections like Robert Bremner's "Scots Reels" (c. 1765). William Chappell claimed the tune was English, citing 1718 appearances.

The oldest documented "Dusty Miller" is a popular and widespread late 17th-century tune in the old triple-time hornpipe metre, published in Scotland in 1730 in a volume labelled Dances, Marches, in Robert Bremner's Scots Reels (c. 1765), in Edinburgh fiddler and writing master David Young's McFarlane Manuscript (c. 1741), and in the Gillespie Manuscript of Perth (1768).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Eadle Alley
description:
American reel from the repertoire of Braxton County, West Virginia, fiddler Melvin Wine (1909-2003), who learned it from the Allen family.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Ebb and Flow
description:
Modern tune composed by Carl Jones. It has been widely adopted in folk sessions in the UK. The B part features crooked, asymmetric phrasing.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Echoes Of the Ozarks
description:
American country rag from Missouri, recorded by Sam Long in 1926. The melody is related to 19th-century songs including "Little Old Log Cabin in the Lane" (1871) and "I'se Gwine Back to Dixie" (1874).

It is melodically similar to the popular song "Little Old Log Cabin in the Lane," written in 1871 (and popularized by Fiddlin' John Carson's 1923 recording), and appears to be, in fact, a song tune. Missouri fiddler Sam Long (1876–1931), originally from Scranton, Kansas, but who also lived in Missouri and Oklahoma, recorded the tune (via acoustic, not electronic methods) in 1926, and despite the rather poor quality of the sound it sold well in the Mid-west and West.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Eli Green's Cakewalk
description:
Published in 1898, this hit was composed by Sadie G. Koninsky (1879-1952) of Troy, New York, with lyrics by Dave Reed Jr. It was the first cakewalk published by a woman.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Emmett Lundy's (Richmond) Cotillion
description:
Emmett Lundy (1864-1950s) learned tunes in his youth from Greenberry Leonard, a fiddler born in the early 19th century who was active in Grayson County, Virginia.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Evening Shade
description:
American reel in G Major, credited to Tennessee fiddler Arthur Smith (1898-1971). It is often played at a slower tempo than his typical breakdowns.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Fair Morning Hornpipe
description:
Simple reel from the repertoire of Wilson Douglas (1922-1999) of Clay County, West Virginia. Paul Mitchell noted a similar tune called "Nancy" recorded by Cape Breton fiddler Joe MacLean.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Farewell Princeton
description:
"Farewell Princeton" is a tune from Clyde Davenport, the Kentucky old-time fiddler widely regarded as one of the great traditional players of the 20th century. The tune appears on the album FRC 104 – Clyde Davenport: Volume 2, released by the Field Recorders' Collective from recordings in the collection of Ray Alden. Specifically, the B part contains two extra beats. The crookedness in the B part is considered very typical of Clyde Davenport's playing style.

It is widely believed that the tune refers to Princeton, West Virginia somehow, a town that was home to several great musicians (Oscar Wright being one notable example). However, no definitive written record of the backstory has surfaced in the old-time community. Emily Schaad played it in the fiddle finals at the Clifftop festival in 2012, and transcriptions of both her performance and Clyde's original are available on taterjoes.com. Emily Schaad won the 2012 Clifftop fiddle contest. The tune has also been passed along informally — at least one player learned it from Adam Hurt, who taught it by playing a slow and clear rendition on fiddle. On banjo, it is commonly arranged in clawhammer style, played in Double D tuning (aDADE).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Fancy Creek
description:
A composition of Fred Campeau, a founding member of the group The Volo Bogtrotters, formed c. 1985.

Retrieved from "https://tunearch.org/w/index.php?title=Annotation:Fancy_Creek&oldid=328147"

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Fat Meat and Dumplings
description:
AB (Siblerberg): AABB (Christeson, Phillips, Williams): AA'BB' (Beisswenger & McCann). The tune is related to "Green Corn." Some fiddlers play all or some of the 'f' notes sharp instead of natural.

Notation sources: Cyril Stinnett (Oregon, Missouri), who learned it from his father [Christeson]; Art Galbraith (Mo.) [Phillips]; Glenn Berry [Silberberg]; Vesta Johnson (b. 1922), learned from Cyril Stinnett [Beisswenger & McCann]; Glenn Berry (1924-, Seabeck, Washington) [Williams].

Published in Beisswenger & McCann (Ozarks Fiddle Music), 2008; p. 71. R.P. Christeson (Old Time Fiddler's Repertory, vol. 1), 1973; p. 43. Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 1), 1994; p. 83. Silberberg (Tunes I Learned at Tractor Tavern), 2002; p. 43. Stuart Williams (The Evergreen Fiddler, vol. I), 2005; p. 10.

Recordings include Marimac 9017, Vesta Johnson (Mo.) - "Down Home Rag." Missouri State Old Time Fiddlers' Association, Cyril Stinnet (1912-1986) - "Plain Old Time Fiddling." Missouri State Old Time Fiddlers' Association VFFA 1001, Vest Johnson - "I'm Old But I'm Awfully Tough" (1977). Rounder C-11565, Art Galbraith (Springfield, Mo.) - "Rounder Fiddle" (1990). Rounder 0157, Art Galbraith - "Simple Pleasures." Red Mountain White Trash - "Sweet Bama" (2002).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Feather Bed
description:
ADae or AEae tuning (fiddle). AAB (Titon): AABB (Milliner & Koken). In the repertoire of John Salyer (1882-1952), Magoffin County, Ky., whose sons, Grover and Glen, made a home recording of him in the early 1940's. Gene Winnans mentions that a black banjo player, Gus Cannon, who worked medicine shows between 1914 and 1929, learned a tune called "Feather Bed" in "strumming style" from "Old Man Saul" Russell, who played for his own amusement around his house. Jeff Titon (2001) remarks that, as far as he knows, Salyer is the sole source for the Kentucky fiddle tune. John Salyer

Notation sources: John Salyer (Salyersville, Magoffin County, Ky., 1941) [Milliner & Koken, Titon].

Published in Milliner & Koken (Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes), 2011; p. 192. Titon (Old-Time Kentucky Fiddle Tunes), 2001; No. 38, p. 70.

Recordings include 5-String Productions, Alice Gerard, Gail Gillespie & Sharon Sandomirsky - "The Road to Agate Hill" (2006. From Martin Marshall). Berea College Appalachian Center AC003, John M. Salyer - "Home Recordings 1941-42, vol. 2" (1993). County CD 2728, Rafe Stefanini - "Hell and Scissors" (1999).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Feed My Horse Corn and Hay
description:
Associated with northeastern Kentucky fiddler Buddy Thomas (1935–1974), who learned the tune from his mother's whistling and other regional sources.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Fiddler's Dream
description:
AABB' (Brody, Milliner & Koken, Songer): AA'BB (Phillips). Charles Wolfe (1978) says the tune, which was fashioned by Tennessee fiddler Arthur Smith, is "based vaguely on the changes of 'Flop Eared Mule,'" although the only similarity appears to be the I-V key change between parts. Some fiddlers start the tune on the first strain, while others on the second.

Published in Brody (Fiddler's Fakebook), 1983; p. 105. R.P. Christeson (Old Time Fiddlers Repertory, vol. 1), 1973; p. 103. Stephen F. Davis (Devil's Box), vol. 22, No. 2, Summer 1988; p. 25. Milliner & Koken (Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes), 2011; p. 194. Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 1), 1994; p. 84. Ruth (Pioneer Western Folk Tunes), 1948; No. 66, p. 24. Susan Songer with Clyde Curley (Portland Collection vol. 3), 2015; p. 71.

Recordings include Heritage 25, "Poor Richard's Almanac." Bluebird 5843-A (78 RPM), Arthur Smith (1935). CMH 9006, Benny Martin- "The Fiddle Collection." County 547, Arthur Smith- "Arthur Smith, vol. 2" (1978). County 762, Lymon Enloe (b. 1906)- "Fiddle Tunes I Recall." Decca DL 78950/MCA 162, Tommy Jackson- "Square Dances Without Calls" (1959). Marimac 9017, Vesta Johnson (Mo.) - "Down Home Rag."

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Fiddler's Reel
description:
Regional reel from Surry County, North Carolina, noted in the repertoire of Benton Flippen. It was also listed in Vance Randolph's 1954 collection of Ozark fiddle tunes.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Fireman's Dance Cotillion
description:
Composed by the African-American bandleader Francis Johnson in 1822, this piece in 2/4 time was written to honor Philadelphia fire companies.

The Philadelphia Fireman's Cotillion is credited to Francis Johnson (1792–1844) and was composed in 1822.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Fishing Limber
description: Fishing Limber is a reel in the key of A from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Five Miles To Town
description:
Sourced to John Sharp (1894–1964) of Wayne County, Kentucky, and recorded by Sergeant Alvin York in 1949. It is distinct from other similarly titled tunes in the region.

The tune was later printed in the Milliner & Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes (2011), p. 203.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Five Miles Out Of Town
description:
A cluster of related but distinct Missouri tunes. Hans Nathan linked the title to minstrel show dance steps. Notable versions come from Frame Davis and Cyril Stinnett.

The notated version comes from the playing of Frame Davis (Des Moines, Iowa), recorded in 1950 by Bob Christeson. Stinnett was born near Savannah in northwest Missouri in 1912; his father was a farmer and a fiddler.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Flatfoot in the Ashes
description:
West Virginia fiddle tune associated with Harvey Sampson. It is played in A modal (AEAE). The title refers to the practice of buck dancing on ash-covered floors.

The recording appears on the Augusta Heritage LP AHR 004 (1986), now out of print.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Ford's One Step
description:
Named in honor of Henry Ford, whose promotion of "old-fashioned" dances and fiddling in the 1920s influenced naming conventions. The "One Step" refers to a popular dance form of that era.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Fork Horned Buck
description:
"Fork Horned Buck" is an old-time fiddle tune in the broader family of "Forked Deer"-related tunes — a cluster of American fiddle pieces sharing similar melodic DNA and titles rooted in frontier hunting culture. The name itself evokes the imagery of a two-pronged (forked) antler buck, which was considered a prize in the pioneer hunting world.

"Forked Deer" is a fiddle tune of the old frontier — old and widely distributed, yet it cannot be traced to the Old World or the northern United States.

Ira Ford's (1940) origin story traces the tune to the days of powder horns, bullet molds, and coonskin caps. It has been traced to the first settlers along the Big Sandy River, on the border of Virginia and Kentucky. In the family which preserved the tune, the story — handed down through several generations — credits authorship to a relative, a noted fiddler of pioneer days. This kinsman was also a famous hunter. There was a spirit of friendly rivalry in the hunt, and he had established a reputation as a champion deer hunter by always bringing in a forked deer. The forked deer, or two-point buck, was considered prime venison.

The tune is fiddled with a fluid bowing style using slurs to create complicated rhythmic patterns, in the manner of the old Upper South. Its title both evokes the forest and names a river in West Tennessee.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Fortune
description:
Galax, Virginia, standard in D Major. It was recorded by Emmett Lundy and John Rector. Tommy Jarrell recalled learning it from his father, describing it as an old flatfoot dance tune.

It was, for example, one of the few tunes recorded by Galax, Va., fiddler Emmett Lundy, and Galax, Va., storekeeper, banjo and fiddle player John Rector was recorded playing "Fortune" in 1926 by collector John Lomax.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Forty Drops
description:
ABAB' (Phillips): AABBAABC (Beisswenger & McCann).

Sources for notated versions: - Jere Canote [Phillips]; Howe Teague (1913-2005, Dent County, Missouri) [Beisswenger & McCann].

Published in Beisswenger & McCann (Ozarks Fiddle Music), 2008; p. 148. Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 2), 1995; p. 52.

Recordings include Gold Standard, Howe Teague - "Ozark Memories" (c. 1986).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Forty Miles From Georgetown Without Any Whiskey
description:
Reel in C composed by Garry Harrison, associated with the Indian Creek Delta Boys.

Harrison is associated with the Indian Creek Delta Boys, and at least one fiddler reports having learned the tune directly from Garry Harrison at Fiddle Tunes in 1998.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Frankie
description:
Reel from the repertoire of Kentucky fiddler Buddy Thomas, who learned it from his mother's whistling. Mark Wilson linked it to Pete Riley's "Rattlesnake."

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Free State Hornpipe
description:
Tommy Jackson and John Ashby credited it to fiddler Ralph Lamp of Winchester.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Full Moon Reel
description:
"Full Moon Reel" is credited to composer Mark Schatz, played by Ryck Kaiser, in the key of A, with AEAE cross-tuning. It appears in the Old Time Fiddle Tunes collection assembled by John Lamancusa, and is referenced in the Old Time Fiddling from the State of Pennsylvania / Gettysburg Collection under the category of Newly Written Fiddle Tunes.

This is a key detail: the tune is categorized as a newly written (i.e., composed) fiddle tune, not an ancient traditional melody passed down anonymously through generations.

Mark Schatz is a well-known bassist and old-time/bluegrass musician who has worked with Tony Rice, Nickel Creek, and many others. He is also an accomplished clogging dancer and tune composer. His background straddles the line between traditional old-time music and the contemporary folk/bluegrass revival world, which fits perfectly with writing new tunes in the old-time idiom.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Galleynipper
description:
Associated with eastern Kentucky and West Virginia fiddlers, notably J.P. Fraley who learned it from his father.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Garfield's Blackberry Blossom
description:
"Garfield's Blackberry Blossom" is one of the great puzzles of the old-time fiddle canon — a tune that exists in the shadow of a more famous melody sharing its name. To call this the "older" Blackberry Blossom is not quite right; it is simply a different tune altogether. When bluegrass fiddler Arthur Smith recorded "Blackberry Blossom" in the 1930s, he created something so it eventually swallowed the older melody's identity. The prefix "Garfield's" — possibly coined by John Hartford, who was meticulous about such distinctions — was retrofitted to preserve the older tune's separate existence.

The melody belongs to northeastern Kentucky. Its primary keeper was Ed Haley (1885–1951), the blind fiddler of Lawrence County whose playing was so singular that fiddlers across the region sought him out directly. Dick Burnett, himself a Kentucky fiddling institution, credited Haley as his source. Buddy Thomas, Snake Chapman, J.P. Fraley, and Ed Morrison — some of the most respected names in the northeastern Kentucky tradition — all carried versions of this tune.

An origin story in Jean Thomas's "Ballad Makin' in the Mountains of Kentucky" connects the "Garfield" name to President James A. Garfield, assassinated in 1881, though the exact nature of that link remains debated. The two Blackberry Blossoms share almost no melodic similarity beyond a vague resemblance in their opening measures, suggesting they developed independently. A close companion tune is "Yew Piney Mountain." The notated version appears in the Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes (2011), p. 226.

Sources: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), Jean Thomas "Ballad Makin' in the Mountains of Kentucky," Milliner-Koken Collection, community discussions, and fiddle music scholarship.

title: Garfield's March
description:
Derived from an 1881 funeral march composed after the assassination of President James A. Garfield. It was recorded by the Kessinger Brothers in 1928, learned by Clark Kessinger from Abe Glenn.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Gaston
description:
Gaston is an American reel in G major. The melody appears in George P. Knauff's Virginia Reels, volume IV (Baltimore, 1839). It is considered cognate to a tune in an anonymous 1862 manuscript and the minstrel tune "Hoop-de-doo-den-doo (2)."

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: General Lee
description: General Lee, also known as "Dubuque," is a reel documented from the playing of South Carolina fiddler Vernon Riddle (1935–2011), recorded by Ashley Carder in 1993. Riddle adapted his style from Texas contest fiddlers.

title: Georgia Row
description:
Georgia Row is an old-time reel in A major (AEae tuning) from northeastern Kentucky. It is associated with fiddler Buddy Thomas (1934-1974). A different tune in D, played by Charlie Osborne, shares the title.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Getting George Bush Upstairs
description:
Getting George Bush Upstairs is a reel in A major (AEae tuning). The source for modern versions is Kentucky fiddler Perry Riley (1893-1986), an itinerant laborer who influenced his cousin, fiddler Buddy Thomas.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Getting Out of the Way of the Federals
description: Getting Out of the Way of the Federals is a reel in the key of G from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Getting Upstairs
description:
Getting Upstairs is a morris dance tune collected in Oxfordshire and Northamptonshire, England. It is an adaptation of an 1830s American blackface minstrel tune by Joe Blackburn. Winston Wilkinson suggested the title relates to the morris processional dance.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Gilroy
description:
Gilderoy is a Scottish/American reel, also known as "Red Haired Boy" or "Little Beggarman." The title derives from the Gaelic 'Giolla Ruadh' (red-haired lad), associated with the Scottish highwayman Patrick McGregor, who was executed in 1636.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Gilsaw
description:
Gilsaw is an old-time breakdown in D major popularized by Missouri fiddler Pete McMahan. Howard Marshall recorded that McMahan learned the tune from a sheriff named Claude Gregory, who heard it played by a traveling fiddler at a train depot.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Glory at the Meeting House
description:
Glory in the Meeting House is a multi-part fiddle reel from eastern Kentucky. The tune was recorded by Luther Strong (1892–1962) in 1937 for Alan Lomax and the Library of Congress. It is played in E modal (EDAE) tuning.

The recording is attributed to Luther Strong, in E Modal tuning (EDAE), and was recorded for Music of Kentucky Vol. 2 (Yazoo 2014), captured by Alan and Elizabeth Lomax on October 18, 1937.

title: Going Across The Prairie
description:
Going Across the Prairie is associated with Missouri fiddler Cleo Persinger, who learned the tune by ear during the early 20th century.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Going Down To Cairo
description:
Going Down to Cairo is a fiddle tune and play-party song from Illinois, associated with river town culture in Cairo. David McIntosh documented it in 'Folk Songs and Singing Games of the Illinois Ozarks' as a circle dance.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Going Down the River
description:
Fraley) (fiddle). "Going Down the River" was recorded for Victor Records in Memphis, Tenn., in September 1928 by the Arkansas group Dr. Smith's Champion Hoss Hair Pullers, although it was not released by Victor until 1929. It featured the twin fiddling of Brian Lackey and Clark Duncan on the cut. However, the a very similar version had been recorded a year earlier by The Hill Billies (Tony Alderman & Charlie Bowman, fiddles) as "Boating Up Sandy (4)," one of many different tunes by that title. The following words were associated with the tune by Kentucky fiddler J.P.

Oh, my little girl, if you don't do better,

Put you on a boat, gonna send you down the river.

Boat began to sink, my heart began to quiver,

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Going To The Free State
description:
Going to the Free State is a two-part fiddle tune in cross A tuning (AEae) from Virginia fiddler John Ashby (1915–1979). Ashby formed the Free State Ramblers in Fauquier County circa 1940.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Going To Town
description:
Going to Town is a version of the tune "Katy Hill," recorded in 1937 by Arthur Smith and his trio in Charlotte, N.C., and released on Bluebird B-8101.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Going Uptown
description:
Going Uptown is attributed to Tennessee fiddler Oscar Stone, who reportedly created the tune by adding a section to "Ragtime Annie." The story was documented by John Hartford and transmitted by fiddler Howdy Forrester.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Going to the Wedding to Get Some Cake
description: Going to the Wedding to Get Some Cake is a reel in the key of C from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Golden Ticket
description:
"The Golden Ticket" is a beautiful creation of fiddler Eric Merrill that has become a jam favorite in many corners of the old-time scene. It was released on October 4, 2004, on his album The Western Star.

The composer credit is well-documented: as Adrienne Young noted in the liner notes to her album Art of Virtue, "This song was written by our fiddle player, Eric Merrill. It is from his record The Western Star."

The Golden Ticket is "perhaps a bit elusive in its melodic and even harmonic structure, with a brief appearance of a D chord to open the tune." It is catalogued in the Traditional Tune Archive as a reel in the key of G, in standard tuning (GDAE).

The tune's path through the folk community is a classic example of oral transmission: Roger Netherton got it from an amateur recording of Rhys Jones playing it at a contra dance. A local friend who gave the recording noted that Rhys used to play it a lot, though it doesn't appear on any of Rhys's CDs. The impression was that it was a modern old-time-style tune, but that Rhys hadn't written it. At the Winfield festival in 2011, Roger was in the fiddle contest finals with Tricia backing him on guitar. As they were about to walk onstage, Roger spontaneously asked if she knew "Golden Ticket." She replied, "Yeah, that's a sweet tune" — and they played it on stage without any preparation.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Gold Rush
description:
Gold Rush is a reel in A major composed around 1967 by Bill Monroe and Byron Berline. Some sources suggest it may have been modeled on "Burt County Breakdown," associated with Nebraska fiddler Bob Walters.

"Gold Rush" was recorded by Mike Yates in 1980 from the playing of fiddler Pug Allen of Stuarts Draft, Augusta County, Va. At the time Allen was adamant that he knew the tune years before Monroe's recording was issued.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Goodbye Girls
description:
Goodbye Girls is an Appalachian reel often played in AEAE tuning. It was collected from Hillard Smith in Hindman, Kentucky, in 1917 by Cecil Sharp. The tune is associated with the Stamper family, including Art Stamper.

Art recorded it on County CD2712 (The Lost Fiddler, c. 1982, taught to him by his father Hiram), and again on County CO-CD-2729, Goodbye Girls I'm Going to Boston (2000).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Goodbye Girls I'm Going To Boston
description:
Goodbye Girls, I'm Going to Boston is an American reel collected in 1917 from Hillard Smith in Hindman, Kentucky, by Cecil Sharp. It is also associated with Jean Ritchie.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Goodbye Liza
description:
Liza Jane songs originated in the folk repertoire of enslaved people in the United States and were later adopted by Civil War regiments. Minstrel versions were popularized in the late 19th century, including an 1871 sheet music publication by Eddie Fox and a 1903 version by Harry Von Tilzer.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Granddad's Favorite
description:
Granddad's Favorite is a West Virginia tune from fiddler Ernie Carpenter, who learned it from his grandfather, Bill Carpenter.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Grand Picnic
description:
Grand Picnic is a Missouri reel in D major, attributed to Joe Politte of Washington County. Gordon McCann suggested a potential French origin for the tune.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Gray Owl
description: Gray Owl is a reel in the key of D from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Great Big Taters
description:
Great Big Taters is a Southern and Southwestern fiddle tune related to "Sail Away Ladies" and "Sally Ann." It has been linked to the "Hound Dawg Song," published in 1912.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Great Eastern Reel
description:
Great Eastern Reel (1)

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Green Fields Of America
description:
Green Fields of America is a transatlantic fiddle tune with roots in Irish emigration ballads. The earliest published version is from a 19th-century collection by S.A. Such. The melody shares similarities with older tunes like "Cossey's Jig" (1774).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Green River March
description:
Green River March is a reel recorded in 1929 by the Roane County Ramblers. Fiddler Uncle Jimmy McCarroll (1892–1970s) learned the tune from his grandmother; family lore associates the tune with the Cherokee Trail of Tears.

McCarroll was born in 1892, in Wheat, Anderson County, Tennessee, and was still playing in the 1970's.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Green Willis
description:
Green Willis is a D major breakdown from southwestern Virginia. The tune became associated with 19th-century fiddler Green Willis. It was historically used as a march for the last day of school. It is likely related to the English tune "New Rigged Ship."

The melody, in 6/8 time, was also in the repertoire of Galax area fiddler Emmett Lundy (b. 1864), who recorded it when he was an elderly man.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Grey Haired Dancing Girl
description:
Grey Haired Dancing Girl is attributed to a Maryland fiddler named Jumahl. It appears in The Gettysburg Collection of Old-Time Fiddle Tunes and was recorded by the Boiled Buzzards in 1994.

There is also a YouTube recording posted in 2017 by at least one other performer.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Grigsby's Hornpipe
description:
Grigsby's Hornpipe is a Texas reel in A major from fiddler Eck Robertson (1887-1975).

From Texas fiddler Eck Robertson (1887-1975), who played it in a medley with "Rye Whiskey," recorded in March, 1963, at Robertson's home in Amarillo, Texas.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Grotts
description:
Grotts is a D major fiddle tune from the Illinois prairie region. A version was transcribed by Stelle Elam in 'Dear Old Illinois,' and it was recorded by Lynn "Chirps" Smith on his 2003 album, 'Down in Little Egypt.'

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Grubb Springs
description: Grub Springs is a Mississippi tune named after a local stream in Monroe County. The most well-known version was recorded by Herbert Halpert from fiddler W.E. Claunch in 1939 and released on 'Great Big Yam Potatoes: Anglo-American Fiddle Music from Mississippi.'

title: Gunboat
description:
Gunboat is a West Virginia breakdown associated with fiddler Ernie Carpenter (1907–1997). Despite the name, there is no evidence the tune dates to the Civil War. It is sometimes known as "Horney Ewe," which researchers believe is a vestige of Scottish pastoral nomenclature.

Melvin Wine, the great Braxton County contemporary of Carpenter's, called it "Gunboat Whistled into Georgi-o." It also appears as "Going Down to Georgie-o" and "Who'll Take Care of the Baby-O." The strangest alias is "Hornio" — which researcher Gerry Milnes traced in 1999 to "Horney Ewe," a Scottish dialect phrase that survived in the Appalachian mountains long after it was lost elsewhere.

title: Half Irish
description:
Half Irish was composed by Kentucky fiddler Owen "Snake" Chapman to emulate an Irish reel. The tune incorporates modal shifts from D Mixolydian to D Ionian.

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: Half Past Four
description:
Half Past Four is a reel in A major (AEae tuning). It was recorded in the mid-20th century by West Virginia fiddler Edden Hammonds as "Paddy on the Turnpike (1)."

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Hanging Around the Kitchen Until the Cook Comes Home
description: Hanging Around the Kitchen Until the Cook Comes Home is a reel in the key of E from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Harrington Valley Two Step
description:
Harrington Valley Two Step is a tune in D major copyrighted by Canadian fiddler Calvin Vollrath, suggesting roots in the Canadian Prairie fiddle tradition.

A widely circulated version of the tune comes from a Missouri fiddle workshop taught by Charlie Walden in January 2015, and an audio recording of that entire workshop is available on Charlie's website.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Happy Hollow
description:
Happy Hollow is a reel in A major (AEac# tuning) recorded from western North Carolina fiddler Marcus Martin (1881-1974) by Artus Moser in 1942.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Happy Thought Reel
description: Happy Thought Reel is a reel in the key of A from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Haystack Blues
description: Haystack Blues is a reel in the key of D from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Hawks And Eagles
description:
Norman Edmonds (1889–1976) of Hillsville, Virginia, is the primary source for this tune, which he recorded in 1973 for the album Train on the Island (Spring Fed Records). It is referenced in the Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Hell and Scissors
description:
Hell and Scissors is an Old-Time breakdown in A Major. The tune is in the repertoire of Bruce Greene, who learned it from a 78 RPM recording by J.W. 'Blind Bill' Day. It also appears in a 1954 list of Ozarks fiddle tunes compiled by Vance Randolph.

"Blind Bill" Day} (recorded 1934 for John Lomax in Ashland Ky).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Hell Broke Loose in Georgia
description:
Hell Broke Loose in Georgia is an American reel associated with a Tennessee fiddling contest in 1899 and cited by A.B. Moore as a standard repertoire tune in his 1934 History of Alabama. The tune appears in Phillips (1994) and Songer (1997) and was recorded by the Skillet Lickers (1975) and Lowe Stokes (1982).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Hell on the Potomac
description:
Hell on the Potomac is a G Major reel documented by Samuel Bayard (1981) in southwestern Pennsylvania. Bayard notes the tune is a floating title attached to various melodies, including those related to Mason's Apron.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Hell Up Coal Holler
description:
Hell Up Coal Holler is a C Major reel associated with West Virginia and southwest Virginia. Versions were recorded by Gerry Milnes and Ed Haley. It appears in Phillips (1994).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Henry King's Reel
description:
"Henry King's Reel" is a fiddle tune written by Trevor Stuart of Haywood County, North Carolina. It is a modern old-time composition — not an ancient anonymous traditional tune — but it has been embraced widely across the old-time music community.

The tune's origin story comes directly from Trevor Stuart himself. He composed it and named it after their great-grandfather, Henry King, born 1856, who was a fiddler, Methodist preacher, mortician, and barber among other things. His grandmother, Myrtle King Stuart, told him many stories about Henry King — including how he'd cut every dead man's hair in Sandy Mush. The stories about Henry King staying up all night and playing for dances inspired Trevor to play fiddle, and as soon as he had a few tunes, he'd play for her and watch the excitement in her eyes.

This is a rare case in old-time music where we know exactly who composed a tune, who it was named for, and why — a deeply personal tribute connecting generations.

Trevor and Travis Stuart learned to play old-time mountain music from members of their community in Haywood County, North Carolina and surrounding counties, including Byard Ray, the Smathers Family, and North Carolina Folk Heritage Award recipient Red Wilson. Trevor passed away in 2016. Travis Stuart is available to play for concerts, festivals, dances, and to teach workshops.

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: Henry Reed's Breakdown
description:
Henry Reed's Breakdown is an A Major reel from the repertoire of Henry Reed (1884-1968) of Giles County, Virginia. Reed was recorded by Alan Jabbour for the Library of Congress in 1967.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Highlander's Farewell
description: Highlander's Farewell is a reel from Galax, Virginia fiddler Emmett Lundy (1864–1953), recorded by Alan and Elizabeth Lomax in 1941. Lundy attributed the tune to his mentor, Green Leonard (1810–1892). The tune is known for a two-voice structure which Lundy described as representing a Highlander and his sweetheart.

title: High Yellow
description:
High Yellow is a C Major breakdown sourced to Henry Reed of southwest Virginia. According to Alan Jabbour, Reed learned the tune from a fiddler identified variously as Mr. Hites, a musician from Texas, or someone from West Virginia. It appears in Phillips (1994) and was recorded by The Red Clay Ramblers (1977).

The tune is sourced to Glen Lynn, southwest Virginia, fiddler Henry Reed (1884-1968), who was visited by folklorist Alan Jabbour in 1966-67 and who collected a wealth of tunes and lore from him.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Hob Dye
description:
Hob Dye is often associated with lore involving a Texas bootlegger of the same name. Other theories suggest a connection to trade terms or alternate title spellings.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Hogeyed Man
description:
Hog-Eyed Man is a tune with origins linked to maritime and American work songs, possibly dating to the mid-19th century. Folklorist Stan Hugill traced its use as a capstan shanty.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Hog Trough Reel (McMichen's)
description:
"Hog Trough Reel" was recorded for Gennett Records by Clayton McMichen's Georgia Wildcats in New York City in August 1932, and released on several subsidiary labels such as Crown, Melotone, Varsity, Beacon, and others. The composition is credited to McMichen, and was also recorded by Pat O'Daniel and The Hillbilly Boys, a Texas string band who recorded for Vocalion in the late 1930s.

The political trail of this tune is notable: In 1938, O'Daniel became a candidate for Governor of Texas and used the band in his campaign stumps. He was elected to that office, and later served as Senator from the state. Each of the band members received patronage jobs after his election, and O'Daniel kept them around to broadcast music from the steps of the Governor's mansion as they helped remind the public of his populist roots.

Clayton McMichen (January 26, 1900 – January 4, 1970) was an American fiddler and country musician. Born in Allatoona, Georgia, he learned to play the fiddle from his father and uncle. He moved to Atlanta with his family in 1913, working as an automobile mechanic. While there, he entered and won several competitions for fiddle.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Hollow Poplar 1
description:
Hollow Poplar is a G Major breakdown popularized by Arthur Smith, who performed it on the Grand Ole Opry. It was recorded by Smith in the late 1950s.

Smith was born in 1898 in Humphreys County, east Tennessee, and died in 1971.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Hollow Poplar 2
description: Hollow Poplar 2 is a reel in the key of C from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Home Town Band
description:
Home Town Band is a G Major American march documented by Samuel Bayard in southwestern Pennsylvania. Bayard identified the tune as a distinct American composition.

The tune was "universally known to Pennsylvania fifers and some fiddlers," according to scholar Samuel Bayard (1981), who was not able to trace it back to British Isles antecedents — meaning it appears to be a distinctly American composition, likely originating in the Pennsylvania tradition rather than being transplanted from older European sources.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Hooker's Hornpipe
description:
Hooker's Hornpipe is a G Major tune collected from Bob Walters (Nebraska) and Taylor McBaine (Missouri). It appears in R.P. Christeson (1973) and Phillips (1995).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Hop High Ladies
description:
'Hop High Ladies' is the American old-time descendant of 'Miss McLeod's Reel,' a Scottish reel that dates to the early 19th century or earlier. The primary melodic difference between the two is telling: the Scottish original ends phrases on the dominant (a harmonically open, questioning gesture), while the American version resolves to the tonic (settled, complete). This subtle shift transforms the feel of the tune from one of anticipation to one of satisfaction — fitting, perhaps, for the communal American dance tradition that adapted it. The tune's famous command — 'Hop high ladies, step lively too / Hop high ladies, the cake's all through' — connects it to the cakewalk tradition of Southern community dances, where the best dancers won a prize. Early recordings include versions by New England fiddlers, Appalachian string bands, and Midwestern dance orchestras, showing how thoroughly the tune permeated American folk music culture.

Included in Viola "Mom's *Pioneer Western Folk Tunes* (1948).

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: Hopping Rabbit (Saut du Lapin)
description:
Saut du Lapin is a French-Canadian reel from the Québécois fiddle tradition. This version is traced to violinist Joseph Bouchard (1905–1980) and transmitted via Philippe Bruneau.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: The Horny Ewe
description:
The Horny Ewe is a composition by West Virginia fiddler Ernie Carpenter. It is included in The Gettysburg Collection of Old-Time Fiddle Tunes by John S. Lamancusa.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Huckleberry Blues
description:
Dykes Magic City Trio

Recordings include Old Homestead OHCS 191, "Dykes Magic City Trio" (eastern Tennessee) {originally recorded for Brunswick, 1927}.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Huntin' for the Buffalo
description:
Hunting for the Buffalo is an American reel rooted in Arkansas. Musician Jimmy Driftwood is the primary source, having learned it from his uncles.

Mike Seeger plays a version learned from singer, songwriter, and fiddler Jimmy Driftwood (1907–1998, born John Morris of Timbo, Arkansas), who had the tune from his two fiddler uncles who lived in Indian Territory for years.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Hut In The Bog
description:
Hut in the Bog is an Irish reel.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Iberia Breakdown
description:
Iberia Breakdown is a tune collected by R.P. Christeson from African-American fiddler Bill Driver (1881-1986) of Iberia, Missouri. The title was supplied by Christeson.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Icy Mountain
description:
Icy Mountain is a D Mixolydian breakdown collected from Ward Jarvis (b. 1894) of Braxton County, West Virginia, who learned it from Frank Santy. It appears in Milliner & Koken (2011).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: I Don't Love Nobody
description:
I Don't Love Nobody is a popular American country rag recorded by numerous fiddlers including Gid Tanner and Earl Johnson in the 1920s. It was also documented in the Ozarks by Vance Randolph.

Charles Wolfe (1983) remarks that it was issued by no less than six labels in the early 1930's, and prior to that it was recorded by Georgia fiddler Gid Tanner (1924), Earl Johnson (1927), and the Dixie String Band (1924). “Red” Steely on fiddle and Red Graham on banjo), resulted in the song being released as “Fatal Wedding.” The tune was recorded for the Library of Congress by musicologist/folklorist Vance Randolph from Ozarks Mountains fiddlers in the early 1940's, and 20th century Ozarks fiddler Art Galbraith noted that he heard many fiddlers play the tune1.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Illinois Rickett's Hornpipe
description:
The specific "Illinois Rickett's Hornpipe" variant traces directly to a single fiddler and a single place. "Illinois Rickett's Hornpipe" is from Dick Reid of Clayville, Illinois. It was collected and documented by the old-time band Volo Bogtrotters, whose members were active in gathering tunes from older Illinois fiddlers. Members of the band and their friend Garry Harrison were active in collecting tunes from older fiddlers in Illinois, and that collecting was an important source for the tunes they played. The Illinois prefix in the tune's name signals what old-time collectors call a local variant — a well-traveled tune that picked up distinct regional character in central Illinois.

The Ricketts being referred to in the title was a circus promoter, one John Bill Ricketts, a Scots immigrant who came from England in 1792 and flourished in America through the 1790s till about 1800, when his Philadelphia enterprise was destroyed in a fire on Dec. 17, 1799. He delighted his audiences by dancing hornpipes on the backs of galloping horses.

He reportedly also hired another famous American hornpipe dancer, John Durang, to produce pantomimes for him. Alan Jabbour (in American Fiddle Tunes) says that circuses under his name appeared in New York City, Philadelphia, Norfolk, Charlestown, Albany, Boston, Hartford, and Montreal.

Both Ricketts and Durang had hornpipes named for them that have endured in American tradition, in both the North and the South, right up through the twentieth century.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: I Love My Wife As Well As Anybody...
I'm Gonna Have My Mustache Blacked When I Get There
description: I'm Gonna Have My Mustache Blacked When I Get There is a tune of West Virginia origin, documented in the Milliner-Koken collection. It is attributed to Taylor Kimbell.

title: Indian Corn
description:
Indian Corn is a tune sourced to Willie O. Ault of Hidalgo, Illinois, recorded by Garry Harrison. It was formerly misidentified as Ol' Woodward's Tune.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Indian Ate the Woodchuck
description:
(Redirected from Indian Ate the Woodchuck)

Back to Indian Ate the Woodchuck (1)

AAAA'BB (Phillips): AABCC (Titon). Jeff Titon (2001) gives its provenance as eastern Kentucky and explains the confusion of titles between the substitution of 'eat' and 'ate' and 'woodchuck', 'woodpecker', 'woodcock' and 'woodhen'. The melody was in the repertoire of Kentucky fiddlers John Salyer (1882-1952), Estill Bingham (1899-1990), Owen "Snake" Chapman, and bluegrass fiddler Kenny Baker (who called it "Indian Killed a Woodcock"). Baker's tune is similar to the tune J.P. Fraley of Rush, Kentucky, plays idiosyncratically called, "Sail away Ladies (4)" (not the tune usually known by that title, and one he obtained from Ed Hayley (1883-1951), who did call it by the "Indian" title--see "Indian Ate the Woodchuck (2)"). Titon seems to think that the Baker/Fraley tune is distanced from the Hayley and Salyer versions, however, and he points out that "Indian Ate the Woodchuck" (and variants) is something of a floating title, noting the similarity, for example to the unrelated "Indian and the Woodhen." Salyer's version is a two-part one that is not as "busy" or 'notey' as Haley's tune. The title appears in a list of traditional Ozarks Mountains fiddle tunes compiled by musicologist/folklorist Vance Randolph, published in 1954. African-American fiddler Frank Patterson recorded the tune under the title "Indian and the Woodchuck" for the Library of Congress around 1942.

Notation sources: John Salyer (recorded 1940-41, Salyersville, Magoffin County, Ky.) [Milliner & Koken, Phillips]; Ed Hayley (Ashland, Boyd County, Ky.) [Titon]; Mark Gaponoff [Silberberg].

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Indians Over the Hill
description:
Indians Over the Hill is a D Major breakdown sourced to John Scotland Hannah (1920-?), a West Virginia fiddler. It appears in the Milliner-Koken Collection (2011).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Indian War Whoop
description:
Indian War Whoop is a Mississippi River region title first appearing in print in Knauff's Virginia Reels (1839). It is associated with Mississippi fiddler Floyd Ming.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Irish Hornpipe
description:
American(?), Hornpipe. Despite the title, the tune does not sound characteristically Irish to my ears, but rather more like the standard 19th century British or American stage hornpipes typical in the Elias Howe publications. It may have been assigned an Irish provenance due to its printing in Patrick O'Flannagan's Hibernia Collection (1860), another of Boston publisher Howe's volumes. Cape Breton fiddler Angus Chisholm recorded the hornpipe in the mid-20th century, pairing it with two of Dan R. MacDonald's compositions, "Miss Marguerite MacNeill" and "Miss Joan MacDonald]]."

"Irish Hornpipe" is on Missouri fiddler Charlie Walden's list of '100 essential Missouri fiddle tunes'. There are similarities in the first strain with the Irish reel "Hand Me Down the Tackle," but perhaps not enough to establish a cognate relationship.

A genericly titled "Irish Hornpipe" was recorded by Joseph Samuels for Edison Records (50900 {78 RPM}) in 1920 (appears as one of tunes of "Miss Johnson's Party Melody").

Published in Cole (1000 Fiddle Tunes), 1940; p. 103. O'Flannagan (The Hibernia Collection), 1860; p. 11. Ryan's Mammoth Collection, 1883; p. 139.
