Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Irish Polka
description:
The polka is of Bohemian origin, Included in the 1840s. It was introduced to New York in 1843 and subsequently influenced Irish traditional music.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Irish Reel
description:
"Irish Reel" is both a genre label and a specific tune title found in the old-time fiddle canon. Fiddle tunes are primarily instrumental melodies, most of which originated for dancing. The terms reel and jig refer both to the type of dance and to the type of tune played to accompany the dance.

Importantly, reels originated in Scotland and were introduced to Ireland in the late 18th century. So the genre itself has a Scottish root that was adopted and transformed into a distinctly Irish tradition before crossing the Atlantic.

The origins of the Scots-Irish lie primarily in the Lowlands of Scotland and in northern England. They were relocated to Ireland's northern province of Ulster starting in 1606, primarily to strengthen royal control over the North of Ireland. Most of the Scots-Irish emigrants settled initially in Pennsylvania. From there, many followed the Great Wagon Road to make their homes in the Appalachian Mountains — Virginia, Tennessee, Kentucky, and the Carolinas.

Once in Appalachia, much of the work on the American frontier — barn raising, molasses making, corn husking, and apple peeling — was done communally. At the end of the workday, people danced the old Scottish and Irish reels and jigs, with the music provided by a fiddle or fiddles.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Jake's Best Reel
description:
Jake's Best Reel is a D Major tune documented by R.P. Christeson (1984) and recorded by Cyril Stinnett and Dwight Lamb. It is a version of Old Jake Gillie.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Jake's Got A Bellyache
description: Jake's Got the Bellyache is an American reel from West Virginia fiddler Edden Hammons, recorded in 1947.

title: JayBird
description:
Jaybird is a breakdown with roots in the British Morris and Sword Dance tradition, documented in Pennsylvania and Indiana. Folklorist Samuel Bayard identified it as a derivative of The Ladies Breast Knot.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Jaybird Died of the Whooping Cough
description:
Jaybird Died of the Whooping Cough,

Squirrel died of the colic;

'Long come a red bird sittin' on a fence,

Call all the young girls to frolic.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Jefferson City
description:
A Missouri breakdown in G Major, associated with African-American fiddler Bill Caton (born 19th century, Tebbetts, Callaway County, Missouri). The tune appears as an unnamed hornpipe in R.P. Christeson's Old-Time Fiddler's Repertory, vol. 1 (1973). Howard Marshall, who notes Caton spelled his name both "Caton" and "Katon," records the tune is a square dance piece requiring specific, rarely heard bowing techniques. The tune is considered essential by Missouri fiddler Charlie Walden.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Jeff Davis
description:
An American reel in C Major, associated with the repertoire of Bert Layne of the Skillet Lickers and Blaine Smith of Flat Top, Tennessee. Smith was recorded in 1977 for Pine Breeze 003.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Jeff Davis County Reel
description:
A C Major reel transcribed in John S. Lamancusa's The Gettysburg Collection of Old-Time Fiddle Tunes, attributed to fiddler Casey Driscoll. The title is associated with Jefferson Davis, a common naming convention for post-Civil War tunes. A related tune, also called "Jeff Davis," comes from Blaine Smith (recorded 1977).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Jenny Comb Your Hair
description:
An A Minor reel from Missouri, sourced to fiddler Cyril Stinnett (1912-1986). It was published in R.P. Christeson's Old Time Fiddlers Repertory, vol. 2 (1984).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Jenny Get Around
description:
An A Major breakdown from Kentucky, played in AEae tuning. Jeff Titon (2001) notes its relationship to the "Liza Jane" and "Sugar Hill" tune families. It was collected by John and Alan Lomax in 1941. A notable version was recorded by John M. Salyer (1882-1952).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Jenny In The Cotton Patch
description:
A Kentucky and Tennessee fiddle tune with a lineage traced to Will Phipps (born 1812, Rock Creek, Tennessee) and later to Clyde Davenport, who learned it from his father, Will Davenport.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Jenny Run Away in the Mud in the Night
description: A tune associated with North Carolina fiddler Marcus Martin (1881–1974), who was recorded by the Library of Congress. Martin, a lifelong musician in western North Carolina, was known for his cross-tuned fiddle style.

title: Jimmy Johnson
description:
An A Major reel in cut time, associated with West Virginia fiddlers Melvin Wine and Ernie Carpenter. It was also recorded by Glen Smith (Galax, Va.).

It was in the repertory of W.Va. fiddlers Melvin Wine (1909-2003) and Ernie Carpenter (1909-1997, who learned it from his father Shelt Carpenter).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Jimmy Shank
description:
A Southern Kentucky/Tennessee reel in A Major, played in AEae tuning. It is in the repertoire of fiddler Bruce Greene, who learned it from a field recording of Sam Dyer.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: John Brown's March
description:
A G Major march or old-time tune documented in various collections including The Portland Collection and the Milliner-Koken Collection.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Johnny Cope
description:
JOHNNY COPE (Seanin Ua Copa). AB (Bayard): AABB (Johnson/2003, Miller & Perron, O'Neill/1850, Perlman, Doyle, Roche, Winstock): AABBCC (Gunn): AABBCCDD (Aird, Gatherer, O'Farrell): AABB'CCDDEEFFAABB' (Johnson): AABBCCDDEEFFGGHH (Howe). The tune is still played by Scottish regiments as their reveille. It is a satirical melody which commemorates the 1745 Jacobite rebellion when Sir John Cope (d. 1760) and the English were defeated by the Scots under Bonnie Prince Charlie at the Battle of Prestonpans, on the 22nd of September, 1745. In 1745, when Prince Charles landed in the highlands, Sir John was commander in chief in Scotland and he bravely resolved to march into the Highlands to oppose him. Cope was ill-prepared and outnumbered however, and soon retreated in the face of opposition in order to regroup. The rebels meanwhile secured Edinburgh and when they learned that Cope was marching to the city's relief they marched to meet him. Both armies neared each other at Prestonpans late in the day, separated by marshy ground, and it was resolved to wait until the next day to begin hostilities.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Johnny Don't Get Drunk
description:
A D Major reel documented throughout the USA, including Kentucky, Virginia, Missouri, and Nebraska. Missouri fiddler Charlie Walden includes it in his list of essential tunes. Scholars such as Jeff Titon suggest a possible derivation from a temperance song or the Irish reel "Miss Monaghan."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Johnny Don't Come Home Drunk
description:
A D Major reel documented in Missouri, Kentucky, Virginia, and Nebraska. Sources include Bob Walters (1954) and Owen "Snake" Chapman (1990). Jeff Titon suggests a link to temperance songs.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: John Rawl Jamieson
description:
A G Major breakdown from northeastern Kentucky, sourced to fiddler Buddy Thomas (1934-1974). Thomas stated the tune was named for an elderly man living on a ridge.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: John Short's Tune
description:
A D Major polka. Fiddler 'Chirps' Smith collected the tune from Erwin Thompson (1915-2015) of Illinois. It is possibly sourced to Illinois fiddler John W. Short (1839-1927).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Johnson Gal
description:
A G Major reel documented in Arkansas and Mississippi. It was included in a 1954 list of Ozark fiddle tunes by Vance Randolph and was also in the repertoire of Archibald Alexander Shaw of Harnett County, North Carolina.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Joke on the Puppy
description:
An old-time breakdown typically played in ADae tuning. Often identified with "Rye Straw," it was published in 1876 by George H. Coes as "Whoop from Arkansas" and by W.H. Morris (1927) as "Acrobat."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Julianne Flanigan
description:
A tune recorded by North Georgia fiddler Lowe Stokes in 1928 for a skit titled "Barn Dance on the Mountain, Part 2."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: JulieAnn Johnson
description: A D Major reel sourced to Grayson County, Virginia fiddler Emmett Lundy (1864–1953). It was recorded in 1941 by Alan and Elizabeth Lomax (AFS 4940-A4). Lundy attributed it to his mentor, Greenberry Leonard.

title: Jump Fingers
description:
A C Major breakdown associated with Nebraska and Missouri fiddlers. It was popularized by Bob Walters, who learned it from George "Jeffie" Pounds.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Jump Jim Crow
description:
A D Major reel associated with blackface minstrelsy, specifically the "Jim Crow" song and character. The tune was documented in the Ozarks by Vance Randolph (1954). The origins are attributed to John 'Picayune' Butler.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Kanawha March
description:
A D Major march recorded in the late 1920s by Kanawha County, West Virginia fiddler Clark Kessinger.

A local West Virginia tune recorded for the Brunswick label by Kanawha County fiddler Clark Kessinger (1896-1975) in the late 1920's.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Katie Bar the Door
description:
An old-time breakdown in D or C Major, sourced from the banjo playing of Roscoe Parrish (1897-1984) of Galax, Virginia.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Katy Did
description:
AAB (Silberberg): AABB (Brody, Reiner & Anick): AA'BB' (Phillips). A tune by this name was mentioned in reports (1926-31) of the De Kalb County (northeast Alabama) Annual (Fiddlers') Convention (Cauthen, 1990). In the 'B' part the 'E' chord played during the accompaniment may be either major or minor. North Georgia fiddler Lowe Stokes recorded the tune in this third session, in 1929, with guitarist Mike Whitten. Stokes' "Katy Did" was backed with "Take Me Back to Georgia," and some confusion of titles existed because many labels were reversed on the 78 RPM record; thus some fiddlers called "Katy Did" by the name "Take Me Back to Georgia"; furthermore, both tunes are in the key of 'C' major. However "Take Me Back to Georgia" is instead related to "Boston Boy"/"Ladies in the Ballroom (2)"/"Rattlesnake Bit the Baby." Fiddlin' John Carson used the minor mode second strain of "Katy Did [1}" as part of his recording of "Billy in the Lowground (1)." Compare also Stokes 1929 "Katy Did" with the western North Carolina "Grey Eagle (6)." The Hometown Boys. Lowe Stokes is on right, with guitar

Notation sources: Lowe Stokes (north Ga.) [Brody, Stecher/Fiddler Mag, Milliner & Koken, Phillips]; Howie Meltzer [Silberberg].

Published in Brody (Fiddler's Fakebook), 1983; p. 154. Larsen (Fiddler Magazine), vol. 25, No. 3, Fall 2018; p. 32. Milliner & Koken (Milliner-Koken Collection of Ameriand Fiddle Tunes), 2011; p. 356. Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes), 1994; p. 130. Reiner & Anick (Old Time Fiddling Across America), 1989; p. 112. Silberberg (Tunes I Learned at Tractor Tavern), 2002; p. 82.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Kelton Cotillion
description: Kelton Cotillion is a reel in the key of D from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Kennedy Rag
description:
An F Major country rag composed by Alabama fiddler Charlie Stripling (1896-1966), named after the town of Kennedy, Alabama. It was recorded by the Stripling Brothers in 1929.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Kentucky Whiskey
description:
AEae tuning (fiddle). The name Kentucky is derived from the Iroquois phrase kenta ke, meaning 'grass land' (Matthews, 1972).

Recordings include Front Hall Records FHR-037, Mark Graham - "Natural Selections" (1987). Rounder CD0403, The Freight Hoppers - "Where'd You Come From, Where'd You Go?"

Back to Kentucky Whiskey

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Kickin' Up the Devil on a Holiday
description:
An American reel in D Mixolydian, published by Thomas F. Briggs in 1855. Its original title, "Kick Up Dee Debbel on a Holiday," indicates its roots in the mid-19th-century blackface minstrel stage.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Kiowa Special
description:
Kiowa refers to the name of a Native American Indian tribe, currently settled in southwestern Oklahoma. Oklahoma fiddler Earl Collins (whose family was from Arkansas) is generally considered the core source for the tune.

Notation sources: Howie Meltzer [Silberberg].

Published in Silberberg (Tunes I Learned at Tractor Tavern), 2002; p. 83.

Back to Kiowa Special

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: L&N Rag
description:
A C Major country rag recorded in 1930 by Alex Hood and the Railroad Boys in Corbin, Kentucky, an L&N Railroad hub.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Lacy Brown
description:
An A Major breakdown in AEae tuning, associated with Kentucky fiddler John Morgan Salyer (1882–1952). Recorded in 1942, it is documented in Jeff Titon's Old-Time Kentucky Fiddle Tunes (2001). Scholars note a melodic relation to "Grey Eagle."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Ladies on the Steamboat
description:
An old-time breakdown in G Major, credited to Burnett & Rutherford, who recorded it in 1927. Dick Burnett likely learned it from Eastern Kentucky fiddler Ed Haley.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Lady of the Lake 1
description:
A widely used title for multiple distinct fiddle tunes. This G-Major version is likely the most common. The title is associated with Sir Walter Scott's 1810 poem. It appeared in the 19th-century manuscripts of Irish piper James Goodman and later in collections by Elias Howe.

Goodman (1828–1896) was an uilleann piper and Irish-language speaker who collected locally in County Cork and elsewhere in Munster, and also obtained tunes from manuscripts and printed collections.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Lady of the Lake 2
description:
Part of a family of at least nine distinct tunes sharing the "Lady of the Lake" title. This numbering system is used in academic collections such as those by Phillips and Milliner-Koken to distinguish various reels, jigs, and hornpipes that share the name, often linked to the 1810 Sir Walter Scott poem.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Lady of the Lake 3
description:
One of nine distinct tunes titled "Lady of the Lake" in the Fiddler's Companion. The title's prevalence is often linked to the popularity of Sir Walter Scott's 1810 narrative poem on the American frontier.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Lady of the Lake 4
description:
A version associated with the New England contra dance scene. Researcher Gary Stanton identified its source as two unnamed schottische and polka renderings recorded by Glen Lyn, Virginia fiddler Henry Reed.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Lady of the Lake 5
description: An American reel in G Major, associated with New England contra dancing. Researcher Gary Stanton traced it to two unnamed recordings of fiddler Henry Reed.

title: Lady On The Green
description:
An A Major breakdown from Nebraska, sourced to Bob Walters (c. 1950). The tune is a version of "Hell on the Wabash," published in 1862, suggesting a migration from military fife-and-drum tradition to civilian fiddling.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Lafayette
description: A D Major reel popularized by Tennessee fiddler Kirk McGee, who recorded it in 1968 for Folkways. McGee described it as an old Civil War tune.

title: Lantern In The Ditch
description:
Missouri fiddler John Jones composed this D major reel in the late 1920s. According to Jones's daughter Leana Hughes, the title commemorates an incident where she and her brother Casey dropped their lantern into a ditch while walking home from a dance, forcing them to finish the journey in the dark. The tune is associated with the fiddling traditions of Iowa, Missouri, and Nebraska.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: The Last of Callahan
description:
"Last of Callahan" is a D major reel found throughout Appalachia and the South. In Patrick County, Virginia, it is regarded as an older, pre-string-band style piece. Folklorist Bobby Fulcher describes it as an archaic tune characterized by cross-tuning and complex bowing. The tune is associated with a common American folk legend about a condemned outlaw who requested to play his fiddle on his own coffin before his execution.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: The Last Of Harris
description:
"Last of Harris" is primarily associated with Kentucky fiddler John M. Salyer (1882–1952), whose 1941–42 home recordings are the earliest documentation. It is an American reel in G major, typically played in standard tuning, though some older Kentucky fiddlers played it in CGDA. While some observers have noted melodic similarities to Doc Roberts' "I've Got a Gal Named Susie," the two are distinct pieces.

The tune is known from a 1941–42 home recording made by his sons Glen & Grover Salyer, documented in the Berea College Appalachian Center collection (AC 003), released as John Salyer: Home Recordings 1941–42 (1993).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: The Last of Sizemore
description:
Hiram Stamper (1893–1992) of Knott County, Kentucky, is the primary source for this mournful, modal tune. Stamper told folklorist Jeff Titon that the title refers to a soldier named Sizemore killed during or after the Civil War. It is considered a example of the Eastern Kentucky fiddle tradition.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Laughing Boy
description:
A cornerstone of the Texas contest fiddling style, "Laughing Boy" is closely associated with Benny Thomasson (1909–1984), who recorded it in AEAc# tuning. While John Hartford noted that Texas Shorty (Jim Chancellor) believed Thomasson composed it, definitive evidence is lacking. The tune gained widespread popularity following a 1968 recording by Kenny Baker.

He recorded it multiple times: County 703, Texas Hoedown (1965); County 724, Texas Fiddler (2005); and Voyager VRCD 345, "Say Old Man Can You Play the Fiddle?" (1999).

title: Laughing Marge
description:
"Laughing Marge" is a modern composition by New Mexico musician Tom Adler, named after his wife. The tune has entered the old-time canon through transmission at festivals and jam sessions.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Lazy Kate
description:
"Lazy Kate" refers to several regional variants. It appears in Vance Randolph’s 1954 Ozark collection and is included in R.P. Christeson's "Old-Time Fiddlers Repertory." The tune was recorded by the Mississippi band the Leake County Revelers in 1930 for Columbia Records.

Here's the full picture: Origin: The tune was described in Adams' book as a typical Ozark Mountain tune of about 1840.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Lead Out
description: Lead Out is a reel in the key of D from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Lightning Hornpipe
description: Lightning Hornpipe is a reel in the key of Bbb from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Lily of the Valley
description:
"Lily of the Valley" is a D major reel associated with Galax, Virginia, fiddler Luther Davis (1887–1986). It is documented in the 1986 booklet "The Old-Time Way," which profiles Davis alongside Roscoe and Leone Parish.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Litchfield
description: Litchfield is a reel in the key of C from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Little Billy Wilson
description:
"Little Billy Wilson" is an A major reel derived from Texas fiddler Eck Robertson's 1929 "Brilliancy" medley. A common three-part version was later synthesized by fiddler Joel Shimberg, incorporating elements from Robertson and Alabama fiddler Bill Owens. It is also linked to the 1926 recording by Uncle Jimmy Thompson.

The tune derives from the playing of fiddler Eck Robertson (1887–1975, Amarillo, Texas), recorded using AEae tuning. His recording was made in Dallas, Texas on October 11, 1929, as part of the "Brilliancy" medley, and the side was issued in 1930 on Victor V40298.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Little Black Mustache
description:
"Little Black Mustache" is a reel associated with Mississippi fiddler Gene Clardy, who recorded the tune with Stan Clements in 1930. Clardy was a mentor to Willie Narmour. According to local lore, Clardy was murdered in the 1930s while refusing a request to continue playing at a dance.

Key recorded sources include: County 3514 — Gene Clardy & Stan Clements, Mississippi Fiddle Bands, Vol. 2 Document 8028 — Gene Clardy, Mississippi String Bands, Vol. 2 Musical Traditions MT 104 — The Nations Brothers (Mississippi), "Where the Southern Crosses the Dog: Mississippi Fiddle Music 1928–35" Harry Bolick recorded the tune, releasing it as part of his album "Carroll County, Mississippi" (2004).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Little Dutch Girl
description:
This reel is associated with the Collins family of Missouri and Oklahoma. The Thede collection attributes the origin to Dutchtown, Missouri, though this is speculative. It is also known as "Goin' Down the River," and Thede collected lyrics associated with the piece.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Little Hornpipe
description:
Collected by Samuel Bayard from Sarah Armstrong of Derry, Pennsylvania, in 1943. Bayard noted stylistic links to "Durang's Hornpipe" and observed that the second strain was particularly unstable in regional versions.

Almost any popular collection of country dances contains a version of 'Durangs;' a good set is in Ford, p. 53; another is in Adam, No. 19" (Bayard, 1944).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Little Pine Siskin
description:
"Little Pine Siskin" is a contemporary composition by British Columbia-based mandolinist John Reischman, recorded on his 2013 album "Walk Along John."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Little Princess Footsteps
description:
This C major reel is associated with Mississippi fiddler Alvis Massengale and the Newton County Hillbillies, who recorded it in 1931. The original title may have been "Little Prince's Footsteps."

The source for the notated version comes from the playing of Mississippi fiddler Alvis Massengale (b. 1897) of the band the Newton County Hillbillies, whose members included Andrew Harrison on guitar and Marcus Harrison on mandolin.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Little Whiskey
description:
"Little Whiskey" is a Missouri reel associated with Nile Wilson, who learned it from his great-uncle Charlie Davis. The tune is considered a "tie-hacker" piece, brought to the Midwest by railroad workers.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Liverpool Hornpipe
description:
The "Liverpool Hornpipe" has been widely published in 19th-century collections and is documented in manuscripts from Irish pipers James Goodman and Stephen Grier. While some critics, such as Father Henebry, dismissed the tune as vapid, it maintained popularity among fiddlers in Ireland and North America.

"Liverpool Hornpipe" was entered into the mid-19th century music manuscript collection of County Cork uillean piper and Church of Ireland cleric James Goodman, and also entered into Book 3 of the large c. 1883 music manuscript collection of County Leitrim musician and piper Stephen Grier.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Log Chain
description: Log Chain is a reel in the key of D from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Loggieville Two Step
description:
"Loggieville Two-Step" was composed by New Brunswick fiddler Matilda Murdoch (1920–2019). The tune is named after her home village. The standard version today is based on a recording by Ivan Hicks with an added 'C' part by the Puslinch Fiddle Orchestra.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Lonesome Blues
description:
"Lonesome Blues" was recorded by the Leake County Revelers in 1929 for Columbia Records.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: The Long Way Home
description: The Long Way Home is a reel in the key of G from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Lost Everything
description: Lost Everything is a reel in the key of G from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Lost Girl
description:
"Lost Girl" is associated with the playing of Kentucky fiddlers John Salyer and Walter McNew. Jeff Titon suggests a possible origin in Virginia, noting that Emmett Lundy played a version. It is sometimes played in G or C major.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Louisiana Hornpipe
description: Louisiana Hornpipe is a reel in the key of C from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Lower Mill Creek
description: Lower Mill Creek is a reel in the key of C from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Lowery's Quadrille
description:
"Lowery's Quadrille" is associated with Indiana fiddler John Summers, who reportedly learned it from a fiddler named Lowery. It is often played at a moderate tempo to suit dance requirements.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: L'ville
description:
"L'ville," also known as "Snake Hunt (L'Ville)," is a modern old-time composition attributed to Fred Campeau. The title likely refers to Louisville, Kentucky.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Maggie Meade
description:
"Maggie Meade," also known as "Maggie Kneed," is associated with the playing of Kentucky fiddler J.P. Fraley.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Maggots in the Sheep Hide
description:
Collected by Samuel Bayard from Sarah Armstrong of Derry, Pennsylvania, in 1943. Bayard noted a unique three-note prelude played only at the start of the tune.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Magpie
description:
"Magpie" is associated with the North Carolina Piedmont fiddling tradition, collected from Harlan Coble and Lonnie Corsbie. It gained popularity during the 1970s old-time revival.

Collected by Eric Olson, Bobbie and Tommy Thompson in 1968, and even earlier by Alan Jabbour (1966, see Library of Congress AFS 13,036), from fiddle/banjo duo Harlan Coble and William Alonzo "Lonnie" Corsbie (Guilford County, north-central N.C.).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Marching Jaybird
description:
"Marching Jaybird," also known as "Walking Jaybird," was popularized by North Carolina musicians Etta Baker and Lacey Phillips. It is often cited as a banjo-based mirror of "Spanish Fandango."

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Marion Reece's Cumberland Gap
description:
William Marion Reece (1874–1939) was a fiddler, fife player, and blacksmith from Zionville, North Carolina. He was known in the Watauga County area for his command of older repertoire, including both standard and cross-tuned pieces.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Martha Campbell
description:
"Martha Campbell" is a known Kentucky reel, recorded by Doc Roberts in 1925. Music historians Charles Wolfe and Jeff Titon suggest the tune may have African-American origins, noting transmittal patterns from black fiddlers to white players in the early 20th century.

"Martha Campbell" was also recorded in the field by the Lomax's from the playing of white Virginia fiddler Emmett Lundy in 1941, when he was 80 years old.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Massa Bill
description:
"Massa Bill," or "Mossy Bill," was played by Missouri fiddler Frank Reed, who learned it from black fiddler Walt Dougherty. The tune is considered cognate with "Kansas City Rag."

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Mays Fork
description:
The web searches did not return any specific results about a fiddle tune called "Mays Fork" — neither its history, origin story, nor any associated fiddler.

"Mays Fork" is not a documented tune in major old-time music databases, discographies, or published collections available on the open web. This is actually quite common in old-time fiddling. "There is no outright way to get fiddle tune history perfect, because there is way more than one straight story for any given tune." For instance, all anyone knows about "Soldier's Joy" is that "a grandpa wrote it" — and whose grandpa exactly remains a mystery.

The titles of many old-time fiddle tunes "add a colorful and evocative dimension," conjuring up people and places that are part of the texture of Appalachian frontier culture. Mays Fork is the name of a real creek/community in Randolph County, West Virginia, which points to a possible West Virginia or central Appalachian origin.

The Appalachian old-time fiddle repertoire began with reels and jigs from the British Isles. Because tunes were generally played and passed on by ear rather than printed music, variations appeared — and sometimes the variations became so different from the original that they were essentially new tunes.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Merriweather
description:
Known as a Kentucky tune, although Bobby Fulcher (1986) says the tune only rarely shows up in traditional Kentucky fiddlers' repertoires. Most modern version are modeled after the "Meriwether" of W.L. "Jake" Phelps of Todd County, Kentucky, recorded in the field in 1973 by fiddler Bruce Greene. Phelps was not originally from the Appalachian part of the state but rather from Purchase, on the western side. Although no one knows for certain what the title refers to, it is likely it refers to the name of a prominent 19th century Todd County family named Meriwether (note spelling). Kentucky fiddler Clyde Davenport recorded the tune for County Records in 1986, although it is likely he learned the tune from Greene. Titon (2001) finds the tune related to the Irish reels "Tom Ward's Downfall" and "Mourne Mountains (1)," and opines that it is a "rare, appealing, and well-constructed tune."

Notation sources: Ky. fiddler Bruce Greene (who learned it from Phelps in 1973) [Phillips]; W.L. "Jake" Phelps (b. 1882, Elkton, Todd County, Ky., 1973) [Milliner & Koken, Titon].

Published in Clare Milliner & Walt Koken (The Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes), 2011; p. 415. Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 1), 1994; p. 151. Songer (Portland Collection), 1997; p. 133. Titon (Old-Time Kentucky Fiddle Tunes), 2001; No. 103, p. 132.

Recordings include Berea College Appalachian Center AC001, Bruce Green - "Celebration! Old Time Music at Berea." County 786, Clyde Davenport (Monticello, Ky.) - "Clydeoscope: Rare and Beautiful Tunes from the Cumberland Plateau" (1986. Probably learned from Bruce Green, says Titon).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Messenger
description: Messenger is a reel in the key of C from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Methodist Preacher
description:
"Methodist Preacher" is an American reel associated with the Kentucky tradition. While often attributed to Bill Monroe, the tune appears to predate him; Monroe likely adapted the tune from his uncle, Pendleton Vandiver.

The composition is sometimes credited to Kentucky mandolin player wikipedia:Bill Monroe (1911-1996), the 'Father of Bluegrass," however it would appear that it predates Monroe in the tradition (he is said to have learned it from his "Uncle Pen", Pendleton Vandiver).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Minnie Put The Kettle On
description: "Minnie Put the Kettle On" (also known as "Minnie Put the Skillet On") is an American Reel in D major, standard tuning, cut time. Its most documented source is Oklahoma fiddler Uncle Dick Hutchison (1897–1986), whose playing is featured in The Milliner-Koken Collection (2011). Hutchison’s version was recorded in the 1960s on the album "Old Time Fiddlin'." A distinct, three-part "crooked" version from Ozarks fiddler Ray Curbow appears on "Traditional Fiddle Music of the Ozarks, Vol. 2."

title: Mississippi Echoes
description:
"Mississippi Echoes" is a fiddle tune in C recorded by the Ray Brothers in 1930 (Document CD DOCD-8028). It appears in the Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes. The Ray Brothers were a Mississippi string band active in the late 1920s and 1930s. The tune's composer is undocumented, as is common for items in the regional string band repertoire.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: (Missouri) Spotted Pony
description:
A staple of the Missouri Ozarks, "Spotted Pony" gained prominence in the early 20th century, with folklorist Vance Randolph documenting it in his 1954 survey of regional tunes. Multiple distinct melodies circulate under this title across Missouri, Arkansas, and Texas, suggesting the name was applied to various tunes rather than a single source.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))
notes: Versions differ in their A parts and keys; check which setting your group plays.

title: Molly In The Window
description:
"Molly in the Window" is a modern composition by Riley, of the band The Onlies, named for banjo player Molly Tenenbaum after she was seen sitting in a window at the Festival of American Fiddle Tunes.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Molly Put the Kettle On
description:
"Molly Put the Kettle On" is a breakdown fiddle tune related to a British song and nursery rhyme dating to the 1790s. The associated melody, "Jenny's Baubie," was cited by John Glen in 1891 as appearing in Dale's Variations for the Pianoforte (1794). A publication titled "Molly Put the Kettle On or Jenny's Baubie" was issued by Joseph Dale in London in 1803; other editions appeared in Dublin and New York shortly thereafter.

It was also printed with "Polly" instead of "Molly" in Dublin about 1790–1810 and in New York around 1803–07.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Molly's Tune
description:
"Molly's Tune" is attributed to Kentucky fiddler Owen "Snake" Chapman (active until the 1990s). It is documented in the Tater Joe's Old-Time Fiddle resource. The tune has been recorded by various performers, including Jeff Norman on banjo in open aEADE tuning.

Chapman had a rich repertoire of old-time tunes, including pieces like "Chapman's Hornpipe," "Snake Chapman's Tune," "Coburn Fork of Big Creek," and others — and was an active performer well into the early 1990s, with a documented concert at Seedtime 1990.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Monkey In The Dog Cart
description: "Monkey on a Dogcart" is an American reel in C major, AA'BB form. Recorded by the Leake County Revelers in 1927 for Columbia, the tune was later documented in the field by Vance Randolph in the 1940s. The Leake County Revelers (Will Gilmer, Dallas Jones, R.O. Moseley, and Jim Wolverton) are considered the primary source for the title.

title: Moon Behind The Hill
description:
"Moon Behind the Hill" was popularized by West Virginia fiddler Melvin Wine (1909–2003). Wine learned the tune from an anonymous fiddler at a roadside dance hall while walking from Fairmont to Clarksburg, an account recorded by fiddler Erynn Marshall. The tune is included in the Milliner-Koken Collection.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Morgan on the Railroad
description:
"Morgan on the Railroad" is a breakdown/reel in D major associated with Madison County, Kentucky. Fiddler Buck Barnes (1902–1994) learned the tune from African-American fiddler Jim Booker, who played with Taylor's Kentucky Boys. John Masters also plays the melody as "Muddy Creek (2)," attributing it to Booker.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Mother's Reel
description:
"Mother's Reel" (also "Reel de mon maton" or "Reel du régiment") is a Canadian and New England reel. While often attributed to Don Messer, the tune was recorded in 1929 by Montreal fiddler Joseph Allard.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Mountain Hornpipe
description:
"Mountain Hornpipe" (also known as "Ice on the Pumphandle," "Mountains of Kerry," and "Old Skeddadalink") is a hornpipe/breakdown in G major. Folklorist Samuel Bayard noted versions in southwestern Pennsylvania; it appeared in Elias Howe's publications starting in 1851 and in O'Neill's Music of Ireland (1903) as No. 1745.

Folklorist Samuel Bayard (1981), who found several versions in the repertory of southwestern Pennsylvania fiddlers, considered it to be "at least a little older" than the 1840s or 1850s — and indeed it was published by Elias Howe in Boston as early as 1851, continuing in Howe's publications and their derivatives for roughly ninety years. The tune's Irish roots are reinforced by its appearance in one of the most important Irish tune collections: it was included in *O'Neill's Music of Ireland: 1850 Melodies (1903), as No. 1745.

title: Muddy Creek
description:
"Muddy Creek" is a "crooked" G reel in cut time, sourced from eastern Kentucky fiddler John Morgan Salyer (1882–1952) via a 1941 recording.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Muddy Creek (aka Morgan on the Railroad)
description: "Muddy Creek" and "Morgan on the Railroad " are versions of a tune learned from African-American fiddler Jim Booker by Jim Woodward and John Masters. "Morgan on the Railroad " was played by Jessamine County fiddler Jim Woodward (1909–1987).

title: Mud Fence
description: "Mud Fence" was in the repertoire of William H. Stepp (1875–1947), recorded by Alan and Elizabeth Lomax for the Library of Congress in 1937 (AFS 01600 B02). The tune is played in D with ADAE tuning. Fiddler J.P. Fraley (1924–2011) released a related version in 1973.

title: Nail that Catfish to the Tree
description:
Despite sounding like a very old tune passed down through generations, "Nail That Catfish to the Tree" was actually written by Steve Rosen. Rosen is a banjo player for the Volo Bogtrotters, and the tune was recorded on their self-titled album. Steve lives in Evanston, IL and, when not playing, teaches at The Old Town School of Folk Music in Chicago.

It is a modern composition, dating to approximately 1985, written by Volo Bogtrotters member Steve Rosen, who wrote the tune on a fishing vacation to Florida.

Of the curious title, Steve himself says: "I wrote this tune on a fishing vacation in Florida. Catfish are hard to clean because of their tough skin, and an old black man told me to 'nail its head to a tree and pull its skin off with pliers.'"

A more colorful version of the story also circulates: Steve was reportedly on the banks of the Mississippi River watching a fisherman haul out a huge channel catfish after a tremendous struggle. Steve exclaimed, "I wonder how you skin one of those monsters?" The fisherman, without missing a beat, replied, "There's only one way to skin a channel cat — you've got to nail that catfish to the tree." He then proceeded to describe slicing around the gills and using vice grips to pull the skin off from head to tail.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Nancy
description:
The "Nancy" title refers to multiple tunes. The most prominent version, often associated with Tom Clough of the Northumbrian piping tradition, is a variation of "My Love is but a Lassie Yet." West Virginia fiddler Wilson Douglas played a version called "Fair Mountain Hornpipe."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Nancy Blevins
description:
"Nancy Blevins" is named for a North Carolina fiddler (1852–1939). Virginia fiddler Albert Hash (1917–1983) is the primary popularizer of the tune, having learned it from Jim Reedy. Kilby Spencer recorded an account of the tune's origin from Hash.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Nancy Dalton
description:
"Nancy Dalton" is an old-time breakdown in D major, documented in the repertoire of Monroe County, Kentucky, fiddlers Jim Bowles, Isham Monday, and Pat Kingery. A recording by Jim Bowles appears on "Railroad Through the Rocky Mountains."

The tune was in the repertoire of Monroe County, south-central Kentucky, fiddler Jim Bowles (1903–1997), who learned it from local musicians. His recording of "Nancy Dalton" appears on Railroad Through the Rocky Mountains (Marimac Recordings, 1994).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Nancy Rollins
description:
"Nancy Rowland" (or "Nancy Rollins") is a traditional G major reel documented by folklorist Vance Randolph in his 1954 list of Ozarks fiddle tunes. It is mentioned in William Percival King's 1891 book "Stories of a Country Doctor."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Natchez Under the Hill
description:
"Natchez Under the Hill" refers to the historic waterfront district of Natchez, Mississippi. The tune was published in George P. Knauff's "Virginia Reels" (1839) as "Natchez on the Hill" and appeared in a Tennessee dialect story in 1845.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Natural Bridge Blues
description:
"Natural Bridge Blues" was composed by Tennessee fiddler Tommy Magness (1911–1972), who played with Bill Monroe, Roy Acuff, and Fiddlin' Arthur Smith. It sits at the crossroads of Old-Time, Bluegrass, and Country Blues traditions, and is associated with the USA/Missouri repertoire.

The tune is in A Major, played in standard fiddle tuning, and follows an AA'B form. It is built on a blues progression — making it an early example of the blues-influenced fiddle writing that was gaining popularity in the 1930s–40s.

The tune is named for Virginia's Natural Bridge, a limestone formation 215 ft. high and 90 ft. long — the remains of the roof of a cave or tunnel through which a creek once flowed. It was a sacred site for indigenous populations and was considered at one time to be one of the seven natural wonders of the world. Thomas Jefferson purchased the land surrounding the formation, calling it "the most Sublime of nature's works," and built a cabin there used by guests and visitors.

Magness first recorded the melody as a member of Roy Hall's Blue Ridge Entertainers. "Natural Bridge Blues" was recorded with the group in Atlanta, Georgia, and released on Bluebird Records. This was released as Bluebird B-8863 (78 RPM) by Roy Hall and His Blue Ridge Entertainers in 1941.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Ned Landry's Tune
description:
Ned Landry (1921–2018) was a Canadian fiddler and composer from Saint John, New Brunswick. He began his professional career on Don Messer's radio show in the 1930s.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Needle Case
description:
"Needle Case" is an American reel in D major associated with southwest Alabama. It was cited as a "popular old-time tune" in the May 9, 1929, issue of the Clarke County Democrat.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Never Mind the Weather When the Wind Don't Blow
description:
This tune is part of the "Miss McCloud's Reel" family, which has roots in the British Isles dating to at least 1779. It spread widely in American fiddle culture.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: New Broom
description:
"New Broom" is a traditional G major reel associated with Texas and Oklahoma. Fiddler Jim Bowles referred to it as "Democrats a-Rising."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: New Five Cent Piece (Buffalo Nickel)
description:
"New Five Cent Piece" (or "Buffalo Nickel") is an old-time breakdown in D major. Kentucky fiddler Isham Monday (1879–1964) is a key source, documented by Jeff Titon in 2001. The "Buffalo Nickel" title likely dates to the coin's 1913 release.

The definitive notated version from Monday was collected at Tompkinsville, Monroe County, Kentucky, in 1959 (published in Jeff Titon's Old-Time Kentucky Fiddle Tunes, 2001).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: New Jordan
description:
"New Jordan" is a traditional Appalachian reel typically played in D or A major, often carrying the sacred connotations associated with the biblical River Jordan in Southern folk tradition.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: The New Leaf
description: The New Leaf is a reel in the key of D from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: New Mexico Polka
description:
"New Mexico Polka" was learned by New Mexico fiddler Antonia Apodaca (1923–2020) from a fiddler named Costales in Wyoming. It was documented on the album "Tonie's Tunes."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: New Money
description:
"New Money" is a C major reel recorded by Kentucky fiddler Doc Roberts in 1927 (Gennett 6775). Roberts learned the tune from Elza Stone of Mt. Sterling, Kentucky.

"New Money" is an indigenous east-central Kentucky tune recorded by Doc Roberts (1897–1978).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Newt Payne's Tune
description:
Newt Payne (1904–1977) was a Tennessee fiddler from the South Pittsburg Mountain area who never recorded commercially.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Ninth of January
description:
"Ninth of January" is a Missouri square dance tune played by Bob Holt (1930–2004), who learned it from his father, who identified it as Charlie Deckard’s version of "The Eighth of January."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Nine Miles Out Of Louisville
description:
"Nine Miles Out Of Louisville" is an old-time G major breakdown sourced from northeastern Kentucky fiddler Buddy Thomas (active 1935–1974).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Nixon's Farewell
description:
"Nixon's Farewell" was composed on the occasion of President Nixon's resignation in the mid-1970s by Curtis (Curt) Bouterse of San Diego, California. Bouterse was a San Diegan and a prominent, important part of the San Diego Folk Festival scene.

Right after Nixon's resignation in 1974, Bouterse figured something that monumental ought to be noted in music. His initial reaction was that the situation resembled the old "Somebody on the Gallows" or "What'shisname's Farewell," and he played around with various lonesome and lone melodies without success. He then imagined a song with the refrain, "And you won't have Old Dick Nixon to kick around anymore," and eventually came up with the tune — occasionally singing "jig words": "Nixon's gone, Nixon's gone" to the ascending melodic run.

The tune is classified as an American Reel (cut time), in D Major, in standard fiddle tuning, with an AABB structure.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: None Of Your Business
description:
The primary source for the reel "None of Your Business" is Noah Beavers, a fiddler from Elkville, in southern Illinois, who was recorded in the field in 1979 when he was 81 years old. This makes Beavers the oldest known documented carrier of the tune, and it is strongly associated with the southern Illinois old-time tradition.

It is classified as an American Reel (cut time), in C Major, played in standard fiddle tuning, with an AABBC part structure — notably a 5-part tune, which is less common than the typical 2- or 3-part reels.

Known recordings and publications include: Lynn "Chirps" Smith – "Midwestern Harvest" (1994, Marimac 9059-CD) Noah Beavers – "Dear Old Illinois, CD 3" (2007, Pickaway Press) Foghorn Trio – "Sud de la Louisiane" (2010)

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: North Carolina Breakdown
description:
"North Carolina Breakdown" was composed by Tennessee's Fiddlin' Arthur Smith (1898–1971). Despite the tune's name pointing squarely at North Carolina, it is firmly a product of Tennessee. It is classified as an American Reel in the key of G Major, played in standard fiddle tuning.

Ernest Smith, Arthur's son, believes his father wrote "North Carolina Breakdown" around 1937, about the same time as "Smith's Breakdown." That places the tune's composition squarely in the late pre-WWII era, a fertile period for old-time string band recordings and radio broadcasts across the rural South.

Smith's recording of the tune was released by Nashville's Starday label in 1962 — meaning it circulated in the oral tradition for roughly 25 years before receiving an official commercial release.

The tune has a notable variant called "Tarheel Breakdown," and is also considered similar to — if not directly descended from — "Whistling Rufus." The connection to "Whistling Rufus" is significant: "Whistling Rufus" is explicitly listed as a related melody to "North Carolina Breakdown" in the Fiddler's Companion, suggesting Smith may have drawn on or reworked that earlier tune's melodic DNA.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Oak Ridge Stomp
description:
Tater Joe's Old-Time Fiddle catalog lists 'Oak Ridge Stomp' among its D-tuning tunes. The listing does not name a composer or source fiddler.

Source: John Lamancusa collection, oldtimefiddletunes.net.

title: Oh My Little Darling
description: "Oh My Little Darling" is an A major/mixolydian reel. It was recorded in 1939 for the Library of Congress by Thaddeus C. Willingham in Gulfport, Mississippi, and also recorded in 1939 from Charles Long of Clarke County, Mississippi.

title: Oklahoma News
description:
"Oklahoma News" is a traditional tune from Kansas fiddler Bert Payne, passed down by Howard Rains and Tricia Spencer.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Oklahoma Redbird
description:
Lyman Enloe (1906–1997) of Miller County, Missouri, is the primary source for this tune. It is listed among Missouri fiddler Charlie Walden’s 100 essential tunes. Although R.P. Christeson credits Enloe with the tune, versions exist that predate Enloe's 1976 recording.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Oklahoma Rooster
description:
An American reel in D major with an AA'BB' structure. It appears as the fourth change of the 'Ten Strike Quadrille' in 'Gems of the Ballroom' (c. 1890s), indicating it predates the title 'Oklahoma Rooster.' It was also in the repertoire of Disney, Oklahoma fiddler John 'Uncle Dick' Hutchison, who played it in C.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Abe
description:
A traditional old-time fiddle tune in A or D, typically in AABB form. While often associated with the Abraham Lincoln era due to its title, no specific composer is known. It circulates in Appalachian and Ozark traditions and appears in various regional tune books.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Aunt Jenny With Her Nightcap On
description:
An American reel in G major from the Appalachian tradition. It is best documented from the playing of Estill Bingham (1899–1990) of Pineville, Bell County, Kentucky, who learned the tune from his father, Noah.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Baldy Kickin' Up
description: Old Baldy Kickin' Up is a reel in the key of C from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Beech Leaves
description:
This breakdown was transmitted through a lineage starting with itinerant teacher James Wallace James to Sid Hudnall (1891–1984) of Logan County, Kentucky, and collected by Bruce Greene in 1975.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Billy Hell
description:
A 'slightly crooked' tune in G major with an AABB form, featuring metric irregularities between C| and 6/4. It is associated with Bell County, Kentucky fiddler Estill Bingham (1899–1990), who is the sole recorded source. Recordings include an 80s session by Bob Butler and a 1989 recording by Bruce Greene.

The known recording is attributed to Estill Bingham, captured in G major, standard GDAE tuning, around 1986 or 1987, recorded by Bob Butler, and preserved in the Digital Library of Appalachia.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Blackberry Blossom (Garfield's)
description:
Sometimes called 'Garfield's Blackberry Blossom' to distinguish it from the unrelated, later version by Arthur Smith. The tune is considered older than the bluegrass standard; the two melodies share little melodic resemblance.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: The Old Blue Tick
description:
An old-time breakdown in G or A major, typically following an AABB form. It was sourced from August Merrill of St. James, Missouri, and recorded in 1973 for the R.P. Christeson Collection.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Ol' Bob
description:
Associated with Gusty Wallace (1890–1985) of Metcalfe County, Kentucky. Recorded by Bruce Greene in 1975, the tune is noted for its irregular phrase lengths (ABCC' structure). A modern version was popularized via Garry Harrison’s 'Red Prairie Dawn.'

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Buzzard
description:
A three-part reel (AABB'C) in G major. It was recorded by Doc Roberts in 1927, who learned the tune from Madison County, Kentucky fiddler Owen Walker (born 1857).

The tune was recorded by Kentucky fiddler Doc Roberts (1897–1978) in 1927 in Richmond, Indiana, backed by African-American guitarist John Booker.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Catville Quadrille
description:
A 6/8 jig/quadrille. Musicologist Paul Gifford notes its relation to 'Whalen's Breakdown' and 'Bride of the Wind(s).' It was recorded by John A. Pattee, a Civil War veteran from New Boston, Michigan, a town once called 'Catville.'

Pattee was born June 5, 1844, in Huron, Wayne County, Michigan.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Cow Crossing the Road
description:
A Country Rag in C and F, attributed to Bert Edwards of Mount Airy, North Carolina. It is featured on his album 'Bert's Bambaree.'

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Cumberland
description:
Recorded by Jon Bekoff in 1990, composed by Pat Conte. The tune is related to the 'Cumberland Gap' family, a cluster of tunes with 19th-century origins debated by folklorists like Alan Jabbour and Mike Yates.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Flannigan
description:
Named for Brack Flannigan, a fiddler who moved from Texas to Kentucky. It was played by Frank Miller and Jarvie Hall and recorded by the Blue Ridge Mountaineers in 1929.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Grey Bonnet
description:
An old-time breakdown in G major. According to Samuel Bayard, it is of Scottish origin and related to the 'Marquis of Hastings' Strathspey' family.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Grimes
description:
A traditional instrumental in D major, likely generations old. It shares a name, though not a melody, with a poem by Albert Gorton Greene (1822). Recorded by Norman Blake and others.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Joe
description:
A American folk song. Joseph Clark (1839–1885) of Clay County, Kentucky, is often cited as the inspiration for the song, though his status as a local figure is well-documented in historical markers.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Ladies Pickin' Chickens
description:
An American reel in D and A major, primarily associated with Iowa fiddler Dwight 'Red' Lamb. It has been recorded by Lamb and by Bob Bovee and Gail Heil.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Man and Old Woman
description:
A reel of French-Canadian origin, originally a song air. It was popularized by a 1930 recording by Mary Travis ('La Bolduc').

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Melinda
description:
A breakdown (AABBCC) listed in the 'Christeson Old-Time Fiddler's Repertory' and recognized as a core Missouri tune. Early recordings include Bob Walters (1948) and Russell 'Casey' Jones.

The most well-known early recording is by fiddler Bob Walters, captured in the key of C (standard GDAE tuning) in 1948, later released on the Old Time Fiddlers' Repertory University of Missouri LP (1976). Nebraska fiddler Bob Walters (1889–1960) announced the tune as "Old Malindee" on his recording. Casey Jones (1910–1967), from northwest Missouri, also recorded the tune — it appears on his Missouri State Old Time Fiddlers' Association release "Rocky Road to Jordan.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Mose
description:
An American reel (C or G major) collected from Illinois fiddler Howard Sims (1896–1977). The tune was brought to the wider community by Garry Harrison and recorded for 'Dear Old Illinois.'

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Pards
description: Old Pards is a reel in the key of A from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Parnell Reel
description:
An alternate title for the tune 'Hotfoot' (or 'Hot Foot Rag'), a variant of 'I Don't Love Nobody' associated with Texas fiddler Benny Thomasson.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Piss
description:
Pisle, a Civil War-era Captain from Franklin County.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Reunion
description:
Documented in 'The Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes' from a Missouri State Old Time Fiddlers Association recording. A notable version is played by Nile Wilson.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Savannah
description: Old Savannah is a reel in the key of A from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Sport
description:
Three distinct tunes share this name. One appears in 'Ryan's Mammoth Collection' (1883) and was recorded by W.B. Houchens. Another, associated with Albert Hash and southwestern Virginia, is also known as 'Callahan.'

Houchens recorded "Miller's Reel And Old Sport Reel" (SILVERTONE 4055-A) in 1924.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Tom of Oxford
description:
An English Morris dance tune from Bampton, Oxfordshire. It was first published as 'Peace and Plenty or Old Oxford' in Daniel Wright's 'Extraordinary Collection' (c. 1713). It is named for the bell in Christ Church College, Oxford.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Time Billy in the Lowground
description:
A crooked G-major tune from 19th-century Franklin County, Kentucky, distinct from the common C-major 'Billy in the Lowground.' Sourced from fiddler Kelly Gilbert (1895–1991), who learned it from Lewis Goins.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Time Fire on the Mountain
description:
A traditional tune dating to the early 19th century. Samuel Bayard identifies its American publication as early as 1814 in 'Riley's Flute Melodies' and an 1801 manuscript. It is part of a broad family of early tunes.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Tune
description: Old Tune is a reel in the key of G from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Voile
description: Old Voile is a reel in the key of D from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Ole Bull Hornpipe
description:
An American hornpipe in F major, named for Norwegian violinist Ole Bull (1810–1880), whose touring in the U.S. influenced many 19th-century musicians.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: One-Eyed Cat
description:
Composed by banjo player Dave Landreth. The tune was originally titled 'One-Eyed Jack' after a cat he rescued, but the name was later changed.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: One More River To Cross
description:
Here's what's known about the old-time fiddle tune "One More River to Cross", drawing from the Traditional Tune Archive and related sources: The tune is rooted in the American old-time tradition, and Mark Wilson (1981) notes that the tune bears a distant resemblance to a Negro spiritual of the same name — suggesting it may have absorbed or been influenced by that well-known spiritual tradition, though the fiddle tune likely developed as its own distinct piece. It is categorized as a traditional spiritual, composed anonymously, which is typical of old-time tunes passed down orally through regional fiddle communities.

The tune was in the repertory of West Virginia fiddler and bagpiper Franklin George, West Virginia fiddler Wilson Douglas, and Indiana fiddler John Summers. These players represent the core regional carriers of the tune — primarily the Appalachian / Upper South fiddle tradition. The tune is played in standard fiddle tuning and follows an AABB form — the classic two-part structure common to most old-time fiddle tunes. Franklin George is a particularly notable figure, being both a fiddler and bagpiper from West Virginia — an unusual combination that hints at Scots-Irish cultural crossover common in Appalachian music. Wilson Douglas was a celebrated West Virginia tradition bearer, known for preserving a deep repertoire of regional tunes. The spiritual of the same name has long been associated with themes of crossing the Jordan River into the afterlife, and also with the Underground Railroad — the fiddle tune may carry echoes of those symbolic meanings.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: On The Banks Of The Kaney
description: On The Banks Of The Kaney is a reel in the key of C from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Ora Lee
description:
A reel (often GDAD tuning) associated with the Southern Appalachian tradition. The earliest known source is Tennessee fiddler Edward Winter, from whom James Bryan learned it.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Over The Stump And Back Again
description: This American breakdown or reel in D major (AABB) is documented by Samuel Bayard in his 1944 collection, Hill Country Tunes. The title is cited as an example of the casual, spontaneous naming conventions found in old-time folk music.

title: Oyster Girl
description:
There are multiple distinct tunes known as "Oyster Girl." A notable old-time version is attributed to Nebraska fiddler Bob Walters (Burt County, 1951), as published in R.P. Christeson's Old Time Fiddler's Repertoire.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Oyster River Hornpipe
description:
Also known as "Oyster River Reel," this G Major tune appears in a Maine music manuscript (1826–1859) titled Melodist. It was later published in Elias Howe's Second Part of the Musician's Companion (1843) and Patrick O'Flannagan's The Hibernia Collection (1860). While the title likely refers to the Oyster River in New Hampshire, its specific origins remain unidentified.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Ozark Mountain Waltz
description:
The title "Ozark Mountain Waltz" refers to two distinct tunes. One version was recorded in Memphis in June 1930 by the Morrison Twin Brothers String Band of Searcy County, Arkansas, featuring twin fiddlers Abbie (1876–1965) and Absie (1876–1964) Morrison.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Paddy On The Pike
description:
A regional West Virginia variation of the "Paddy on the Turnpike" tune family, "Paddy on the Pike" was documented from the playing of Wilson Douglas (1922–1999) of Clay County, West Virginia, who played it in AEae tuning. It is related to Irish tunes found in O'Neill's Music of Ireland (1903) and Henebry's A Handbook of Irish Music (1928).

It appears in O'Neill's Music of Ireland: 1850 Melodies (1903) under two separate entries (Nos. 1196 and 1555). It has been in various tune books since Howe published it in 1864 in the key of D. The notation for "Paddy on the Pike" is drawn from the playing of Wilson Douglas (1922–1999, Clay County, central W.Va.), recorded on Boatin' Up Sandy (Marimac AHS CS 01, 1989), played in AEae cross-tuning.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Paddy On The (PA) Turnpike
description:
"Paddy on the Turnpike" is a widespread Irish reel appearing in many North American fiddle traditions. Samuel Bayard (1981) links the tune to the Scottish air "Waulkin' o' the Fauld," noting it has not been traced earlier than the 18th century. It appears in Ryan's Mammoth Collection (1882) and The Roche Collection (1912). Patrick J. Gaffney made the first known recording in 1923.

The tune has also been called "Jenny on the Railroad" and has been in various tune books since Howe published it in 1864 in the key of C.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Paddy Won't You Drink Some Good Old Cider
description:
An American reel first recorded by Fiddling Bob Larkin & His Music Makers in 1928. It belongs to a family of cider-themed tunes; researcher Kerry Blech identifies an early recording of the related "Down to the Stillhouse to Get a Little Cider" by Ernest Stoneman (1928). The tune is also included in Ira W. Ford's Traditional Music in America (1940).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Pagosa Hornpipe
description: Pagosa Hornpipe is a reel in the key of D from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Party Tune
description: Party Tune is a reel in the key of A from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Pat 'Em On The Back
description:
This Old-Time breakdown in G major was documented from Owen "Snake" Chapman (1919–2003) of Chapman's Holler, Kentucky, and included on his 1990 release "Fiddle Ditty." It also appears in Phillips' Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 1 (1994).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Pegleg
description: Pegleg is a reel in the key of D from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Perrodin Two Step
description:
A Cajun two-step in D Major, first recorded in 1929 by Angélas LeJeune, Dennis McGee, and Ernest Frugé. The tune is associated with the Perrodin family, who frequently requested it at dances.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Pickin' on the Ol' Banjo
description: This tune is documented on the 1990 album Galleynipper by J.P. and Annadeene Fraley (June Appal Recordings JA0058). J.P. Fraley was a traditional eastern Kentucky fiddler.

title: Piedmont
description:
A D-major schottische, this tune is associated with fiddler Art Galbraith (1909–1993) and his lineage, which traces to Uncle Tobe Galbraith (born 1853). It is likely named for Piedmont, Missouri.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Pike's Peak
description:
An American breakdown in C major, "Pike's Peak" was recorded in 1933 by Ted Sharp and his band. It was previously recorded in 1930 by Clark and Luches Kessinger under the title "Rat Cheese Under the Hill."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Piney Woods Gal
description:
Galax, Virginia, fiddler Eck Dunford described "Piney Woods Gal" to Elizabeth Lomax in 1941, noting it was the original title for a tune sometimes called "Katy Hill." The tune is traced to Galax fiddler Green Leonard (1810–1892) through Emmett Lundy and Luther Davis.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Pleasure House Rag
description: This tune is attributed to Virginia fiddler Kelly Perdue and appears in the collection Old Time Fiddling From The State Of Virginia and John Lamancusa's The Gettysburg Collection of Old-Time Fiddle Tunes.

title: Plowboy Hop
description:
A country rag in the key of B, recorded in 1930 by Ben Tinnon (1891–1975) and the Grinnell Giggers (Victor 23675). Tinnon was a dance fiddler from New Madrid County, Missouri.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Polly Put the Kettle On
description:
Derived from the British song "Jenny's Baubie," known since the 1770s, the tune was associated with the lyrics "Polly Put the Kettle On" by the early 19th century. A song titled "Molly Put the Kettle On" was published in London in 1803.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Poor Little Johnny's Gone To War
description: Poor Little Johnny's Gone To War is a reel in the key of D from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Porter
description:
A two-part square tune in D, this piece is from the repertoire of Nacogdoches County, Texas, fiddler Stafford Stephen Harris (1927–2010).

Harris was born in Laneville, Rusk County, TX, to Porter "Port" Stephen Harris (1903–1964) and Edna Faye Fryman (1911–1977).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Porter's Reel
description:
Also known as "Porter's Two-Step," this East Texas reel is attributed to Stafford Stephen Harris, who stated the tune was handed down from his grandfather.

Harris was born in Laneville, Rusk County, TX to Porter "Port" Stephen Harris (1903–1964) and Edna Faye Fryman (1911–1977).

title: Portsmouth Airs
description:
This G-major breakdown, named for Portsmouth, Ohio, is associated with the West Virginia fiddler Clark Kessinger (1896–1975), who recorded it in 1930.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Possum On A Rail
description:
Ellis stated he learned the tune from his brother, Homer.

On their 1930 recording, Ellis played fiddle, Pete Herring played guitar, and John M.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: The Possum's Tail is Bare
description:
This modal tune is primarily associated with West Virginia fiddler Melvin Wine (1909–2003). While not commercially recorded by Wine, it was documented through field recordings and direct instruction.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Possum Trot 1
description:
Attributed to Bill Shelor of Patrick County, Virginia, and documented on the 1978 release Old Originals, Vol. 1. Researchers Carter and Owen noted the tune remained regionally specific to Patrick County.

Researchers Tom Carter and Blanton Owen (1976) reported that the tune had not been recorded outside of Patrick County, Virginia.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Possum Trot 2
description:
A D-major tune documented from the Patrick County, Virginia, tradition, specifically from fiddler Bill Shelor. It appears in the Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes.

Folklorists Tom Carter and Blanton Owen (1976) say the tune has not been recorded outside of Patrick County, Virginia.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Possum Up A Simmon Tree
description:
A traditional American tune documented in Southern Appalachian and African American traditions. Related titles like "Possum up a Gum Stump" appear in sources dating to before 1830. Verses were collected from Black informants in North Carolina in 1908.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Pretty Betty Martin
description:
A mid-18th-century song and fiddle tune. Elizabeth Smith, wife of John Paca and mother of William Paca, has been identified in genealogical lore as the daughter of the "Betty Martin" referenced in the rhyme.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Pretty Little Indian
description:
The tune's origin, like most old-time fiddle tunes, is murky by nature. In old-time circles, saying "this is Pretty Little Indian, from Ward Jarvis" means he was the earliest source we know of, but it doesn't necessarily mean he actually wrote the tune himself.

Ward Jarvis (1894–1982), from Braxton County, West Virginia, who later moved to southeastern Ohio, is the primary attributed source. Jarvis is credited as the source for many old-time versions.

The tune also traveled through a parallel Kentucky lineage. Multiple recordings trace it back through Van Kidwell (a Kentucky/Ohio fiddler) and Buddy Thomas (a Kentucky fiddler): The West Orrtanna String Band recorded it in 1978, having learned it from Kentucky/Ohio fiddler Van Kidwell. Bob Carlin recorded it in 1980 on Fiddle Tunes for Clawhammer Banjo, having learned it from Van Kidwell via the Hotmud Family. Roger Cooper recorded it in 2006 on Essence of Old Kentucky, having learned it from Kentucky fiddler Buddy Thomas.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Pretty Little Shoes
description:
"Pretty Little Shoes" is actually the name applied to two distinct West Virginia old-time breakdown tunes that share a title but sound quite different from each other. Both are rooted in the Appalachian fiddle tradition of Clay County, West Virginia. The source for this tune is Clay County, West Virginia, fiddler French Carpenter (1899–1965), passed down via Wilson Douglas. It is classified as an Old-Time Breakdown in A Mixolydian. The notated version comes from Jim Ketterman, and was printed in Silberberg's Tunes I Learned at Tractor Tavern (2002). It was recorded by Wilson Douglas (West Virginia) on "Boatin' Up Sandy" (Marimac Recordings, 1989).

This is the version most commonly played today in old-time circles. This week's tune is "Pretty Little Shoes" from the playing of James Warden "Ward" Jarvis (19 March 1894 – 18 September 1982). He was the son of Josiah "Si" Jarvis and Amanda Melissa Siers, and married Susie Ellen Fulks in 1920.
