According to Milliner-Koken, Jarvis moved to Athens County, Ohio in the late 1940s to work in the timber industry. He played banjo with Ed Haley and John McIlwaine, frequently visited Henry Reed, and never recorded commercially — but was captured in various field recordings. Jarvis's repertoire was typical of his West Virginia origin, with many archaic-sounding cross-tuned pieces as well as tunes popular in the 1920s and 1930s. The tune was also played by West Virginia fiddlers Doc White and Lester McCumber.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Pretty Little Widow
description:
A traditional Kentucky tune. Documented sources include W. H. Stepp (1875–1957) of Magoffin County, recorded for the Library of Congress, and John Ashby of Virginia.

John Ashby — Virginia Another well-known version comes from John Ashby, recorded in the key of A with AEAE cross-tuning, sourced from the album Down on Ashby's Farm (County LP 745, 1974).

title: Pumpkin Vine
description:
A two-step from northeastern Kentucky. Sources include Alfred Bailey (1918–1996) and Buddy Thomas (1935–1974). Bailey attributed his knowledge of the tune to Asa Neil.

One of the primary documented sources for "Pumpkin Vine" (also called "Old Pumpkin Vine") is Alfred Bailey (1918–1996), from Fleming County, northeastern Kentucky, who was recorded in the field in 1986 by folklorist John Harrod.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Puncheon Floor
description:
Associated with Dobson, North Carolina, fiddler Esker Hutchins, who learned it from Crawley Hamlin. The title refers to the construction of log cabin floors, though a secondary meaning involving liquor barrels has been suggested.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Purcell's Reel
description:
The primary documented source for Purcell's Reel in the old-time tradition is Bob Walters, a Nebraska fiddler. Robert E. "Uncle Bob" Walters was born on June 16, 1889, in Decatur, Burt County, Nebraska. His grandfather, Ike Walters, and his father, William Wilson "Wilse" Walters, were both noted fiddlers — meaning Bob came from a deep multi-generational fiddling family.

Purcell's Reel is attributed to artist Bob Walters, played in the Key of A with standard GDAE tuning, recorded around 1950, and later released on the Old Time Fiddlers' Repertory University of Missouri LP (1976). It appears in the collections The Old Time Fiddler's Repertory and Old Time Fiddling From The State Of Nebraska.

Bob Walters was a titan of the Midwestern old-time fiddling scene. He won a number of contests sponsored by KFNF in Shenandoah, Iowa — so many that other contestants protested and he was eventually hired as a judge and "guest artist." He competed in radio contests in Omaha and Sioux City, and his last regular radio stint was on KMMJ out of Grand Island, Nebraska, where he played from the mid-1940s until around 1954. He was a consistent winner in local contests, at one point having won 34 out of 38 he had entered. His biggest win was the 1931 Tri-State Championship held in Sioux City, Iowa, where he took first prize along with a silver cup.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Queen Of France
description:
A tune within the American old-time tradition. The title follows naming conventions prevalent during the American Revolution, often commemorating foreign political figures or powers in an ironic or aspirational manner.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Quince Dillion's High D
description: Quincie Perry Dillion (c. 1810–1827) was a fifer in the Confederate Army. This tune is documented in the Henry Reed collection at the Library of Congress (AFC 1999/016).

title: Rabbit in the Grass
description:
Popularized by Luke Hignight's Ozark Strutters in 1928, the tune also appears as "Soapsuds Splash" in Marion Thede's The Fiddle Book (1967). Alabama fiddler James Bryan learned the tune from Mack Blalock.

It also appears in R.P. Christeson's Old Time Fiddlers Repertory, Vol. 1 (1973), sourced from Bill Driver of Missouri.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rachel
description:
An American reel in D major. While sometimes associated with Rachel Jackson, there is no corroborating evidence for this attribution.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Railroad Runs Thru Georgia
description:
'Railroad Runs Through Georgia' was in the repertory of the Collins family of Pottawatomie County, Oklahoma. Gary Stanton and Tom Carter made a field recording of Max Collins playing it. The tune is also associated with Marion Thede's Fiddle Book, page 42, in a setting notated by Walter Baker.

The documented setting uses AEae fiddle tuning.

Source: John Lamancusa collection, oldtimefiddletunes.net.

title: Railroading Thru the Rockies
description:
This Kentucky Old-Time breakdown is played in D Major. Fiddler Jim Bowles, the primary source, learned it as "Goin' Down to Shirley's" from his uncle, Wash Carter, as documented by Jeff Titon (2001). The title "Railroad Through the Rocky Mountains" is the name by which it is known in the broader old-time community.

He was a great old Kentucky fiddler known for "lots of weird, awesome tunes... with plenty of blue notes to go around." Jim Bowles (1903–1993) learned the tune from his uncle, Wash Carter, who called it "Goin' Down to Shirley's", according to Jeff Titon (2001).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rattlesnake Bit The Baby
description:
This reel, played in C Major, is frequently known by the name recorded by Lowe Stokes, "Take Me Back to Georgia." Mandolinist Kenny Hall used the title "Rattlesnake Bit the Baby." Fiddler John Ashby learned the tune from Walter Graham and John Sinclair.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rebel Raid
description:
"Rebel Raid" is a title applied to multiple unrelated Appalachian breakdown tunes. A version attributed to Kentucky fiddler Ed Haley is thought by Jim Taylor (1996) and Jeff Titon (2001) to refer to the 1864 Confederate incursions into eastern Kentucky by General John Hunt Morgan.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Red Apple Rag
description:
"Red Apple Rag" is an American Country Rag in G Major popularized by Tennessee fiddler Arthur Smith. It was also documented in 1972 from the playing of farmer and fiddler Sammie Dyer of Macon County, Tennessee.

The tune is also documented from the playing of farmer and fiddler Sammie Dyer (1906–1983, Macon County, north-central Tennessee), recorded in the field in 1972.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Red Bird
description:
Two distinct tunes are known as "Red Bird." The first is an Oklahoma breakdown featuring plucked notes, learned from Jubal Anderson and Byron Berline; scholar Guthrie Meade notes its similarity to Uncle Jimmy Thompson's "Billy Wilson (2)." The second is a showpiece associated with West Virginia fiddler Clark Kessinger.

It appears in print in *Phillips' Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 1 (1994), p. 197, and in Thede's The Fiddle Book (1967), p. 152. Scholar Guthrie Meade notes the tune is very similar to Uncle Jimmy Thompson's "Billy Wilson (2)," recorded for Columbia in 1926. It is also related in some parts to the separate tune known as "Red Bird Reel." Red Bird is considered a showpiece tune for West Virginia fiddler Clark Kessinger (1896–1975), who recorded it several times, albeit later in life.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Red Haired Boy (Little Beggar Man)
description:
"Red Haired Boy" is an English translation of the Gaelic "Giolla Rua," a title associated with the 17th-century Scottish outlaw Gilderoy. 17th-century song versions, which pre-date the popular association with Rob Roy McGregor, were laments. The tune appears in Baring-Gould's 1895 "Garland of Country Song" and "The Scots Musical Museum."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rhymer's Favorite
description:
"Rhymer's Favorite" (or "Rymer's Favorite") is an old-time tune attributed to fiddler Allen Sisson. It is part of the public domain repertoire with no known authorship.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Richmond
description:
"Richmond" refers to a family of fiddle tunes, some of which modulate from D major to A major. It is a well-known tune in the Upper South.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Richmond Cotillion (Emmett Lundy's version)
description:
This tune was played by Grayson County, Virginia, fiddler Emmett Lundy and recorded for the Library of Congress in 1941. It is unrelated to the common "Richmond Cotillion" and is sometimes called "Lundy's Cotillion" because the original title remains unknown.

This tune was played by Dalhart (near Galax), Grayson County, southwest Virginia fiddler Emmett Lundy (1864–1953) and recorded for the Library of Congress in 1941.

title: Richmond Cotillion
description:
"Richmond Cotillion" is a D Major tune that modulates to A major. Its origin is debated; some argue the title "Richmond" was paired with "Cotillion" due to labeling on 1920s Da Costa Woltz records.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rickett's Hornpipe
description:
"Rickett's Hornpipe" is named for John Bill Ricketts (1769–1800), a Scottish immigrant and circus promoter who presented performances in Philadelphia and other American cities beginning in 1793. Alan Jabbour (in "American Fiddle Tunes") documents the spread of Ricketts's circuses.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Road to Malvern
description:
"Road to Malvern" is a modern composition by West Virginia fiddler Jim Childress, named for the Arkansas town where his wife was raised. It is an A Major breakdown.

Jim originally recorded it on the *2004 CD Turkey Sag with old-time stringband Uncle Henry's Favorites.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Roaring River
description: "Roaring River" is an Ozark fiddle tune listed by Vance Randolph (1954). Another tune by the same name was composed by Solomon Northup and published in his 1853 memoir "Twelve Years a Slave."

title: Robinson County
description:
"Robinson County" is a D Major breakdown from central Arkansas, also known as "Robertson." A 1933 recording by Ted Sharp, Hinman & Sharp is documented in the Milliner-Koken Collection.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rochester Schottische
description:
At least three distinct tunes are known as "Rochester Schottische," leading to significant confusion. The tune originates from upstate New York.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rock that Cradle Joe
description:
"Rock that Cradle Joe" is an old-time breakdown in D Major associated with the traditions of Virginia and West Virginia. Modern versions are based on the recordings of J.W. "Babe" Spangler from the 1940s.

Roane County, W.Va., fiddler Franklin George (1928–2017) also recorded a version captured in a 2008 field recording.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rock the Cradle Lucy
description:
"Rock the Cradle Lucy" is a D Major breakdown associated with north Georgia and Oklahoma. Gid Tanner and His Skillet Lickers recorded the most version for Columbia in 1929.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rocky Mountain Goat
description:
"Rocky Mountain Goat" is a D Major reel popularized by a 1927 Paramount recording by Doc Roberts and his band. Roberts learned the tune from Dude Freeman of Beattieville, Kentucky.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rocky Road To Jordan
description:
"Rocky Road to Jordan" is a D Major reel included in the "100 Essential Missouri Tunes" by Charlie Walden. It is mentioned in Edgar Lee Masters' 1942 book "The Sangamon" regarding a visit to fiddler John Armstrong in 1914.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rocky Pallet
description:
"Rocky Pallet" is a C Major reel associated with north Georgia and North Carolina. The Skillet Lickers recorded it in 1927 for Columbia.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rodes' Division
description:
"Rodes' Division," also known as "Rose Division" or "Rowe's Division," is a reel in C or B-flat Major. Revival interest stems from a 1974 recording by the Hollow Rock String Band, who credited fiddler John Lewis.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Roger Sprung's #2
description:
Roger Sprung (1930–2023) was a banjo player and teacher whose repertoire extended beyond bluegrass to ragtime, jazz and other styles. He learned by ear from Earl Scruggs records and took lessons from Tom Paley. Those biographical details do not establish that he composed this tune.

Source: John Lamancusa collection, oldtimefiddletunes.net.

title: Rolling the Logs
description: Rolling the Logs is a reel in the key of C from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Root Hog or Die
description:
"Root Hog or Die" is an idiomatic expression for self-reliance dating to the early 1800s. It resulted in several pre-Civil War songs, some of which appear in minstrel and patriotic contexts.

By 1829, the Vermont Gazette recorded: "In Ohio, they have a vulgar proverb which runs thus — 'Root, hog, or die.' It is usually spread in staring capitals among idlers and it is said often has an admirable effect in promoting habits of industry." By 1834, Davy Crockett used it in his autobiography: "We therefore determined to go on the old saying, root, hog or die" — from A Narrative of the Life of David Crockett, of the State of Tennessee.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rosebud Hornpipe
description:
"Rosebud Hornpipe" was published in George Saunders' 1847 tutor and later circulated in the Missouri Valley tradition via fiddler Cyril Stinnett. Vivian Williams is credited with bringing the tune to modern attention.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Roscoe
description:
"Roscoe" is a G Major breakdown from the repertoire of Kyle Creed, who named it for his friend Roscoe Russell.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rose in the Mountain
description:
"Rose in the Mountain" is a D Major reel attributed to John Morgan Salyer of Magoffin County, Kentucky. It is noted for its "crooked" AABC structure, documented in 1941-42 home recordings.

The tune is attributed to John Morgan Salyer (1882–1952, Salyersville, Magoffin County, eastern Kentucky), and the foundational recording comes from a 1941/42 home recording made by his sons, Glen & Grover.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Round The Horn
description:
"Round the Horn" was composed by New York fiddler and mandolin player Jay Ungar. It is a G major reel in 4/4 time, copyrighted in 1978 by Swinging Door Music/BMI.

Despite sounding deeply traditional and being widely absorbed into the old-time and Irish session repertoire, this is a modern composition — not an anonymous folk tune passed down through generations, though it circulates as one.

The title refers to making the trip around Cape Horn (the southern tip of South America) — the tune is played with "Off to California" and "Road to California" as a medley called "Bound for California" on a James Galway, Jay Ungar, and Molly Mason CD, which confirms the title's nautical/westward journey meaning.

It is an American reel in G Major, played in standard fiddle tuning, with an AABB / AA'BB' structure.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rundown Boot
description: Rundown Boot is a reel in the key of C from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Run Rebel Run
description: Run Rebel Run is a reel in the key of G from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rush and the Pepper
description:
This tune is documented on the Indian Delta Creek Boys, Vol. 1 album, where the liner notes describe it as follows: "RUSH AND THE PEPPER (Key of D): Jesse James Abbott of rural Toledo said that he learned this hornpipe as a young boy in Missouri."

J.J. (Jesse James) Abbott turned 82 in the Fall of 1975, placing his birth around 1893 and his learning of the tune likely sometime in the early 1900s in Missouri. The tune is documented from the playing of Jesse James Abbott, and was collected by Gary Harrison — one of many fine tunes Harrison collected in Illinois. The tune is catalogued in old-time tune directories as "Rush And The Pepper, D-ADae — Jess Abbott via G. Harrison", referencing the non-standard ADAE fiddle tuning used to play it. Key of D, played in ADAE cross-tuning (also written D-ADae) Classified as a hornpipe — hornpipes are typically in 4/4 time and played somewhat slower than reels, often involving melodically complex and elaborately arpeggiated tunes.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rustic Dance
description:
"Rustic Dance" was composed by Cyrus R. Howell and Included in 1887. It is widely played across the U.S. and Canada, often for schottisches.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Ruth's Rag
description:
"Ruth's Rag" was composed by fiddler Ben Tinnon and named for his wife, Ruth. It was recorded in 1930 in Memphis by Tinnon's group, the Grinnell Giggers.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rye Straw
description:
"Rye Straw" was published in an 1876 collection by George H. Coes as "Whoop from Arkansas (A)." The title is a polite substitution for an unprintable original name.

Morris (Old Time Violin Melodies, 1927, No. 28) as "Acrobat." Marion Thede published Ozarks region versions as "Preacher's Favorite" and "Ladies Fancy (4)" in her The Fiddle Book (1960).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Saddle Old Kate
description:
"Saddle Old Kate" is an A Major reel from Missouri and Arkansas. Fiddler Lum Varner composed it in the 1920s, naming it after his horse; the version "Saddle Old Spike" originated from his brother Jim's renamed take on the tune.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Saddle Old Paint
description:
"Saddle Old Paint" is a G minor air learned by Ohio fiddler Forest Pick from a Cherokee fiddler named Chief Red Bird (William A. Sanders, 1899–1978).

Chief Red Bird was a Detroit-area bandleader and dance fiddler who played on the radio and even recorded 78rpm records with Otto Gray's Oklahoma Cowboys from 1927 to 1933.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sadie At The Back Door
description:
"Sadie At The Back Door" is a D Major breakdown composed by Jere Canote. It is a "crooked" tune associated with Greg Canote's playing in ADae tuning.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Safe Harbor Rag
description:
"Safe Harbor Rag," also known as "Safe Harbor Reel," was composed by Dick Walton of Safe Harbor, Pennsylvania.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sail Away Ladies
description:
"Sail Away Ladies" traces back to the "Sally Ann" family of tunes. Uncle Bunt Stevens recorded it in 1926, and Uncle Dave Macon added the lyrics in 1927.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sailing Over England
description:
"Sailing Over England" comes from the playing of West Virginia fiddler Fitzhugh Lee Triplett (1897–1981). It is a D Major reel.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Saint Ann's Reel
description:
St. Anne's Reel is a Canadian reel historically traced to Québec. It is also known as "St. Agathe" and "La Reel de la Baie Ste. Anne." Researcher Jean Duval suggests the title refers to Sainte-Anne-de-Bellevue, Montreal, while Father Stanislas Paulin noted its popularity in New Brunswick's Catholic culture.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: St. Joe Hornpipe
description:
"St. Joe Hornpipe" is an American reel in C-flat Major associated with Nebraska and Missouri. The title likely refers to St. Joseph, Missouri. It is considered an essential Missouri fiddle tune, popularized by players such as Bob Walters and Cyril Stinnett.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sally Ann Johnson
description:
"Sally Ann Johnson" encompasses two distinct tunes: a D Major reel associated with West Virginia fiddler Henry Reed, and a G Major reel ("Sally Johnson") associated with Texas/Midwest fiddlers. Henry Reed's 1967 recording by Alan Jabbour is archived at the Library of Congress (AFS 13703B10).

Henry Reed (1884–1968) lived in Glen Lyn, Giles County, Virginia, and his recording is preserved at the Library of Congress as AFS 13703B10.

title: Sally Cooper
description:
"Sallie Cooper" is an old-time breakdown in G Major from Kentucky, sourced from John Morgan Salyer of Magoffin County, recorded in the 1940s. It features an unusual structure where the second part is played only once.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sally Will You Marry Me
description:
"Sally Will You Marry Me" is a West Virginia reel in G Major, with most modern versions tracing to Braxton County fiddler Melvin Wine. It is notated in the Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes (2011) and Phillips' Traditional American Fiddle Tunes Vol. 1 (1994).

The most referenced recording is by Melvin Wine on the album Hannah at the Springhouse (August Heritage CD AHR 021, 1989), collected by Gerry Milnes.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sal's Got Mud Between Her Toes
description:
"Sal's Got Mud Between Her Toes" is a three-part D Major tune sourced to southern Kentucky fiddler Pat Kingery (ca. 1912–1976), recorded in 1976 by Bruce Greene. Kingery provided the traditional lyrics for the piece.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Salt Sack Behind the Door
description: Salt Sack Behind the Door is a reel in the key of C from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Salt Spring
description:
"Salt Spring" is an original composition by West Coast mandolinist John Reischman, released on his 2001 debut album with the Jaybirds.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Salty River Reel
description:
Here is a thorough breakdown of everything known about "Salty River Reel" — its origin, associated fiddlers, and relationship to the broader "Salt River" tune family.

"Salty River Reel" (or "Salt River Reel") is not the same tune as "Salt River" or "Salt Creek" — experienced fiddlers are clear that these are distinct pieces. The similar-sounding names cause frequent confusion in the old-time community.

The tune "Salty River Reel" is most closely identified with Cyril Stinnett, a northwest Missouri fiddler who became one of its most celebrated carriers: Cyril Stinnett was born near Savannah, in northwest Missouri, on January 27, 1912. His dad was a farmer and a fiddler. The family moved to southwest Missouri for a while, but Cyril eventually returned to the Filmore area where he spent the rest of his life. Cyril began playing fiddle around age eight, practicing secretly in the basement on his dad's fiddle for months before surprising his dad with his new ability. Within a couple of years he was playing for dances. His tremendous memory for tunes and precision in playing led some folks to refer to him as a "fiddling computer," but his playing was far from being mechanical. Although Cyril's renditions were melodically complex, they were in a sense, quite simple — no bow effects (double shuffles, etc.) other than the occasional use of 32nd notes, and little double string playing. Most of his tunes were two-part reels and hornpipes.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sam and Elzie's
description:
"Sam and Elzie's" is named for Sam and Elzie Crutchfield, who organized square dances near Omega, Illinois. The tune is associated with Illinois fiddler Wilson Bray (1918–?), who learned dance tunes from his father.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sam Hill
description:
"Sam Hill" is considered an Alabama tune, placing it firmly in the Southern Appalachian / Deep South old-time tradition. Detailed written documentation of its origins is sparse, which is typical of many old-time tunes passed down through oral tradition.

It is described as a "crooked tune" — meaning it has an irregular or asymmetrical phrase structure (e.g., bars that don't fall into a strict 8+8 form), a hallmark of many older Southern fiddle pieces. Ralph Whited — The tune is attributed to Ralph Whited, as documented on Tater Joe's Old-Time Fiddle resource, transmitted via James Bryan. James Bryan — James Bryan, a celebrated Alabama fiddler, plays "Sam Hill" on the CD Cricket's Lullaby with Carl Jones. Bryan is Norman Blake's longtime fiddler and is known for his smooth, immediately recognizable personal style — his playing on Bob Carlin's album Banging and Sawing is considered especially exemplary.

The phrase "what in the Sam Hill" is a recognized American euphemism — Sam Hill was reportedly a prominent man of the Northwest known for his prolific profanity, and his name came to be used as a substitute for foul language. Whether the tune's name connects directly to this folk etymology or to a specific person named Sam Hill in Alabama fiddling tradition is not definitively documented.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sand Mountain Drag
description:
"Sand Mountain Drag" is an American Country Rag in C Major. It was recorded in March 1930 by Dilly & His Dill Pickles in Atlanta, Georgia, and is attributed to the group's fiddler, Harry Kiker from Hiram, Georgia.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sandy Boys
description:
"Sandy Boys" is from the repertoire of Pocahontas County, West Virginia fiddler Edden Hammons (1875–1955), recorded in 1947 by Louis Chappell. The tune has roots in the American minstrel repertoire, appearing in period tutors like Phil Rice's Correct Method for the Banjo (1857).

The original can be found in the American minstrel show repertoire — a similar version appears in *Phil Rice's Correct Method for the Banjo (1857), a period tutor, and also in an 1844 minstrel songbook (reproduced by the Harvard Theatre Collection, Cambridge, Mass.).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Santa Anna's Retreat
description:
"Santa Anna's Retreat" is a southwestern Virginia reel in A Mixolydian/Dorian. According to Henry Reed, the tune was learned from fifer Quince Dillon, who believed it was used by Antonio López de Santa Anna’s army during the Mexican War.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sarah Armstrong's Tune
description:
Sarah Gray Armstrong (1883–1957) was a Pennsylvania fiddler from Gray Station. She grew up in a musical family and learned to play at age five from her uncle Laney. Her family band was known as "The Gray Boys."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Satisfied
description: Satisfied is a reel in the key of A from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Saturday Night Breakdown
description:
"Saturday Night Breakdown" was recorded in 1929 by Wil Gilmer and The Leake County Revelers of Sebastopol, Mississippi. The group was regionally popular and performed regularly on WJDX radio.

They were already regionally popular when they recorded in Atlanta, Georgia, in 1929, and had accompanied Louisiana politician Huey Long on his campaign for governor in 1928.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Scotland Yard
description: Scotland Yard is a reel in the key of C from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Scott #1
description: Scott #1 is a reel in the key of G from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Setauket
description:
William Sidney Mount (1807–1868), a painter and fiddler from Setauket, New York, documented several fiddle tunes in his manuscripts, now held at the Long Island Museum. These manuscripts include an untitled hornpipe and "Roscommon's Hornpipe."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Shag Poke
description:
"Shag Poke" is associated with fiddler Dwight Lamb of Moorehead, Iowa. It is recorded on the CD Joseph Won a Coated Fiddle (1999) and cataloged in the Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Shenandoah Falls
description:
"Shenandoah Falls" is an old-time breakdown in A Major. It was transmitted through Carol Robinson of Sebastopol, California, who learned the tune from a mandolin player known as "Cookie."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Ship in the Clouds
description:
"Ship in the Clouds" is a crooked Virginia reel in D Major. It is notably played by Galax fiddler Uncle Norm Edmonds (1889–1976) and Laurel Fork fiddler Taylor Kimble (1892–1979).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Shippingport
description:
"Shippingport" is named for the former town of Shippingport, Kentucky, a river port near the Louisville and Portland Canal that was absorbed by the city of Louisville.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Shoes and Stockings
description:
"Shoes and Stockings" was learned by Henry Reed (1884–1968) from his mentor, Civil War-era fifer Quince Dillon. It was entered into the old-time canon via Alan Jabbour's recordings of Reed.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Shoo Fly
description:
"Shoo Fly" is an American reel associated with the late 19th century. Thomas Brigham Bishop of Wayne, Maine, claimed authorship in 1869, stating he wrote the song during the Civil War.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Shooting Creek
description: "Shooting Creek" is a common tune in the Franklin/Floyd County area of Virginia. The version is an American reel in D Major, sourced from West Virginia fiddler Oscar Wright.

title: Shucking The Brush
description:
When asked directly, fiddler Earl White confirmed he was told the tune is called Shucking the Brush and has always called it that — though he acknowledged that names and versions of old-time tunes can be, as he put it, "fluid."

One competing theory holds that the original name is "Shuck in the Bush" — as in a corn shuck stuck in a bush — a story passed down from someone who supposedly spoke directly with the fiddler who composed the tune.

The variant title "Chuck in the Bush" also appears in Silverberg's Tunes I Either Did or Did Not Learn at the Tractor Tavern and the Phillips collection, and may have also been published in The Devil's Box, which some believe is the original title. Earl White (SF Bay Area) is the most-cited player associated with the tune's wider spread. The tune was first heard by at least one community member around 1980, likely played by Billy Hornung fiddling with the Jubilo String Band from the Philadelphia area, and later circulated widely through Earl White and his Bay Area band. A fancier, multi-part version also exists in the Texas-style fiddle tradition, performed under the name "Shuck in the Bush," with fiddler Tashina Clarridge noted for a particularly spectacular rendition. The tune has had a revival in sessions in the Albany, NY area, where players also debated its name.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Shuffle About
description:
"Shuffle About" is a D Major reel from Kentucky. It was recorded in 1975 by Bruce Greene from fiddler Everett Kays (1905–1996) of Anderson County.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Silver Bells
description:
"Silver Bells" is a 1910 Tin Pan Alley song composed by Percy Wenrich with lyrics by Edward Madden. It was recorded by Ada Jones and Billy Murray in 1910.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Silver Lake
description:
"Silver Lake" refers to several tunes; this version is from West Virginia fiddler Emory Bailey (1900s), recorded by Malvin Artley in 1953. Bailey's version is noted for its D Major AEad cross-tuning and B-part variations.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sleepy Eyed Joe
description:
"Sleepy Eyed Joe" exists in multiple versions, including one in A from Bob Walters (1889–1960) of Nebraska, and one in E from John Ashby (1915–1979) of Virginia.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Slippin' Around
description: Slippin' Around is a reel in the key of G from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Smith's Reel
description:
"Smith's Reel," known in Ireland as "Kitty's Wedding," is an American breakdown. It appears in George Saunders' 1847 tutor, where Saunders claimed authorship.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Snake Chapman's Tune
description:
Owen "Snake" Chapman (1919–2002) was a lifelong resident of Chapman's Hollow, Canada, Pike County, in northeastern Kentucky. His personal story is almost an archetype for the experience of Kentucky mountain people in the 20th century — born and raised in a log cabin, he worked as a coal miner from his late teens to middle age, retiring early with black lung, and working briefly in the auto plants of Detroit before returning to the family home in Chapman's Hollow in the late 1960s.

Snake knew as many melodies as any fiddler his peers had ever met, ranging from very old tunes learned from his father to modern bluegrass fare. Growing up in an isolated mountain hollow, Owen developed an astonishingly accurate ear for the nuances of a fiddle tune and could diagnose very sharply how the playing of certain popular fiddle tunes had evolved over his own lifetime.

Among all the melodies Snake played, the most astonishing were the tunes he learned as a boy from his elderly father, "Doc" Chapman, who had been born in 1850 — Doc's own father, according to family tradition, split logs with Abraham Lincoln before the family resettled in Kentucky.

Doc Chapman was born around 1850 (he was 67 when Snake was born) and thus learned his music from the antebellum generation. Snake learned fiddle when he was "eleven or twelve" from a father who must have been around 78 by then. If Doc had done the same, he would have been learning from someone born in 1783 — a mere seven years after the Declaration of Independence!

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Snake River Reel
description:
The original was composed by musician and dance caller Peter Lippincott (formerly of St. Louis, now living in Arkansas). The tune has a contemporary composition date of 1985. He is described as a fiddler and potter from Missouri.

Lippincott himself described the tune's creation: "I just came up with it noodling around one day, oh so long ago. String bands, in St. Louis where I lived, took it to Galax and other fiddle venues and it caught on. Who knew? I named it after the Snake River, but other than sounding like a cool name there is no added significance. I also wrote an contra dance by the same name at about the same time."

He named it after the Snake River, but noted that "other than sounding like a cool name there is no added significance." Despite this, some in the old-time community have drawn colorful associations — it is described as a tune that "changes mode whilst keeping the same tonal centre," and at least one player hears it in the context of the Lewis and Clark expedition, pairing it in medleys with Over the Waterfall due to their shared mixolydian character.

The tune is described as an old-time reel "that changes mode whilst keeping the same tonal centre" — it begins in D-Major, then switches to D-Mixolydian in the second part. This modal shift between parts is part of what makes it distinctive and memorable in jam settings.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Snake Winder
description:
"Snakewinder" is a G Major reel from northeastern Kentucky. It is attributed to Morris Allen, transmitted through fiddler Buddy Thomas (1935–1974), and featured on the album Buddy Thomas – Traditional Fiddle Music of Kentucky, Vol. 1 (1997).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Snouts and Ears of America
description:
"Snouts and Ears of America" was collected from Sarah Gray Armstrong (1883–1957) of Derry, Pennsylvania, by Samuel Preston Bayard for his 1944 volume, Hill Country Tunes: Instrumental Folk Music of Southwestern Pennsylvania.

This tune is one of thirty-seven tunes collected in 1943 by musicologist Samuel Preston Bayard, from Derry, Pennsylvania fiddler Sarah Gray Armstrong (1883–1957).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Snow Deer
description:
"Snow Deer" is a Tin Pan Alley song composed by Percy Wenrich around 1910. The piece, depicting a cowboy's love for an indigenous woman, entered the fiddle repertoire and was played by Arizona fiddler Kenner C. Kartchner.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Snowflake Breakdown
description:
"Snowflake Breakdown" was composed in 1959 by Canadian fiddler Wally Edward Traugott (1934–2010), who played on The Tommy Hunter Show. The tune has circulated in New England and Missouri.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Snow Shoes
description:
"Snow Shoes" is an American reel in D Major, AABB form. It was popularized by Nashville session fiddler Tommy Jackson, who recorded it on the 1962 album *Tommy Jackson – Swing Your Partner* (Dot DLP-3454).

"Snowshoes" was popularized by Nashville, Tennessee, session fiddler Tommy Jackson (1926–1979), who recorded it in 1962.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Soapsuds Over The Fence
description:
"Soapsuds Over the Fence" is a traditional American breakdown. It was listed as "Pouring Soapsuds over the Fence" in Vance Randolph's 1954 collection of Ozarks fiddle tunes and appears in earlier dance records from Missouri. Alternate titles include "Soap Suds."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Somebody's Buried in the Graveyard
description: Somebody's Buried in the Graveyard is a reel in the key of G from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Soppin' Up the Gravy
description:
"Soppin' Up the Gravy" is an old-time breakdown in D Major, also known as "Sopping the Gravy," with roots in Missouri and Texas. It has been noted for stylistic connections to "Year of the Jubilo."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Speed Of The Plow
description:
This tune has a surprisingly rich and documented history, unusual for a piece of folk music. It also exists in several distinct, melodically unrelated versions that share the same name, which causes considerable confusion.

What is most unusual about this tune is that we do know who composed it — unlike many older tunes whose origins are typically unknown. Captain Francis O'Neill researched the melody and reported his findings in Irish Minstrels and Musicians (1913), tracing it to one John Moorehead (also spelled Morehead or Muirhead), of County Armagh, Ireland.

Moorehead was an Englishman who emigrated to Armagh, Ireland, in 1782. A talented young violinist, he became employed by London's Covent Garden Theatre in 1798 and wrote the tune the following year, originally entitling it "The Naval Pillar" after a military victory. It spread rapidly throughout Great Britain and the English colonies, and the melody was later used in a theatrical play, Speed the Plough, which led to the song's current title.

Francis O'Neill (1913) believed the tune to be Irish in character and stated it was regarded as English due to its being first heard in English theaters, though he regretfully determined it too associated with England to include in his Dance Music of Ireland (1907).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Speed The Plow
description:
"Speed the Plow" (sometimes "Speed the Plough" or "God Speed the Plough") is a well-traveled tune, popular with fiddlers for over 200 years. Although it is considered a chestnut in many circles, it has a deserved place in the core fiddle repertoire in several genres, for it seems to flow off the fiddle yet is melodically interesting in both its parts. The reel is extremely widespread in English-speaking traditions and can be found in the repertoires of fiddlers throughout North America, Ireland, Scotland, and England.

What is most unusual is the fact that we do know who composed "Speed the Plow," unlike many older tunes whose origins are typically unknown. Captain Francis O'Neill researched the melody and reported his findings in Irish Minstrels and Musicians (1913), basing his remarks on entries from the British Musical Biography. Therein he found that the reel was the work of one John Moorehead (whose name has also been given as Morehead or Muirhead), of County Armagh, Ireland.

A talented young violinist, Moorehead became employed by London's Covent Garden Theatre in 1798 and wrote the tune the following year, originally entitling it "The Naval Pillar" after a military victory. The melody was then used in a theatrical play called "Speed the Plough," leading to the song's current title.

The phrase "God speed the plough" goes back at least to the 14th century as a prayer for a successful crop and as a song sung by gangs of mischievous revelers on Plough Monday rampages at the end of the Christmas season.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Spotted Pony
description:
"Spotted Pony" is a popular Missouri Ozarks tune documented in Vance Randolph's 1954 survey. Multiple unrelated melodies share this name across Missouri, Arkansas, and Texas, suggesting a regional naming convention for lively tunes.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))
notes: Versions differ in their A parts and keys; check which setting your group plays.

title: Spring Creek Gal
description:
"Spring Creek Gal" is a D-major breakdown. Alabama fiddler James Bryan learned the tune from Iowa fiddler Al Murphy after hearing Murphy’s band, Grasslands, at a 1981 festival in Seven Ponds Park, Iowa.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Springfield
description: Springfield is a reel in the key of D from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Spring In The Valley
description:
"Spring in the Valley" is a D-major reel composed in the mid-1970s by Tom McCreesh of the Hotmud Family. The title references Spring Valley, Ohio, where band members Dave and Suzanne Edmundson resided.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Squirrel Hunters
description:
"The Squirrel Hunters" is an Allegheny fiddle and fife tune. Samuel Bayard collected the tune in southwestern Pennsylvania, noting it as a member of a widespread melodic family. The title references 1862 Ohio militiamen nicknamed by Major Malcolm McDowell.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Star Of Bethlehem
description:
"Star of Bethlehem" is a D-major march from southwestern Pennsylvania. Scholar Samuel Bayard (1981) suggested a Scottish origin. The tune is associated with military marches from the Peninsular War and appears in various 19th-century collections, including the "Centenary March."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Steamboat Round The Bend
description:
"Steamboat 'Round the Bend" is a G-major reel associated with the Missouri-Nebraska fiddling tradition. It was recorded by Bob Walters in 1956, appearing on the 1976 collection *Old Time Fiddling From The State Of Nebraska*.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Step to the Music Johnny
description: Step to the Music Johnny is a reel in the key of A from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Stillhouse Branch
description:
"Stillhouse Branch" is associated with Kentucky fiddler Buddy Thomas (1935–1974), who learned it from his cousin Perry Riley. Thomas also identified it as "Brown Stream," a mishearing of "Brown's Dream." The name refers to mountain streams used for distilling liquor.

Thomas knew the tune as "Stillhouse Branch," and learned his version from his cousin, Perry Riley (1893–1973).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Stonewall Jackson
description: Multiple unrelated American tunes share the name "Stonewall Jackson," likely named for Confederate General Thomas "Stonewall" Jackson. The Traditional Tune Archive catalogs at least three distinct melodies under this title.

title: Streak O' Lean Streak O' Fat
description:
Recorded around 1930 by Seven-Foot Dilly and His Dill Pickles, "Streak O' Lean, Streak O' Fat" is associated with fiddlers Harry Kiker or A.A. Gray. The melody is related to "Hell Broke Loose in Georgia" and was used in 1899 at a Gallatin, Tennessee, fiddle contest.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Stumptail Dog
description:
"Stumptail Dog" is a variant of a fiddle tune family, also known as "Stumptail Dolly." The name refers to a regional working dog breed in West Virginia and Kentucky, traditionally believed to have descended from Briard stock.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Stumptail Dolly
description:
"Stumptailed Dolly" is an old-time reel in G Major associated with eastern Kentucky. A 1937 Library of Congress recording by W.H. Stepp (AFS 568) is a primary source. John Salyer (1882–1952) also recorded a version.

Jeff Titon (2001) says John Salyer (1882–1952) recorded a similar version of this local tune as "Stumptailed Dolly." John lived not far from the home of Stepp, and the two played together frequently, sharing repertoire. Salyer's home recording of "Stumptailed Dolly" from 1940/41 is archived at the Berea Sound Archives.

title: Sugar In Coffee
description: "Sugar in Coffee" is an American reel documented in the Ozarks by Vance Randolph in 1954. It is associated with regions including Arizona, Oklahoma, Arkansas, and Missouri.

title: Sugarbaby
description:
"Sugar Baby" is a traditional old-time tune widely circulated in the American South. A definitive recording was made in the late 1920s by Virginia banjo player Dock Boggs, whose modal style influenced its revival in the 1960s.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sugar Hill
description:
Researcher Mike Yates (2002) attributed "Sugar Hill" to George Washington Dixon (pre-1827). The title appears in Vance Randolph’s 1954 Ozark collection. The tune is strongly associated with Galax, Virginia, and Surry County, North Carolina, styles.

Music researcher Mike Yates (2002) reports that "Sugar Hill" is "believed to have been composed by George Washington Dixon some time prior to 1827," a version of which was published in New York in 1855 in Christy's Negro Songster, a mid-19th century collection of blackface minstrel songs.

title: Sunflower Hornpipe
description:
"Sunflower Hornpipe" is an American old-time hornpipe played in 4/4 time with a dotted, swung rhythm. Like many American instrumental tunes, it shares roots with earlier British traditions.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sunnyside
description:
"Sunnyside" is a traditional major-key old-time tune with a standard AABB structure. Its authorship is undocumented, as is common for tunes of this tradition.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sweet 'Bama
description:
"Sweet 'Bama" is associated with Stanley Bailey (1914–1988) of Berrien County, Georgia, a state fiddle champion in 1932 and 1934. Bailey was recorded in the field by several collectors in the 1980s.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sweet Bundy
description:
"Sweet Bundy" is a D-major reel. Fiddler Lotus Dickey learned it from his brother Cyprien, who learned it from Lee Trinkle of Orange County, Indiana.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sweet Dixie
description:
"Sweet Dixie" was composed by bluegrass banjo player Bill Emerson and recorded with Jimmy Martin around 1964. Martin suggested the title, noting its similarity to "Home Sweet Home," and insisted on the key of D after consulting fiddler Vernon Derrick.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sweet Jenny
description:
This tune originates as "Cader Idris," composed by Welsh harper John Parry (1776–1851) and published in *The Welsh Harper* (1839). It became popular in 19th-century England and was named after a Welsh mountain.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sweet Little Julie
description:
"Sweet Little Julie" is a D-major reel from the Blue Ridge mountains of southwest Virginia, typically played in cross-tuning (ADAE). The most documented source is fiddler Norman Edmonds.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sweet Marie Sheet Music 1893
description: "Sweet Marie" was composed by Raymon Moore with lyrics by Cy Warman in 1893. It was debuted in the musical comedy *Africa* in Cleveland. The song became a hit after singer Charles Hopper performed it.

title: Sweet Marie (NC version in D)
description:
"Sweet Marie" originated as a sentimental ballad written by Raymon Moore and Cy Warman in 1893 for the musical comedy *Africa*. It eventually entered the folk repertoire, where parodies were written using its limerick-like meter.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sweet Marie (WV version in A)
description:
"Sweet Marie," a song by Raymon Moore and Cy Warman (1893), transitioned from a pop ballad into the old-time repertoire, similar to the tune "Redwing."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sweet Nell
description:
"Sweet Nell" is a modern tune by Rob Pine and Jim Mullany. It is named for Nell Newman, daughter of actor Paul Newman, whose image appeared on the packaging of snacks the musicians ate during practice.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sycamores Along The Brandywine
description:
"Sycamores Along The Brandywine" appears on a 2003 recording by Walt Koken and Clare Milliner. The title likely refers to the Brandywine Valley of Pennsylvania and Delaware, a region historically significant to the old-time revival.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sycamore Shoals
description:
"Sycamore Shoals" is associated with the muster of the "Overmountain Men" militia prior to the 1780 Battle of Kings Mountain. The tune is named for a historical location in Elizabethton, Tennessee.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Tar River
description:
"Old Tar River" was written by minstrel performer Joel Sweeney around 1840. The Virginia Minstrels popularized the song, and Frank Brower is credited with performing it in 1841 with bone accompaniment.

The original song was written and composed by Joel Sweeney (1810–1860) around 1840.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Tater Patch
description:
Tommy Jarrell attributed "Tater Patch" to banjo player Ike Leonard, who reportedly composed it around 1910. Jarrell learned the tune from his uncle Charlie Barnett Lowe.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Taylor's Quickstep
description:
"Taylor's Quickstep" was recorded in 1929 by Leonard Rutherford and John D. Foster for Gennett Records. The tune was named for Dennis Taylor, a Gennett talent scout and the duo's manager, and was released under the pseudonym "Fox and Davis" on the Supertone label.

The tune was recorded in 1929 for Gennett Records in Richmond, Indiana, by fiddler Leonard Rutherford (1898–1951) paired with Kentucky singer John D. This is confirmed by Rick Kennedy's book "Jelly Roll, Bix, and Hoagy: Gennett Records and the Rise of America's Musical Grassroots" (2013), which agrees with Tony Russell, who also described Taylor as Rutherford & Foster's manager.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Temperance Hall
description:
"Temperance Hall" is a traditional old-time fiddle tune found in the American folk repertoire. Like many old-time tunes, its precise origin is difficult to pin down with certainty, as it was passed down orally through generations of fiddlers before being formally documented.

The name "Temperance Hall" is a direct reference to the temperance movement in 19th-century America, which advocated against the consumption of alcohol. Temperance Halls were physical meeting places — community buildings — where temperance societies gathered. It was common practice in old-time music to name tunes after local landmarks, events, or community institutions, and many tunes were played at dances held in such halls (somewhat ironically, given the halls' anti-alcohol mission). Key & Mode: Typically played in A major or D major, depending on regional tradition. Time: Standard 4/4 (or cut time) dance feel. Style: Falls in the category of hoedown/breakdown — a lively, rhythmically driving tune well-suited for square dancing and old-time sessions. Structure: Standard AABB 32-bar form, common to the old-time repertoire. The tune appears in old-time jam and session repertoire lists, particularly in the Appalachian and Midwestern traditions. It has been referenced in online old-time tune databases such as [The Session](https://thesession.org) and [ibiblio's tunebooks](https://www.ibiblio.org), though its documentation is sparse compared to more known tunes. Like many tunes of its era, no single composer is definitively credited — it is considered a traditional tune of unknown authorship.

title: Ten Cents
description: Ten Cents is a reel in the key of C from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Tennessee Politics
description:
John Hartford, a Nashville musician and newgrass pioneer, composed this tune; it was transcribed from his personal notebooks by Matt Combs. Hartford's archive contained over 2,000 original fiddle tunes composed during the final eighteen years of his life. [L1-L6]

He won four Grammy Awards, including two for his 1967 recording of "Gentle on My Mind." Hartford's journals date back to 1983, essentially coinciding with the sessions for his 1984 album Gum Tree Canoe, recorded at the Cowboy Arms Hotel and Recording Spa in Nashville.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Texas
description: This tune is associated with Henry Reed of Glen Lyn, Virginia. Alan Jabbour named the tune 'Texas' because Reed initially had no title for it, though Reed later attributed the source to a 'Mr. Drummond(s)' from Texas and also referred to it as 'New Castle'. [L16-L23]

title: Texas Barb Wire
description:
Popularized by Kenny Hall, who learned the tune in the late 1930s from Warren Raley. It is an American reel in G major. The title refers to Joseph F. Glidden's 1874 patent for barbed wire. [L27-L35]

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Texas Gals
description:
Recorded by Alonzo Elvis 'Tony' Alderman and Charles Bowman on Vocalion 5021 in 1927. The tune is in C major and features a three-part structure. [L40-L46]

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Texas Quickstep
description:
The tune carries one of the most storied attributions in American fiddle music. It was also known as "Rachel's Hornpipe," and is attributed to Rachel Jackson, wife of President Andrew Jackson. This makes the tune's roots stretch back to the early 19th century, long before it was commercially recorded — though whether Rachel Jackson actually composed it or merely inspired its name is unverifiable, as with many folk attributions.

The tune is also listed under the alternate titles "Missouri Quickstep" and "Texas Quickstep," with "Rachel" sometimes used as the primary title.

The tune's most important popularizer was Albert L. "Red" Steeley, the anchor of the Red Headed Fiddlers, a Dallas–Fort Worth duo. The recording is credited to the Red Headed Fiddlers (Dallas–Ft. Worth, Texas), specifically A.L. "Red" Steeley (1893–1969) and J. Warner "Red" Graham. The Red Headed Fiddlers featured fiddler A.L. "Red" Steeley and Red Graham on banjo, and they had a radio program in Ft. Worth for about 10 years during the 1920s up to about the time of the Depression. The program was almost entirely fiddling. Steeley and Graham recorded "Texas Quickstep" in 1928, and it stands as a prime example of a very tight and unified fiddle and banjo duet.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: The Third of July
description:
It is classified as an Old-Time Breakdown, played in G Major, with an AA′BB′ repeating structure.

The primary source for the tune is the Red Brush Rowdies, a West Virginia string band featuring fiddler Miller Wikel, who recorded in the 1930s.

The tune is also known as — or closely related to — "Cornshucker's Frolic."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Thread The Needle
description:
Here's what's known about the old-time fiddle tune "Thread the Needle" based on available sources: Classification: Traditional old-time fiddle tune. No single composer is credited — like many tunes in the old-time canon, it was passed down orally through regional playing communities. A catchy tune that fiddler Carl Jones first heard in Alabama in the 1970s, played by Joe Sharp. This is one of the clearest documented transmission stories for the tune — connecting it to the Deep South old-time tradition. The tune has been recorded and performed by Erynn Marshall, a prominent figure in the old-time world. Erynn Marshall is an old-time fiddler who resides in Galax, Virginia, and has played for over 30 years, performing and teaching at music camps and festivals across North America, Europe, Australia, and China. She won 1st place in fiddle at both the Clifftop and Mt. Airy Fiddlers Conventions. The recording was released as a traditional track on the album Old-Time Sweethearts - Vol. 1 & Vol. 2, performed by Erynn Marshall, Carl Jones, Rachel Eddy, and Em Hammond. On that recording, Rachel Eddy plays a Slim Jim banjo. "Thread the Needle" is also a well-known play-party and square dance figure in American folk tradition, where participants form an arch and "thread" through it — strongly suggesting the tune's title and character are tied to this social dance tradition. The lively, rhythmic nature of the melody fits perfectly for calling such figures.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: The Three Forks of Cheat
description:
A traditional tune known throughout West Virginia, most commonly associated with the Hammons family of Pocahontas County. The name refers to the local Cheat River geography. [L94-L100]

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Three Thin Dimes
description:
It was later recorded by the Hutchison Brothers band around 1976. [L104-L108]

According to Seattle fiddler and old-time music expert Kerry Blech, the source for the tune is Barnesville, Ohio, fiddler Old John Hutchison (1915–1979), who never formally recorded.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Tie-Hacker Hoedown #1
description:
Named for itinerant railroad tie cutters in late 19th-century Missouri. The labor of tie-hackers was a regional source of income for Ozark farmers before the industry declined in the 1930s. [L113-L117]

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Tie-Hacker Tune #2
description:
The name of the tune is rooted in a forgotten chapter of American labor history. A "tie-hacker" was an itinerant worker who cut ties from the north Missouri forest for the railroads in the late 1800s, following the Civil War. These tie-hackers helped construct the railway across northern Missouri by cutting railroad ties from the once abundant stands of white oak in the region. They were often Irish or Scots-Irish who lived in camps in the white oak woods, and some of their music was preserved in the playing of the Wilson family of Linn County, north-central Missouri.

Tie-Hacker Hoedown No. 2 comes from the playing of Nile Wilson (1912–2008), of Linn County, north-central Missouri. Wilson was the key figure through whom this tune family survived. The tunes come from the repertory of this northern Missouri fiddler, who played them (some in the form of a country rag) as fast breakdowns. Nile played a lot of tunes in C, a desirable key for square dance music, as the fiddle rings out nicely in that key.

Tie-Hacker Hoedown No. 2 is a Reel in cut time, in the key of C Major, played at a "Moderately Quick" tempo. It is part of a small family of related tunes — there is also a Tie-Hacker Hoedown #1 and a Tie-Hacker's Rag — all traced back to Wilson.

> ️ Note on labeling: The tune has been mislabeled on at least one compilation — appearing as Tie Hacker #2 on the Now That's A Good Tune: Masters of Traditional Missouri Fiddling CD when it is actually a different tune ("Old Reunion").

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Tilden to the Whitehouse
description:
Published in The Gettysburg Collection of Old-Time Fiddle Tunes, this G major tune is attributed to Ernie Carpenter (1909–1991) via Sandy Hofferth. [L133-L138]

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Tippy Get Your Hair Cut
description:
Learned by Bob Wine from a single performance by a fiddler named Jilly Grace. The tune was later popularized by his son, Melvin Wine (1909–2003). [L142-L148]

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Tomahawk
description:
Bob Holt learned this tune from Nashville fiddler Tommy Jackson, who recorded it in the 1950s and 60s. [L152-L156]

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Tom Fuller's Reel
description:
Tom Fuller (1890–1979) grew up in Indian Territory, later Oklahoma, and worked in farming, ranching and oilfields in Oklahoma and west Texas. He bought his first fiddle around 1905 and learned by ear. In the early 1920s he took lessons in Hulen, Oklahoma, and learned to read music.

Source: John Lamancusa collection, oldtimefiddletunes.net.

title: The Tune The Old Cow Died On
description:
The tune for the original comic song was written by Joseph Eastburn Winner — composer of the famous "Little Brown Jug" — with words by George Russell Jackson, and published in 1880 by John F. Perry & Co., Boston. The original full title was "The Tune that the Old Cow Died On." The sheet music is preserved and viewable at the Library of Congress: [loc.gov/item/sm1880.05588](https://www.loc.gov/item/sm1880.05588/).

The song tells of old Farmer John who came home one summer afternoon, sat beneath a maple tree, and sang himself a tune — drawing all the cows running up to form a ring around him, for they had never heard him attempt to sing before.

The oldest cow in the herd tried hard to join in the song, but she could not strike the melody, though her voice was loud and strong. The farmer laughed until tears ran down his cheeks, but the cow was so determined that she tried to sing until she dropped down dead.

title: Turkey Buzzard Laughed at Crow
description: Turkey Buzzard Laughed at Crow is a reel in the key of G from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Turkey in the Pea Patch
description:
An American reel in D major, first recorded by Uncle Dave Macon in 1927. It is distinct from 'Turkey in the Straw'. [L183-L188]

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Turkey Sag
description:
"Turkey Sag" is a composed old-time fiddle tune, not a tune of anonymous folk tradition — though it has spread so widely through the old-time community that many players assume it to be traditional.

Jim Childress wrote the tune in 1977 or 1978, and considers it the tune that made him take composing seriously. Remarkably, it came to be very widely played years before he ever officially recorded it — prompting him to finally record it so he could have some say in how the tune actually goes.

The tune was finally released on Childress's 2004 CD also titled Turkey Sag, a collection of 16 original fiddle tunes composed over roughly 25 years. Several of these tunes have become known and played by old-time musicians around the world. The original versions were performed by Uncle Henry's Favorites, Rick Epping, Jimbo Cary, and Barbara Payne.

The tune is catalogued in the Traditional Tune Archive as a Reel in D major, played in standard GDAE tuning, attributed to Jim Childress (as sourced from Eric Zorn's YouTube performance).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: 28th of January
description:
Sourced from West Virginia fiddler Franklin George, who learned it from Jim Farthing. George noted the title's origin was unclear. [L202-L208]

Modern revival fiddlers source the tune from Bluefield, West Virginia, fiddler Franklin George, who learned it from his mentor Jim Farthing, who called the tune "28th of January." Franklin George — William Franklin "Frank" George (6 October 1928 – 15 November 2017) was from Roane County, WV.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: 22nd of February
description:
Composed by Zeke Backus and first released by Snuffy Jenkins in 1962. The title commemorates George Washington's birthday. [L213-L215]

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))
notes: Snuffy Jenkins recorded a banjo version.

title: Twinkle Little Star
description:
Based on the 18th-century French melody 'Ah! Vous Dirai-Je, Maman', first printed in 1761. The lyrics were written by Jane Taylor and published in 1806. [L219-L224]

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Twinkle Twinkle Little Star
description:
This melody is derived from the 1761 French tune 'Ah! Vous Dirai-Je, Maman'. The lyrics are from Jane Taylor's 1806 poem 'The Star'. Mozart composed variations on the French tune in the late 18th century. [L228-L236]

Jane Taylor, who died in 1866, is unlikely to have seen any proceeds from her creation, and certainly had no idea of the millions of children she would end up delighting. Historians believe Mozart would have likely heard and composed on the French melody while he was in Paris between April and September of 1778.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Twin Sisters
description:
A floating title applied to multiple tunes, most commonly a D-major reel related to 'The Boys of Bluehill' or a modal tune from Carroll County, Virginia. [L240-L246]

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Two Bits
description: Two Bits is a reel in the key of G from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Uncle Frank's Piece
description:
According to The Gettysburg Collection of Old-Time Fiddle Tunes by John S. Lamancusa, "Uncle Frank's Piece" is played in the key of D, and its known transmission chain is: Bill Wellington ← Wilber Terry ← Frank Vance. This is the clearest documented lineage for the tune — it was passed down through oral/aural tradition from fiddler Frank Vance to Wilber Terry to Bill Wellington.

The violinist.com blog "Uncle Frank's Fiddle" offers a richly detailed portrait of a real-life "Uncle Frank" fiddler that provides context for how tunes with this kind of name originate: A cousin named Lee Williams, an accomplished fiddler, taught Frank "a few chords and the tune of 'Old Dan Tucker'" around 1907–1908, and another cousin, Harvey Walker, later taught him to tune his instrument and play by ear. Frank recalled: "I kept the folks away at night, practicing on that fiddle." He would work in the fields all day, whistling tunes he'd heard, then try to play them after supper into the night. Frank eventually wrote down the names of 120 songs he could play and sing from memory, including at least 40–50 old-time fiddle tunes. His repertoire included "Arkansas Traveler" (in D), "Whistlin' Rufus" (in G), and "Ft. Smith" (in G). Frank played his fiddle until he was 90 years of age, then gave it up at 91.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Uncle Pink
description: Uncle Pink is a reel in the key of G from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Valley Forge
description:
Named for the American Revolutionary War encampment, this tune was learned by Jimmie Driftwood from Arkansas fiddler Absie Morrison. [L265-L268]

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Vince Crawford's Tune
description: This tune originated with Vincent Crawford of Anderson County, Kentucky, and was recorded by Gus Meade and John Harrod in 1979. [L273-L277]

title: Wagoner
description:
Despite what the name conjures, "Wagoner" has nothing to do with Conestoga wagons. The title honors a Tennessee thoroughbred horse that competed in a hugely popular Louisville, Kentucky, horse race in 1839. John Hartford accepted that the tune "Grey Eagle" melody was once known as "Miller of Drone," and that the "Grey Eagle" title became attached to it in America following this famous late 1830s race between horses known as Grey Eagle and Wagner — a race that took place at the Oakland Racetrack in Louisville in 1838. The tunes "Wagner" and "Grey Eagle" both commemorate those two competing horses. Wagner was the smaller of the two; Grey Eagle stood 16 hands high and was legendary. The race attracted national attention — and Wagner beat Grey Eagle not once but twice.

These other "Wagoner/Wagner" tunes in the key of C descended from a "Wagner" tune first published in 1838 or 1839 under that title, in honor of the racehorse "Wagner."

The tune's melodic DNA is older than its American name. The first part is thought to be derived from "Billy in the Lowland/Lowground," while the second is a strain from an old Scottish air "Gaberlunzie," the earliest version of which can be found in Thompson's Orpheus Caledonius, 1725. This second strain has an old and venerable history in folk process; the second half of both "Wagoner" and "Gaberlunzie" greatly resemble the Scots tunes "Johnny Cope" and "Keep Off the Grass." Even the second half of the well-known "Mississippi Sawyer" may be derived from this element.

The tune was published as "The Hero" in George P.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Wagoner One Step
description:
A square dance tune in the key of C, named for an 1839 Kentucky racehorse. It is documented in the 1843 G. McMillan manuscript. [L293-L296]

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Waiting for the Boatsman
description:
This tune was in the repertoire of West Virginia fiddler Melvin Wine, who adapted it from a hymn his mother sang. [L300-L302]

The melody was in the repertoire of fiddler Melvin Wine (1909–2003), of Copen, Braxton County, West Virginia, who played it quickly, almost at dance tempo.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Waldorf Reel
description: Sourced from Guthrie Meade, this tune is named for both Waldorf, Maryland, and the reel-to-reel tapes used in field research. [L309-L313]

title: Walk Along John
description:
"Walk Along John" is an American reel (cut time), rooted in the states of Missouri, Arkansas, Oklahoma, and Texas, played in G Major with standard fiddle tuning. It is also known as "Come Along John" and "Johnny Walk Along with Your Paper Collar On."

The tune's story begins on the antebellum American stage. A minstrel song called "Walk Along John" or "Come Along, John" was published in 1844, with music and words attributed to J.P. Carter of the Virginia Serenaders in their published songbook, though it also states it is "an Old Southern Refrain" — possibly based on an African-American corn (shucking) song called "Shock Along John."

The tune quickly entered popular culture: it was popular enough to be employed in the 1844 Presidential race between Henry Clay (Kentucky) and James K. Polk (Tennessee), with each side sculpting the lyric to their political advantage.

Remarkably, an early version also appears in print far from America's South: there is a close version of the tune in The Boston Collection of Instrumental Music (1910), and it appears in the J. Roose manuscript from Manchester, England (1850). The tune was also notated in Thomas Briggs' Instructions for the Banjo (1855).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Walk Along John to Kansas
description:
Sourced from Arizona fiddler Kenner 'K.C.' Kartchner, though he suggested it had Southern roots. Field recorded by Alan Lomax in 1941. [L327-L331]

Kenner was born in Snowflake, Arizona in 1886 and is considered an important figure in the old-time music world.

title: Walk Chalk Chicken with a Necktie On
description:
This tune is a family heirloom of Melvin Wine (1909–2003) of Braxton County, West Virginia, who learned it from his father. [L335-L339]

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Walking in My Sleep
description:
A syncopated, ragtime-influenced breakdown from the Round Peak, North Carolina tradition, associated with Tommy Jarrell and Fred Cockerham. [L343-L345]

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Walking Uptown
description: Walking Uptown is a reel in the key of F from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Washington Courthouse
description:
Here is everything the web sources were able to surface about the old-time fiddle tune "Washington Courthouse", combined with the broader context that helps explain how a tune like this gets named, circulated, and preserved.

"Washington Courthouse" is named after Washington Court House, Ohio — the county seat of Fayette County in south-central Ohio. This type of place-name title is extremely common in old-time music; tunes were frequently named after the towns, counties, crossroads, or landmarks where they were popularized or first heard.

The most documented thread connecting this tune to a specific person and place comes from a 1983 field recording. A field recording from 1983 captures Jeff Goehring playing the tune, with Goehring citing his source as Estill Adams of Washington Courthouse, Ohio. This suggests Adams was a local traditional fiddler from Fayette County, Ohio, who preserved and transmitted the tune — a classic example of the oral folk transmission chain. The Canote Brothers (Greg and Jerry) also recorded the tune with the Small Wonder String Band, helping bring it to a wider old-time audience.

The story of "Washington Courthouse" reflects patterns common to the entire old-time canon: The titles of many fiddle tunes "conjure up people and places, incidents and functions" that are part of the texture of Appalachian frontier culture. The first fiddle tunes were passed from one generation to the next; as settlers spread out and mixed with other immigrant cultures, their different fiddle tunes and techniques began to mingle.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Washington's March
description:
"Washington's March" is a celebrated old-time Appalachian fiddle tune most closely associated with the Hammons family of West Virginia — one of the most storied fiddling dynasties in American folk music history. Despite its title, the tune is played in reel tempo, and may possibly be a very distant derivative of "Washington's Grand March," though there were many melodies in America that carried the Washington name — an indication of his influence even in backwoods areas.

The tune's definitive custodian was Edden Hammons (born Edwin Hammons, 1875–1955) of Pocahontas County, West Virginia. Allan Jabbour, in his 1984 liner notes to the Edden Hammons recording, says this is one of the tunes in the Hammons family repertoire that has special family associations — it was considered to have been composed by early family members, "or at least uniquely preserved by them."

Its original composer is unknown, said to have been written or simply collected by someone further down the Hammons family tree.

One of the most vivid pieces of lore around this tune comes from a 1947 field recording session. The folklorist Louis Watson Chappell stated that Edden Hammons won the 1939 Greenbrier Valley fiddle championship playing "Washington's March," and that he had learned it "59 years ago and first played it on a gourd covered by a deer skin."

title: Waterloo
description:
This tune belongs to a family of fiddle and pipe tunes composed in response to the Battle of Waterloo (June 18, 1815). John Gow (1764–1826), son of Scots fiddler Niel Gow, composed "Highland Brigade at Waterloo." Gow's publishing firm also issued "Lamentation for the Fallen Heroes of Waterloo" and "Royal Highlanders Welcome from Waterloo."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Waverley
description:
"Waverley" is associated with fiddler Art Galbraith (1909–1993) of the Missouri Ozarks. Galbraith reported learning the tune from his Uncle Tobe. Beisswenger & McCann note family tradition identifying it as an old Scottish tune.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Waynesboro
description:
"Waynesboro" is an American version of the Irish reel "Over the Moor to Maggie." Kentucky fiddler Doc Roberts popularized the tune, attributing it to African-American fiddler Owen Walker, from whom Roberts learned much of his repertoire.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Ways of the World
description: "Fiddling Bill" Stepp (William Hamilton Stepp, 1875–1947) of Magoffin County, Kentucky, is the source for this tune. He was recorded by Elizabeth and Alan Lomax for the Library of Congress in 1937. His name was long misidentified in indices as "W.M. Stepp."

title: The Week Before Christmas
description:
