Associated with Appalachian holiday customs, this tune is linked to the tradition of house-to-house dances. It may have been composed by Preston "Pet" McKinney, a Civil War veteran from Lambsburg, Virginia. Fiddler Tommy Jarrell cited McKinney as an early influence.

This account comes from Lawrence Bolt, a fiddler born in 1894 in Galax, VA.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Weller's Reel
description:
'Weller's Reel' is listed in the Traditional Tune Archive, which supplies notation but no composer or historical annotation. The listing is also reproduced at abcnotation.com.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org).

title: Wes Muir's Tune
description:
"Wes Muir's Tune" is a Missouri reel from the repertoire of fiddler Nile Wilson (1912–2008). It is named for a contemporary of Wilson's father, William Randolph "Dolph" Wilson, who lived in Linn County, Missouri.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Western Country/Susanna Gal
description:
This tune is known by various names including "Western Country," "Susanna Gal," and "Fly Away My Pretty Little Miss." It is a staple in the Galax, Virginia and Mt. Airy, North Carolina region. The melody is often traced to the English publication Wit and Drollery (1658).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Whistling Rufus
description:
Composed in 1899 by Kerry Mills (Frederick Allen Mills), "Whistling Rufus" was a "characteristic march" of the Tin Pan Alley ragtime era. The title refers to a solo performer who used guitar and whistling. Joyce Cauthen (1990) identifies it as a minstrel-style composition that entered the fiddle tradition.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: White Creek
description: "White Creek" is attributed to the Collins family and comes from Oklahoma fiddler Earl Collins (1911–1975). It was transmitted through the old-time community by fiddler Rafe Stefanini and is documented in Library of Congress recordings (AFS 14458).

title: Whiteface
description:
"Whiteface" was composed in the 1980s by Surry County, North Carolina fiddler Joe Thrift, who named it after a cow. It was first recorded on the 1989 album Ready to Roll by Thrift's band, The Red Hots.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: White's Polka
description: White's Polka is a reel in the key of C from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: White River
description:
Named for the White River in Missouri and Arkansas, this breakdown is attributed to Ozark fiddlers including Howe Teague, Gene Goforth, and John Hartford. Teague credited local fiddlers Roy Wooliver and Buck Sullivan.

Gene Goforth: His family treated it as a treasured heirloom piece, recorded on Eminence Breakdown (Rounder, 1997). John Hartford: Recorded it on Hamilton Ironworks (Rounder, 2001), helping bring it to a wider audience.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: White River Bottoms
description:
"White River Bottoms" is associated with Lotus Dickey (1911–1989) of Orange County, Indiana. Researcher Paul Tyler documented Dickey's account that the tune was a common square dance piece among older Indiana fiddlers.

The primary notated version is sourced from Lotus Dickey (1911–1989, Orange County, Indiana), recorded on Marimac CS 9030, Lotus Dickey – Fiddle Tunes from Orange County, Indiana, Vol. 2 (1992).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: White River Breakdown
description: "White River Breakdown" is an Ozark tune documented in the 1940s by folklorist Vance Randolph. Primary sources include Howe Teague, who learned it from fiddlers Roy Wooliver and Buck Sullivan.

title: White River Stomp
description:
"White River Stomp" was first recorded by Jack Cawley’s Oklahoma Ridge Runners in 1931. The tune shares melodic material with "Beaumont Rag," which was recorded by Smith's Garage Fiddle Band in 1928.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Who Hit Nellie with the Stovepipe
description:
Associated with the tune "Crooked Stovepipe," this name is primarily noted as an example of humorous fiddle nomenclature. "Crooked Stovepipe" is attributed to John Burt, pianist for George Wade and his Cornhuskers.

Authorship of Crooked Stovepipe is usually attributed to Jim Magill, a fiddler from Toronto and leader of Jim Magill and the Northern Ramblers, but it was most likely composed around 1932 by John Burt, piano player for George Wade and his Cornhuskers (a dance orchestra from Toronto).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Who Shit in Grandpa's Hat
description:
This tune is credited to fiddler Sandy Hofferth. It has been recorded by various performers, including the New Southern Cowtippers and the Dust Settlers.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Wild Goose Chase
description: "Wild Goose Chase" refers to a family of American reels from the Appalachians. Fiddler Emmett Lundy (1864–1953) of Grayson County, Virginia, was recorded playing this tune by the Lomax family in 1941. Lundy learned the tune from Greenberry Leonard, born c. 1810.

title: Wild Rose Of The Mountain
description:
"Wild Rose of the Mountain" was the signature tune of Kentucky fiddler J.P. Fraley (1924–2011). Fraley learned the tune from June Rice and Bun Oney in the 1950s. It was popularized by his 1974 release with Annadeene Fraley on Rounder Records.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Willits or Wontits
description: Willits or Wontits is a reel in the key of E from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Willow Creek
description:
"Willow Creek" is a three-part reel composed by Ralph Whited (1919–1994) of Blount County, Alabama. Named for a local fishing spot, the tune was documented in 1983 and released on the Field Recorders Collective album FRC 717.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Wilson's Clog
description:
"Wilson's Clog" is associated with minstrel performer Fred Wilson, who appeared with various companies starting around 1843 and was a prominent clog dancer in early American minstrelsy.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Wilson's Hornpipe
description:
"Mr. Wilson's Hornpipe" was composed by Edinburgh fiddler Robert "Red Rob" Mackintosh (c. 1745–1808) and appeared in his Fourth Collection of New Strathspey Reels (c. 1804).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Winder Slide
description:
"Winder Slide" is a 1980 composition by Joe LaRose of Kent, Ohio, written in the style of 1930s North Georgia recordings. Kerry Blech documented its transmission through the old-time community, noting that an early demo recording used intentional misdirection by posing as an old 78rpm track.

"Winder Slide" is a modern old-time tune composed around 1980 by Joe LaRose of Kent, Ohio, written in the style of Gus and Theodore Clark, who recorded two sides in North Georgia around 1930 — "Barrow County Stomp" and "Wimbush Rag." Despite being a relatively recent composition, it still sounds as if it could've been around for a century or so.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Wink the Other Eye
description:
"Wink the Other Eye" is an American reel documented in Kentucky, Tennessee, and Missouri. Music historian Charles Wolfe associated it with Sequatchie Valley, Tennessee fiddlers.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Wolf Creek
description:
The source for this tune is fiddler Roy Bennett (born c. 1895) of Meade County, Kentucky. The name is derived from Wolf Creek Road, where Bennett resided.

The sole source for the tune is fiddler Roy Bennett (born c. 1895), who in the 1940 census was living on Wolf Creek Road in Meade County, Kentucky, with his wife and five children.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Wooden Nickel
description:
"Wooden Nickel" is a modern composition written in the late 1970s by Mark Gaponoff of Seattle, Washington.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Wrassled With A Wildcat
description: "Wrassled With A Wildcat" is associated with fiddler Earl Collins (1911–1975). A recording by Collins is preserved in the Library of Congress (AFS 14458).

title: Yellow Barber
description:
"Yellow Barber" (also known as "Arthur Berry") is a Kentucky reel dating to the mid-1800s. Researcher John Heine linked the tune to a barber and fiddler named William B. Taylor (born 1821), who led an orchestra in Minnesota.

He died in 1862. Taylor, a fiddler born in Kentucky in 1821, who called the figures as he played — Taylor's Band, composed of barbers, played for hundreds of balls, banquets, and steamboat excursions in the Minnesota territory from 1849 until his death in 1862.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Yellow Gals
description:
"Yellow Gals" is a breakdown related to a family of tunes including "Buffalo Gals." It was documented by folklorist Vance Randolph in his list of Ozark fiddle tunes (1954).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Yellow Jacket
description:
"Yellow Jacket" was composed by Midwestern fiddler Garry Harrison and spread through oral transmission. The tune is typically played in cross-A tuning.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Yew Piney Mountain
description:
"Yew Piney Mountain" is a central West Virginia tune. Alan Jabbour (Digital Library of Appalachia) notes that the melody was historically identified as "Blackberry Blossom" before that title was adopted by a different tune.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Zack Wheat's Piece
description:
"Zack Wheat's Piece" is another instance of a tune known only by the name of a man who played it. Zack Wheat was an earlier fiddler of some renown who lived near Argyle, Missouri. According to Christeson (1973), this fiddler was an earlier musician who lived in that area. The tune belongs to the broader Missouri/Ozarks old-time tradition, a regionally rich fiddle culture.

There is an intriguing and unresolved overlap with a famous athlete of the same name. There was a baseball player named Zack Wheat whose career spanned 1909 to 1927. He was born in the north Missouri town of Hamilton in 1888. Wheat played primarily for the Brooklyn Dodgers and was proficient enough to have been elected to the Hall of Fame in 1959. His batting was prodigious — he won the National League batting title in 1918 (.335) and batted over .300 a total of fourteen times, compiling a lifetime average of .317.

It is unknown whether there is any connection between the ballplayer and the tune; however, there is a small state park dedicated to Zack Wheat (the ballplayer) in the Camden/Morgan County area of Missouri, not far from Osage County, where the town of Argyle — home of Christeson's fiddler — is located; a strange coincidence.

The tune was first formally documented by R.P. Christeson in his landmark 1973 collection. The source for the notated version is George Helton (Maries County, Missouri), as documented by Christeson, and Ike Helton (1907–1983, Maries County, Missouri) as documented by Beisswenger & McCann.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Batchelder's Reel
description:
Associated with Alvah Batchelder (1879–1968) and Albert Quigley (1891–1961), this reel appears as "Atlanta Hornpipe" in Ryan's Mammoth Collection (1883). It is a staple in contra dance circles.

The reel predates Batchelder, however, and was printed in Ryan's Mammoth Collection (1883) and its succesor, Cole's 1000 (1940), as the "Atlanta Hornpipe." The tune has been a staple among North American contra dance circles, particularly associated with New Hampshire, but can be found in the Pacific Northwest as well as New England.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: La Belle Catherine
description:
"La Belle Catherine" is a popular Québécois reel. The title refers to a longways dance dating to the 18th century, which folklorist Marius Barbeau attributed to French origins.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Brenda Stubbert's Reel
description:
AAB (Songer): AABB' (Cranford/Holland, Fiddler Magazine, Martin & Hughes, Shears). One of the most famous compositions by Inverness, Cape Breton, fiddler, teacher and composer Jerry Holland (originally from Brockton, Mass.) in honor of another Cape Breton fiddler and composer, Brenda Stubbert.

Notation sources: Carl & Jackie Webster (Cardigan, Central Kings County, Prince Edward Island) Perlman.

Published in Cranford (Jerry Holland's Collection), 1995; No. 40, p. 12. Fiddler Magazine, vol. 3, No. 2, Summer 1996; p. 17. Martin & Hughes (Ho-ro-gheallaigh), 1990; p. 18. Perlman (The Fiddle Music of Prince Edward Island), 1996; pg. 91. Shears (Gathering of the Clans Collection), 1986; p. 61 (pipe setting). Songer (Portland Collection), 1997; p. 40.

Recordings include BM-91, Buddy MacMaster - "Glencoe Hall." Boot Records, Jerry Holland - "Master Cape Breton Fiddler" (1982). Green Linnet SIF 1077, Capercaillie - "Crosswinds" (1987). Green Linnet SIF-1109, Altan - "The Red Crow" (1990). Green Linnett SIF1156, Jerry Holland - "Fiddlesticks Collection." SG155, Alasdair Fraser - "The Road North." Smithsonian Folkways SFW40491, Kinnon & Betty Beaton - "The Heart of Cape Breton" (2002, various artists). Patty Furlong - "Traditional Irish Music on the Button Accordion" (1999).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Campbell's Farewell To Red Gap
description:
This tune is a version of the Scottish march "Campbell's Farewell to Redcastle," which appeared in Robert Bremner's Scots Reels (1757). An earlier version of the melody appeared as a country dance titled "Hob or Nob" in Walsh's Caledonian Country Dances (c. 1745).

The melody is to be found as a country dance called "Hob or Nob" in collections earlier than Bremner — in Walsh's Caledonian Country Dances (4th book, c. 1745), in Johnson's Collection of 200 Favourite Country Dances (1748), and other contemporary dance books.

title: Charlie MacKerron's Reel (Islay Rant)
description:
Charlie McKerron is widely regarded as one of Scotland's finest fiddle players, having won the Daily Record Golden Fiddle Award. He first joined the Scottish Celtic supergroup Capercaillie in 1985 and has toured extensively throughout the world with the band.

Beyond Capercaillie, McKerron is an award-winning performer in his own right, leading his own fiddle supergroup Session A9. He is also an accomplished composer whose music has been widely recorded.

An accomplished composer, Charlie's music has been widely recorded and he has contributed to the film Rob Roy. Over the years he has performed with a wide variety of artists including Fish, The Pearl Fishers, and Fred Morrison.

The tune is a composition by Charlie MacKerron, the fiddler with the band Capercaillie. The dramatic and lyrical melody of the tune definitely comes from the northern [Scottish] tradition.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Chorus Jig
description:
One part (Burchenal): AB (Silberberg): ABCC or ABAC (ending on the A or B part)[Brody]: AABC (Ditson, Miller & Perron/1977): ABCD (Sweet): AABCCB (Kaufman): AA'BCC'B (Phillips): AABCCD (Miller & Perron/1983): AABCC'DD (O'Neill). Despite the title, the tune is a reel, with long histories both in Ireland and the United States. Linscott (1948) explains: "The 'Chorus Jig' has always been a favorite with pipers. It is an Irish melody whose author and date are unknown. Jigs were originally tunes sung after a play by the clowns. During the 17th century everyone sang them, and the dances were performed by persons of all ranks. They are generally thought of as Irish, but jigs were common in England and Scotland. The word 'jig' applied to a form of rhyme and is of uncertain derivation."

Perlman (1996) suggests the contra-dance reel called "Chorus Jig" originated from the jig form of the tune (see "Chorus Jig (3)"). In non-modal versions (as Randy Miller points out) it is the companion tune for a country dance of the same name in New England, and although the tune is Irish, the dance figures seem English according to experts.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Culburnie Cottage
description:
Culburnie Cottage is a D major reel composed by Alasdair Fraser. Fraser and pianist Paul Machlis began collaborating in 1983, recording the album Skyedance.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Dancing Bear
description:
The Dancing Bear is an American reel in E minor, composed by New Hampshire musician Bob McQuillen (1923–2014) on February 2, 1978. It was dedicated to a friend named Oso and Barry Nielson.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Dick Gossip's
description:
Dick Gossip's is an Irish reel in D major. While sometimes linked to an 18th-century highwayman, historical evidence for this figure is lacking.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: The Earl's Chair
description:
The Earl's Chair is an Irish reel attributed to flute player Patrick 'Pakie' Moloney of Woodford, East Galway, likely composed in the 1940s or 1950s.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Eddy's Reel
description: Eddy's Reel is a reel in the key of G from the Celtic tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Frenchie's Reel
description:
Frenchie's Reel is a Canadian reel in B-flat major, composed by Ward Allen and Mel Lavigne. It was recorded by Allen in 1957.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Homage a Belle Gaspesie
description:
Hommage à la Belle Gaspésie is an A major reel composed in the early 1980s by Québécois accordionist Marcel Messervier.

Hommage à la Belle Gaspésie is a French-Canadian Reel in the key of A Major, composed in the early 1980s by Québécois accordion player Marcel Messervier, born in Montmagny, Québec, in 1934.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Homage a Edmund Parizeau
description:
Hommage à Edmond Parizeau is a French-Canadian reel in A major. It is sometimes attributed to accordionist Marcel Messervier, who arranged it based on a 1953 recording by fiddler Edmond Parizeau, originally titled Reel du Commonwealth.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Joys of Quebec
description:
Joys of Quebec is an A major French-Canadian reel popularized in the 1920s by fiddler Fortunat Malouin (1870–1935). Its authorship is disputed, with rival fiddler A.J. Boucher publishing a competing version as a demonstration of technical variations.

His recording of "Les Joyeuses Québécoises" appeared on Columbia 34144-F (78 RPM) in 1928.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Reel Laurentides
description:
Reel Laurentides is a French-Canadian reel named for the Laurentian region of Québec. A documented version was transcribed from fiddler Isidore Soucy (1899–1963) in 1930.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: MacLeod's Farewell
description:
MacLeod's Farewell is a Scottish reel in E major, composed in the late 1980s by Donald Shaw for fiddler Martin MacLeod.

Composed in the late 1980's by Donald Shaw, a Scottish musician, composer, producer, and one of the founding members of the group Capercaillie.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: McQuillen's Squeezebox
description:
McQuillen's Squeezebox is a 4/4 march in C major, composed by Ralph Page (1903-1985) in honor of Bob McQuillen.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Reel de Montreal
description:
Reel de Montréal is a French-Canadian reel with a shifting G to D key structure. Different tunes circulate under this title; notable recordings include those by Joseph Allard and J.O. LaMadeleine in the 1930s.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Mouth of the Tobique
description:
Mouth of the Tobique was composed by Francis Sowish between 1910 and 1930. Originally titled French Mary, the current title stems from an attribution error by Don Messer.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Gray Cat
description:
Old Grey Cat is a reel of uncertain origin, appearing in Scottish and Irish traditions. The earliest known printed source is Kerr's Merry Melodies (c. 1880s).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Pays du Haut
description: Pays du Haut is a reel in the key of D from the Celtic tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Pointe Au Pic Reel
description:
Pointe-au-Pic is a small town on the St. Lawrence River near Charlevoix, northeast of Quebec City. It sits in one of the most storied regions for traditional Québécois fiddling, where French-Canadian folk music thrived for centuries in relative geographic isolation, preserving older modal styles and dance forms.

The Reel du Point-au-Pic is a Québécois fiddle tune written by Joseph Bouchard. Joe Bouchard was a great fiddler from the Charlevoix region, which is the region east of Quebec City.

Jos Bouchard started on the violin at the age of 8, probably with some classical training, as well as coaching from Huron fiddler Élie Sioué; by 14 he was playing dance. Fiddling was a sideline for Jos, who worked for the CNR railroad for 32 years, but he participated in local festivals.

Pointe-au-Pic was Bouchard's hometown — the tune is essentially a musical tribute to the village where he was born and raised. Bouchard had the habit of renaming tunes from his repertoire, so it is possible that the Reel de Pointe-au-Pic exists under another name somewhere.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Prince Charlie
description:
Prince Charlie is a cluster of related tunes commemorating Prince Charles Edward Stuart (1720–1788). The tune remains a fixture in Scottish and North American fiddle traditions.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Quickstep in the Battle of Prague
description:
Quickstep in the Battle of Prague is a programmatic composition by Bohemian musician František Kocžwara (c. 1750–1791), who was active in London.

He had been born in Prague, in the land of Bohemia, in 1730, and may well have witnessed the event in 1757 — Prussia vs. He roamed around Europe as a double bass player for hire, and by 1775 had ended up in London where he composed prolifically.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Reconciliation
description:
The Reconciliation is an A major tune of Irish, Canadian, and American tradition. It was renamed from The Olive Branch by Francis O'Neill, likely sourced from Ryan's Mammoth Collection (1883).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Reel des Jeunes Maries
description:
Réel des Jeunes Mariés is a French-Canadian reel in D major. Harmonica player Louis Blanchette recorded it in 1931. The modern contra dance version is attributed to Ralph Page.

"Le Réel des jeunes mariés" was recorded in 1931 (released January 1932) by harmonica player Louis Blanchette (1905–1969), who produced several marriage-themed reels among his many recordings in the 78 RPM era, among them "Reel des noces de diamant" (Diamond Wedding Reel, 1936), "Reel des fiançailles" (Betrothal Reel, 1932), and "Reel des noces d'or" (Golden Wedding Reel, 1935).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Road to Skye
description: Road to Skye is a reel in the key of A from the Celtic tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Ross's Reel (#4)
description: Ross's Reel No. 4 is an F major reel from the United States, popular in the late 20th-century New Hampshire contra dance repertoire.

title: St. Ann's Reel
description:
St. Anne's Reel is a French-Canadian reel in D major, now widely played in North American and Irish sessions. Early recordings include versions by Willie Ringuette (1927) and Joseph Allard (1930).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Thomas Tourish's Tune
description: Thomas Tourish's Tune is a reel in the key of D from the Celtic tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: The Trip To Pakistan
description:
The Trip to Pakistan is an E minor reel composed by flute player Niall Kenny in 1998.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Crabs In The Skillet
description:
Crabs in the Skillet is an Irish jig in 6/8 time. Collected by P.W. Joyce in 1854 from piper James Buckley, the tune is associated with the coast of Clare and Limerick.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Holm Band Tune
description:
The Holm Band Tune is a traditional jig in A major from Orkney, Scotland. It is named for the local Holm Band, the origins of which are not documented.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: I Buried My Wife and Danced on Her Grave
description:
I Buried My Wife and Danced on Her Grave is a 6/8 air in D Mixolydian. The tune is associated with Inagh, West Clare, piper Garret Barry (1847-1899).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Joanie's Jig
description:
Joanie's Jig is a D major jig composed by Nancy Martin of Vancouver, Washington, for Joan Hathaway.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Kerfunken Jig
description:
Kerfunken Jig is an Irish jig composed by Belfast-born flute player Hammy Hamilton. He named the tune after a suburb of Quimper, Brittany, though the spelling was altered.

The tune was composed by flute player and flute maker Hammy Hamilton, born in Belfast in 1953, although he makes his home (and his flutes) in County Cork, Ireland.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Little Burnt Potato
description:
AB (Begin): AABB (Brody): AA'BB' (Barnes, Bayard, Carlin, Messer, Miller & Perron, Perlman, Phillips). "Little Burnt Potato" was popularized by Canadian Maritime radio and TV fiddler Don Messer. The tune has been characterized as Irish in origin, although in fact it is the composition of Canadian fiddler Colin J. Boyd, who was himself of Scottish descent. Boyd was born in West Lakeville, Nova Scotia, in 1891, and learned to play the fiddle as a child, inspired by his uncle Hughie MacGillivary (whose fiddle he inherited). Like many in the community, he learned and spoke Gaelic. Due to a declining ecomony, Boyd found work in 1909 in Ontario, then moved to Boston for the years 1911-1916 where he studied violin and learned to read music. It was during his Boston years that he composed "Little Burnt Potato." Boyd had the distinction of being the first Nova Scotian fiddler to record in 1932, in Montreal for the Brunswick label. He later settled in Ontario, and passed away in 1975.

"Little Burnt Potato" is Boyd's adaptation of an old Scottish jig passed on to him by Dan “The Ridge” MacDonald, formerly of Mabou, Cape Breton, and then Antigonish, Nova Scotia, according to Mary Boyd (liner notes to Shanachie Records, CB-1). His jig proved popular and has been widely disseminated, and has been interpreted in a number of styles. It has been a staple of New England contra dances.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Da Lounge Bar
description:
Da Lounge Bar is a tune written by Norwegian fiddler Annlaug Børsheim, named for a session venue in Lerwick, Shetland.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: One Horned Sheep
description:
One Horned Sheep is a jig with disputed origins, linked to both Scottish and Irish traditions. The tune appeared in Ryan's Mammoth Collection (1883) titled The Boss.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Paddy Fahy's Jig
description:
Paddy Fahey (also spelled "Fahy," 17 August 1916 – 31 May 2019) was an Irish composer and fiddler considered one of the finest living composers of tunes in the style of traditional Irish music.

Born in the year of the Rising, 1916, and a native of Kilconnell in east Galway, Paddy Fahey grew up on a farm in Killaghbeg House. From a musical family, he began playing the fiddle at the age of five. His father, Jack Fahy, was a notable fiddle player and founder of the Aughrim Slopes Céilí Band. Paddy became a member of the band in the 1940s and toured throughout the UK and America — but the bright lights of the city weren't for him, and he chose to remain in his beloved East Galway, living and working as a farmer.

Paddy Fahy's Jig (Irish title: Port Phádraig Uí Fhathaigh), also known simply as "Paddy Fahey's," is an Irish Double Jig in G Major, in standard fiddle tuning, with an ABB (or AA'BB') structure.

It is a modern composition of Kilconnell, east County Galway, fiddler Paddy Fahey that has gained wide currency. Written by Paddy Fahey, it is one of his most popular tunes and is considered an Irish standard today — a must-know tune for any Irish fiddle session player.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: R. Aim's Compliments to J. Craigie
description:
Ronnie Aim's Compliments to Jimmy Craigie is a D major jig. The tune appears on the recording Mither o' the Sea by Orcadian fiddlers Jennifer and Hazel Wrigley, suggesting an Orcadian origin.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Strayaway Child
description:
"The Strayaway Child" is a 6-part traditional Irish jig composed by Michael Gorman, rooted in the Sligo area of Ireland. It is a dance tune in compound time (6/8 or 9/8), with a characteristic lilting rhythm.

The tune has one of the most romantically unusual origin stories in Irish traditional music. It was composed by Margaret Barry around 1956, with the help of Sligo fiddler Michael Gorman (who lived in London most of his life). Parts of the tune came to Barry in a dream, which was then developed by Gorman.

From the sleeve notes of Portrait: Margaret Barry — Margaret's jig "The Strayaway Child" is now well known among Irish musicians. She describes how it came to her in a dream. In its final form, it was too complex to tackle on the banjo, and it was left to her collaborator Michael Gorman to popularize it.

In her own words, Barry said: "Now and again, I do dream, of music all the time. And there's music coming into my head, when I'm dreaming, that I've never heard in reality. It's just one of those things that even — I composed a jig of me own. It was true, a bit of dreaming that I got the parts of that dream. I only remembered a couple of parts of that."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Swelkie
description: Swelkie is a jig in the key of G from the Celtic tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Tripping Up the Stairs
description:
Tripping Up the Stairs is a traditional Irish jig. It is attributed to the Co. Mayo fiddler John McGrath (1900–1955), who reportedly called it The Jew Jig.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: The White Petticoat
description:
"The White Petticoat" (Irish: An cota-beag ban) is an Irish double jig in 6/8 time. It is a well-known two-part traditional Irish jig played out of the key of E minor. The tune follows an AABB structure in standard fiddle tuning.

This is where things get interesting. Unlike many Irish tunes with clearly traceable roots, The White Petticoat's origins are genuinely murky: The provenance of the tune is not known — many have remarked on its unusual nature in the context of the bulk of O'Neill's collection, and the melody is only sourced to Francis O'Neill himself (a very loose source attribution, as O'Neill often put his name to tunes he learned from in the course of years of playing with Irish musicians from Chicago and other areas). It is one of the few tunes in O'Neill's in aeolian minor — nearly all minor-sounding tunes in that collection are in dorian. This alone makes it stand out as something of an outlier in the Irish traditional canon. It's a very eerie, pretty tune with a bit of a Spanish/Mediterranean feel in the second half due to the D# implying the harmonic minor. It kind of feels like a Morris Dance tune to some, but no such link has been found.

The earliest printed source is Francis O'Neill's landmark 1903 collection: It appears in O'Neill's Music of Ireland (1903), also known as O'Neill's 1850. It was also reprinted in O'Neill (Krassen), 1976, p. 74, and Knowles' Northern Frisk (1988), No. 38.

Captain Francis O'Neill (1848–1936) was Chicago's chief of police and an obsessive collector of Irish traditional music.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: DeDannan Polka Set (Julia Clifford's/O'Keefe's Polka/Johnny I Do Miss You)
description:
A polka medley from the Sliabh Luachra region of Ireland, featuring three tunes associated with local fiddlers. The set was recorded by De Dannan on the 1980 album The Mist Covered Mountain. "Julia Clifford's" (polka) is also known as "Johnny Leary's," "Johnny O'Leary's," and "Tarrant's."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Ducks of Magheralin
description:

title: Toormore Polka
description:
The Toormore Polka (also spelled Tournmore, Tuar Mór, or Crosaire De Bhalis) is a traditional Irish polka, not an American old-time tune. It is part of the rich polka tradition of Munster (southwest Ireland), closely associated with the West Kerry / Sliabh Luachra region. There are actually two Toormore Polkas — a First and a Second — both circulating widely in Irish traditional sessions and fiddle instruction. "Toormore" is the anglicized form of the Irish Tuar Mór, a place name in County Cork, on the Mizen Peninsula in West Cork. The tune takes its name from this locality — a common naming convention in Irish traditional music where tunes are named after the townland, parish, or area where they were played or collected. It is also known by alternate titles including Tuar Mór Polkas 1, The Tuar Mór, and Wallace's Cross.

The tune belongs to the broader Irish polka tradition: The polka (polca in Irish) is one of the most popular traditional folk dances in Ireland, particularly in Sliabh Luachra, a district spanning the borders of counties Kerry, Cork, and Limerick. Many figures of Irish set dances, developed from Continental quadrilles, are danced to polkas. Introduced to Ireland in the late 19th century, there are today hundreds of Irish polka tunes. The Irish polka is a dance music form in 2/4 time, typically 32 bars long, subdivided into four parts played AABB. Irish polkas are typically played fast, at over 130 bpm, with an off-beat accent.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: The Poppy Leaf (Hornpipe)

title: Haughton House
description:
"Haughton House" is a Scottish march, not an American old-time tune in the traditional Appalachian sense — but it has traveled widely across traditions and appears in Irish, Shetland, and folk revival repertoires, making it feel like a shared old-time/traditional tune today. Haughton House is a manor in Aberdeenshire, near the village of Alford on the banks of the River Don, and the tune was composed by a James Mitchell, published on a single sheet with variations by James Scott Skinner. It is classified as a Scottish March in G Major, in standard tuning, with an AABB structure. The tune was played in the Shetland Islands (especially Uist) as a wedding march and was sometimes labeled a Shetland tune; however, the melody is mainland Scottish in character and appears to have been originally called "Haughton House." The tune was known for a time as "Auchadon House" (probably a mishearing), and was thought to be from Shetland — but it was composed by James Mitchell and published as a single sheet with variations by James Scott Skinner. Shetland fiddler Debbie Scott confirmed this confusion: she knew nothing about the tune's history "other than it is not a Shetland tune," was not aware of it being used as a wedding tune in Unst, and speculated "maybe someone used it once and it got picked up on" — agreeing it is "probably plain Scottish." A related tune, "R.O.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sonny Brogan's Mazurka (#1)
description:
Mazurkas originated in Poland and spread across Europe in the 1800s, both as tunes and as a dance form. They found their way to Ireland in the mid-1800s and became a traditional tune form there, particularly in County Donegal.

"Sonny's Mazurka" is perhaps the most well-known of all Irish mazurkas.

Patrick Joseph "Sonny" Brogan (4 July 1906 – 1 January 1965) was an Irish accordion player from the 1930s to the 1960s, and was one of Ireland's most popular traditional musicians. He was one of the earliest advocates of the two-row B/C button accordion in traditional music and popularized it in the 1950s and '60s.

Sonny was born in Dublin on the 4th July 1906, the eldest of three children born to Andrew Brogan and Alicia Brown. It has been suggested that Sonny first developed an awareness of Irish music as a young boy while on holidays in Kildare and heard his uncle Thomas Cleary playing the accordion. He taught himself to play the accordion and as a young man attended piano lessons for a while.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sonny Brogan's Mazurka (#2)
description:
"Sonny's Mazurka" is perhaps the most well-known of Irish mazurkas. It is in D Major, in 3/4 time, and typically follows an AABB structure. The "#2" designation (vs. #1) refers to the fact that two distinct mazurkas circulate under Brogan's name — these two are often played together, and it is suspected they were both in Sonny Brogan's repertoire, which accounts for them both being tagged with his name, despite their differences and similarities.

Mazurkas originated in Poland and spread across Europe in the 1800s, both as tunes and as a dance form. They found their way to Ireland in the mid-1800s, and became a traditional tune form there, particularly in County Donegal.

Patrick Joseph "Sonny" Brogan (4 July 1906 – 1 January 1965) was an Irish accordion player from the 1930s to the 1960s, and was one of Ireland's most popular traditional musicians. Despite the tune being closely associated with fiddle playing, Brogan was actually an accordionist, not a fiddler. He was one of the earliest advocates of the two-row B/C button accordion in traditional music, and popularised it in the 1950s and 60s. He originally played on a single-keyed Hohner melodeon, and later the two-row Paolo Soprani, which he used until he died. Sonny Brogan was born in Dublin, the eldest of three children. On a holiday trip to Kildare as a young boy, he first heard Irish music played on the accordion by his great uncle, Thomas Cleary.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Black Hills Waltz
description:

His early career as an itinerant fiddler — which began around the time his father was serving a Mormon mission — made him a sort of "rock musician" of his day.

He is the central figure associated with the Black Hills Waltz, and the tune's transmission to modern players runs entirely through him.

title: Country Waltz
description:
The tune simply called "Country Waltz" is one of those old-time gems whose precise origins are somewhat murky — a common fate for tunes that traveled through oral tradition across North America.

The most detailed paper trail for "Country Waltz" leads to Canada. Missouri fiddler and researcher Charlie Walden first heard this waltz on the old K-TEL record 25 Old-Tyme Fiddle Hits, which was actually an American reissue of a Canadian record on the Arc label (FH-2). On the U.S. K-TEL version none of the fiddlers were identified, but the Canadian issue told the names — and the fiddler playing "Country Waltz" on that album was Ned Landry of New Brunswick.

Ned Landry (1921–2009) was one of the most celebrated Maritime Canadian old-time fiddlers, known for his smooth, melodic style. The K-TEL/Arc record was a major vehicle by which the tune spread southward into American old-time circles.

Several of the old-time fiddlers around Mid-Missouri picked up this tune — Taylor McBaine being among them. This mirrors the pattern of many Canadian tunes filtering into Midwestern fiddle communities via records and radio.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Don't You Remember The Time
description:
"Don't You Remember The Time" appears in the repertoire catalogued at Tater Joe's Old-Time Fiddle resource, listed among a broad collection of traditional G-tuning fiddle tunes. Unlike many neighboring tunes in that same list — such as Dandy Jim (attributed to Clyde Davenport), Double File (Gaither Carlton), or Devil In The Strawstack (Tommy Jarrell) — "Don't You Remember The Time" is listed without a specific attribution or source fiddler, which is common for tunes that have entered the general old-time commons without a traceable single originator or collector. Regional tradition: The tune sits comfortably in the Southern Appalachian and Upper South old-time tradition, a genre where tunes passed orally through communities over generations, making pinning down a single composer or "inventor" nearly impossible. Naming convention: The title follows a classic old-time pattern of question-phrase titles (e.g., "Did You Ever See the Devil Uncle Joe", "Don't You Mind the Weather"), often connected to older songs or dances that predated formal recording. No commercial recording credit: Unlike tunes recorded in the 1920s–30s commercial hillbilly era (e.g., by Fiddlin' John Carson or Henry Gilliland), this tune does not appear to have a well-documented early 78rpm recording tied to a named fiddler.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Julia Waltz
description:
The most specific attribution found comes from the fiddle community itself. A member of the Fiddle Hangout forum notes that the tune was written by Jeff Kaufman of Free Raisins, and that "Julia" is believed to be his wife or daughter. The poster also mentions loving the way "Audrey (the Fiddler)" plays it. This suggests the tune is a composed waltz by a known modern author, rather than an anonymous traditional piece passed down through generations.

European dance styles that became popular in the United States during the 19th century — including the quadrille, polka, schottische, two-step, and waltz — provided new tunes and additional fodder for original compositions. New types of fiddle tunes emerged in the US, including breakdowns, blues, and rags.

Despite the fact that the majority of the old-time fiddle tradition consists of very old tunes with no known authorship, new fiddle tunes have always been written and are still being written today. The Julia Waltz fits squarely into this category of newer original compositions in the old-time style.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Kansas Waltz
description:

title: Keys To The Kingdom
description:
"Keys to the Kingdom" is an old-time fiddle tune that appears in various old-time and American folk music collections. It is sometimes listed under alternate titles and is part of the broader Appalachian and American fiddle tradition.

The tune is associated with the old-time fiddle repertoire of the American South and Appalachian region. Like many old-time tunes, its exact composer and precise origin are difficult to pin down definitively, as the tradition was largely oral and passed from fiddler to fiddler across generations rather than through formal composition or publication.

The title "Keys to the Kingdom" reflects a strong thread of sacred and gospel-influenced imagery that runs through old-time fiddle music, particularly tunes from the American South, where religious life and community music-making were deeply intertwined.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Kiss Waltz

title: Lament Of The First Generation
description:
This tune was composed by Liz Carroll, one of the most celebrated Irish-American fiddlers of the modern era. It was released on Liz Carroll's album "Lost in the Loop" on February 1, 2000. The oldest known source for the tune, considering indexed recordings and transcriptions, dates to 2000.

Liz Carroll is a Chicago-born Irish-American fiddler and composer, widely regarded as one of the foremost composers of new Irish traditional music. She is known for writing tunes that feel deeply rooted in the traditional idiom while carrying a distinctly personal voice — the title "Lament of the First Generation" is widely understood to reflect themes of immigrant identity, the experience of first-generation Irish-Americans caught between two worlds.

It is a waltz (3/4 time) in G major, with four known settings documented in the Irish traditional music community. The standard transcription is an exact copy from Carroll's own handwritten sheet music, which was previously available on her website.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Mr. Fisher's Old German Waltz
description:
The tune's name is quite literal — it traces directly to a real person. "Mr. Fisher's Old German Waltz" was learned from a Mr. Fisher of Bowling Green, Missouri, who described the tune as "an old German waltz" — which became the basis for the title.

The fiddler who collected and popularized it was Lynn "Chirps" Smith, a celebrated Midwestern old-time fiddler from Illinois. Along with the waltz, Chirps also learned a tune called "Bowling Green" from Mr. Fisher.

Chirps Smith is the figure most responsible for preserving and spreading this tune. Described as "the Midwest's premier fiddler," Smith presents tunes that evoke memories of front-porch music-making on the Illinois prairie and dances in the hollers of Little Egypt, in a style he calls simply "Midwestern."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: My Pretty White Kitty
description:
John Dee Kennedy (1914–1997) was a self-effacing man who, in his prime, was considered by many to be the best breakdown fiddler in Pawnee and Osage counties, Oklahoma.

In a generation where most of his contemporaries were playing Western swing, bluegrass, or Texas contest style fiddle, John perpetuated an older family and community tradition that can be traced through the mountains of Arkansas all the way back to earlier roots.

"My Pretty White Kitty" is catalogued as a waltz, attributed to John Dee Kennedy, and appears in old-time fiddle tune indexes alongside similarly rare and regionally specific pieces.

title: Olga Blom's Waltz
description:
This waltz is in the key of C and sourced from the collection Across the Fields – Traditional Norwegian-American Music from Wisconsin. It is associated with the Norwegian-American immigrant tradition in the Upper Midwest. The title refers to Olga Blom, likely the composer or the dedicatee, following a common naming convention in Scandinavian-American music.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Over The Waves
description:
José Juventino Policarpo Rosas was a Mexican composer and violinist, known worldwide for the waltz "Sobre las olas" ("Over the Waves"). He was born to an indigenous Otomí Mexican family in 1868 in a village in Guanajuato, which was later renamed in his honor in 1939 as Santa Cruz de Juventino Rosas.

His father, Juan de Jesús Rosas, had made a career playing harp in a military band and encouraged his children's talent. Taught by his father, Juventino became a violin prodigy and was joined by his brothers Manuel (guitar) and Patrocinio (singer) to form a traveling band. Together, with their father on harp, they performed at festivals and other celebrations.

In 1875, the family headed to Mexico City in search of better opportunities. Equipped with a simple fiddle, the child Juventino played folk tunes and popular songs in the streets of the densely populated barrio known as Tepito, then notorious for its poverty and crime.

The waltz "Sobre las olas" ("Over the Waves") is the best-known work of Rosas, who first published it in 1888. Casino owners Vicente Alfaro and Calixta Gutiérrez de Alfaro, important arts funders, commissioned Rosas to write a festival piece in the mid-1880s, which resulted in "Sobre las olas" (dedicated to Calixta). The specific origins of its inspiration are shrouded in lore.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Ook Pik (Ootpik) Waltz
description:
"Ookpik Waltz" is a late 20th-century composition by Mission, British Columbia fiddler Frankie Rodgers (1936–2009), who published it in his tune book and copyrighted it in 1965. It was first recorded in 1973 on the album Maple Sugar, Fiddle Favourites by Canada's Old Time Fiddle King.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Orvetta Waltz
description: "Orvetta Waltz" is a 19th-century piano piece composed by E.B. Spencer and published in 1879 by the Oliver Ditson Company in Boston. It is written in 3/8 meter in the key of A and dedicated to Miss Mary E.R. Johann.

title: Ozark Waltz
description:
Recorded in June 1930 in Memphis by the Morrison Twin Brothers String Band of Searcy County, Arkansas, this old-time waltz is in F major and uses standard tuning. Scholar Guthrie Meade suggests it may be based on an early 20th-century song, noting an Earl & Joe recording from 1930.

"Ozark Waltz" was originally recorded in Memphis, Tennessee, in June 1930, by the Morrison Twin Brothers String Band of Searcy County, Arkansas, featuring the twin fiddles of Abbie (1876–1965) and Absie (1876–1964, sometimes "Apsie") Morrison, who were themselves twins, backed up on guitars by Abbie's sons Claude and Lawson.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Paris Waltz
description:
Composed by Arthur Smith (1898–1971), "Paris Waltz" is named after Paris, Tennessee. Smith recorded the piece for Bluebird Records in 1938 in Charlotte, North Carolina, backed by guitarists Alton and Rabon Delmore.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Peek-A-Boo Waltz
description: "Peek-a-Boo Waltz" is derived from a song by Irish-American composer William J. Scanlan (1856–1898), published in 1881 and performed in the play Friend & Foe. In 1883, L.A. Benjamin arranged the melody as a waltz, which was published by T.B. Harms in New York.

title: Pinedale Waltz
description:
"Pinedale Waltz" is associated with Arizona fiddler Kenner Casteel Kartchner and the town of Pinedale, Arizona. Authorship is sometimes attributed to Frank Pruitt (Shumway, 1990). The tune is documented in Frontier Fiddler and the Milliner-Koken Collection.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Poor Girl Waltz
description:
This waltz, also known as "Poor Girl's Waltz," was recorded in May 1929 by West Virginia fiddler Reese Jarvis (1900–1967) and guitarist Dick Justice for Brunswick Records in Chicago.

The tune is classified as an American/Canadian waltz in 3/4 time, and goes by both "Poor Girl's Waltz" and "Poor Girl Waltz." The waltz was recorded in May 1929 for Brunswick Records by fiddler Reese Jarvis (1900–1967, of Clendenin, West Virginia) and guitarist Dick Justice (1906–1962), in Chicago, Illinois.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Poughkeepsie Waltz
description: Poughkeepsie Waltz is a waltz in the key of F. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Pretty Waltz
description: Pretty Waltz is a waltz in the key of C. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Quabbin Waltz
description:
"Quabbin Waltz" is an English Country Dance devised by Gary Roodman in 2023 and published in Countable Calculated Figures.

The track "Quabbin Waltz" by Gary Roodman was released on July 18, 2024, and also appears on the album Summersweet.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Ranger's Waltz
description:
"Ranger's Waltz" was composed by Quentin Ratliffe, saxophonist for the Spokane, Washington band The Mom and Dads. The group recorded the waltz in 1971, and it was later released on the 1980 album 20 Favorite Waltzes.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Red Fox Waltz
description:
"Red Fox Waltz" is a D major old-time waltz attributed to fiddler Harold Allen (1925–2012), who credited it on his album Fiddling Around. It is frequently associated with Missouri fiddlers and became popular at the Weiser, Idaho, national fiddle contest in the 1960s.

There is also a field recording of Harold Allen playing the waltz at the Weiser, Idaho national fiddle contest in 1966, preserved courtesy of Vivian & Phil Williams.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rockin' The Babies to Sleep
description: Rockin' The Babies to Sleep is a waltz in the key of D. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rosalita Waltz
description: Rosalita Waltz is a waltz in the key of C. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rose Waltz
description:
This tune is associated with Nebraska fiddler Uncle Bob Walters (1889–1960) and is documented in the 1976 collection Old Time Fiddler's Repertory.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sonny's Mazurka
description:
"Sonny's Mazurka" is a known Irish mazurka, a dance form that arrived in Ireland from Poland in the 1800s. It is named for Dublin accordionist Sonny Brogan (1906–1965), a member of Ceoltóirí Chualann.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Stars And Stripes Waltz
description:
"Stars and Stripes Waltz" is associated with the Missouri/Ozark fiddle tradition. A documented version in the key of C was performed by fiddler Lonnie Robertson, sourced from Luther Hampton and featured on Fiddle Tunes Ozark Style Vol. 2.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Swedish Waltz
description:
The "Swedish Waltz" in the American old-time tradition—notably that of Bob Walters of Nebraska—is distinct from other catalogued tunes of the same name.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Tears Of Love
description:
"Tears of Love" is a sentimental waltz-style tune within the American old-time tradition. It exists in various regional variants and is typically played in a slow, expressive style.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Terra Mollada
description: Terra Mollada is a waltz in the key of Am. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Tombigbee Waltz
description:
"Tombigbee Waltz," also known as "Gum Tree Canoe," is a G major waltz with roots in 19th-century minstrelsy. The song "Tom Big Bee River" is attributed to S.S. Steele, with sheet music appearing in various collections including the 1909 Heart Songs.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Tommy Bhetty's Waltz
description:
This waltz was composed by fiddler Tommy Maguire from Kinawley, County Fermanagh, Ireland. "Bhetty" is a traditional patronymic/matronymic addition to his name, derived from his mother, Betty.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Tuscaloosa Waltz
description:
"Tuscaloosa Waltz" was composed by Mississippi fiddler Will E. Ray of the Ray Brothers. It was recorded in Memphis in 1930 and released on Victor 23552 in 1931. The waltz is in the key of C.

Alabama fiddler James Bryan recorded the tune on the Rounder Records album "Lookout Blues" (1983), having learned it directly from the original 78 RPM recording by the Ray Brothers of Mississippi.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Valse Gisele
description:
"Valse Gisèle" is a 1994 composition in D major by French-Canadian fiddler Yvon Cuillerier of Saint-Bruno, Quebec.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: La Vie Est Pas Donne
description: La Vie Est Pas Donne is a waltz in the key of A. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Waltz of the Little Girls
description:
Also known by various French titles, this waltz was learned by American multi-instrumentalist Grey Larsen in 1978 from Belgian fiddler Raymond Honay.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Wednesday Nite Waltz
description:
The Leake County Revelers, featuring fiddler Wil Gilmer, recorded this tune for Columbia Records in 1927, where it became a notable seller. Scholars debate its origins, with some linking it to a popular song and others noting Gilmer picked it up in Texas.

The Leake County Revelers' version was the second best-selling country music record of 1927 (backed by "Goodnight Waltz") and the biggest old-time seller of 1928, recorded for Columbia Records.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Wednesday Night Waltz
description:
Scholars debate whether this tune originated from a popular song or from the Mississippi-based Leake County Revelers. Fiddler Wil Gilmer noted he learned the tune in Texas.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: West Leyden Waltz
description:
"West Leyden Waltz" is a G major waltz composed by Jimmy Nelson (1900s) from Oneida County, New York, and named for the nearby hamlet of West Leyden.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Westphalia Waltz
description:
"Westphalia Waltz" is a Texas fiddle tune credited to Cotton Collins of the Lone Star Playboys. Its melody is derived from a Polish song known variously as "Pytala Sie Pani" or "Wszystkie Rybki," which was known among Polish-American immigrant communities.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Ali Oidak Polka
description:
"Ali Oidak Polka" is a fiddle tune from the Tohono O'odham nation in Southern Arizona. It was recorded by the Gu-Achi Fiddlers on the album Old Time O'odham Fiddle Music.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Biscuit Cheeks Two Step
description: Biscuit Cheeks Two Step is a reel in the key of G from the Texas tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Cababi Polka
description:
"Cababi Polka" is an instrumental tune from the Tohono O'odham tradition, specifically associated with Elliott Johnson of the Gu-achi Fiddlers, who lived in Cababi, Arizona.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Caballito Blanco
description:
"Caballito Blanco" (Little White Horse) is a widely distributed folk song found throughout the Spanish-speaking world, appearing as a jump rope rhyme and a children's song. Its exact origin remains contested between Spain and Latin American variants.

One correspondent noted that she read the tune is from Chile, but was born in northern Mexico where her grandmother (born in 1899) sang it to her, and her grandmother's grandmother also sang it to her.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: La Cadena Waltz
description: La Cadena Waltz is a reel in the key of C from the Texas tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Celeya Polka
description: Celeya Polka is a reel in the key of G from the Texas tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: La Comancha Waltz
description: La Comancha Waltz is a reel in the key of A from the Texas tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Cuadrilla
description: Cuadrilla is a reel in the key of G from the Texas tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: E. J. Special Polka
description:
"E. J. Special Polka" was released on Canyon Records in 1997 on the album Old Time O'odham Fiddle Music by the Gu-Achi Fiddlers. The Tohono O'odham (formerly Papago) people of southern Arizona developed a fiddle tradition incorporating polkas, two-steps, and mazurkas.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

description: Valse de Escoba is a reel in the key of C from the Texas tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: First Choice Two Step
description: Recorded as a 2/4 two-step by the Gu-Achi Fiddlers on the album Old Time O'odham Fiddle Music (Canyon Records CR-8092). The Gu-Achi Fiddlers are a Tohono O'odham group from Arizona; the tune reflects the Southwestern fiddle tradition.

title: Hohokum Polka
description:
"Hohokum Polka" is recorded by Bayou Seco and is associated with the Tohono O'odham fiddle tradition of southern Arizona, which utilizes violins, guitar, and drums.

The "Cababi Polka / Hohokum Polka" medley also appears on the 1998 album Unbuttoned by Katie Howson & Jeannie Harris.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Its In There

title: Josefinita

title: Libby Bird Song Mazurka
description:
Recorded by the Gu-Achi Fiddlers on their 2001 Canyon Records release. The tune originates from the Tohono O'odham fiddle tradition of southern Arizona.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Lonnie's Polka
description:
The Fiddler's Companion reports that Bob Holt thought he had learned 'Lonnie's Polka' from a radio broadcast by Missouri fiddler Lonnie Robertson. Holt was uncertain about the source and title, so this is a tentative account of transmission, not a composer credit.

Source: John Lamancusa collection, oldtimefiddletunes.net.

title: Memories in Ajo
description:
"Memories in Ajo" is a polka from the Tohono O'odham fiddle tradition, recorded by the Gu-Achi Fiddlers for Canyon Records. The title refers to Ajo, Arizona.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Mi Suegra Aprietan Mis Botas Polka
description:
Commonly known as "La Polka 'e la Suegra" (Mother-in-Law Polka), this Northern New Mexican tune appears in the repertoire of Gregorio Ruiz and Cleofes Ortiz.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Valse de los Panos
description:
A 3/4 waltz attributed to New Mexican fiddler Cleofes Ortiz, who learned it from his cousin Emiliano Ortiz. The title translates to 'Waltz of the Cloths/Shawls.'

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Paul's White Sox Polka
description: Paul's White Sox Polka is a reel in the key of G from the Texas tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: La Pecosita
description:
"La Pecosita" is a tune from the Tohono O'odham tradition of southern Arizona and northern Mexico. The genre blends Spanish colonial fiddle traditions with Indigenous O'odham musical sensibilities.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Pinto Beans Two Step
description: Pinto Beans Two Step is a reel in the key of G from the Texas tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Polfa (Polka in F)
description: Polfa (Polka in F) is a reel in the key of C from the Texas tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Polka de Rapho
description: Polka de Rapho is a reel in the key of G from the Texas tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Purple Lilies Polka
description:
"Purple Lilies Polka" is a tune that sounds almost like a Mexican polka, but it is actually a polka from the Native American Tohono O'odham tradition. The Tohono O'odham are an Indigenous people of the Sonoran Desert, straddling southern Arizona and northern Mexico.

It is a Tohono O'odham tune from southern Arizona, specifically associated with the Gu-Achi Fiddlers — a fiddle ensemble rooted in the Gu-Achi (Santa Rosa) community on the Tohono O'odham Nation.

The Gu-Achi Fiddlers are the primary source group for this tune. Their style blends Indigenous O'odham musical sensibility with the influence of Mexican norteño/polka rhythms — a natural result of the Tohono O'odham people's deep cultural and geographic ties to the Sonoran borderlands. A free collection of 39 fiddle tunes from Arizona and New Mexico — including tunes from the Gu-Achi Fiddlers and others — has been transcribed and compiled by John S. Lamancusa, making it one of the key documentary sources for this regional repertoire.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: El Quelite
description:
"El Quelite" is a traditional Mexican ranchera song attributed to composer Alfonso Esparza Oteo. It is named for the town of El Quelite near Mazatlán.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Redondo de Leyba
description: Recorded by New Mexican fiddler Cleofes Ortiz, this tune is documented in the Strachwitz Frontera Collection. The title likely refers to a circular dance form.

title: St. Rose of Lima Mazurka
description: St. Rose of Lima Mazurka is a reel in the key of G from the Texas tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Santa Rosa Processional
description:
"Santa Rosa Processional" is an old-time fiddle tune associated with Southwestern / Native American and Mexican musical influences, rather than the more commonly known Appalachian old-time tradition. Its name and character suggest a ceremonial or parade-style piece — a processional being music composed or used for a formal procession, likely connected to a feast day or religious celebration associated with Santa Rosa (a common Catholic saint's day honored in many indigenous and mestizo communities of the American Southwest and Mexico).

The tune appeared as a Tune of the Week (TOTW) on Fiddle Hangout on September 12, 2010, and that discussion thread generated notable comments on Native American and Mexican music and influences. This places it firmly in a conversation about Southwestern and Mexican fiddle traditions, distinct from Appalachian roots.

The tune appears to be part of a broader tradition of fiddle music from the U.S. Southwest and northern Mexico. Examples of this tradition include Raweali/Huichol fiddling (documented on the CD Wood That Sings: Indian Fiddle Music of the Americas), and music compiled by ethnomusicologist Jack Loeffler in the three-CD set La Musica de los Viejitos (Music of the Old Men), recorded along the Rio Grande and heavily flavored with Mexican influence.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Second Time in San Javier Two Step
description: Second Time in San Javier Two Step is a reel in the key of G from the Texas tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Squash Fields
description: Squash Fields is a reel in the key of G from the Texas tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Tampico Hermosa Polka
description: Tampico Hermosa Polka is a reel in the key of C from the Texas tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Uncle Charlie's
description:
This tune is often associated with the Round Peak, North Carolina, fiddle tradition and figures such as Charlie Lowe, though specific provenance remains oral.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: La Vaquera
description:
A chotis (schottische) popular in northern New Mexico, documented in the repertoire of Cleofes Ortiz, who learned the piece from his cousin Emiliano Ortiz.

Cleofes Ortiz was born in 1910 on the Pajarito Plateau near Rowe, New Mexico.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Ho Detta al Sole
description: Ho Detta al Sole is a reel in the key of G. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Isaac Nelson's Hoppwaltz
description: Isaac Nelson's Hoppwaltz is a polska in the key of D from the Scandinavian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Hazel's Waltz
description: Hazel's Waltz is a polska in the key of D from the Scandinavian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Mabel Polka
description:
Direct historical documentation for "Mabel Polka" specifically is sparse in publicly indexed sources. Like many old-time fiddle tunes, it may belong to the large category of tunes with obscure or entirely oral origins. "Mabel Polka" is likely part of the old-time fiddle repertoire, most of which is in the public domain and has no known authorship — though many of these tunes have rich historical significance.

Polkas originated in Bohemia (Czech Republic) in the 19th century — a surprisingly recent period — but spread quickly in German and Polish folk music, throughout Europe, and were easily picked up by American fiddlers.

The polka's origin story first appears in the periodical Bohemia in 1844, attributed to a young Bohemian woman named Anna Slezáková. As told by Čeněk Zíbrt, music teacher Josef Neruda noticed her dancing in an unusual way to a local folk song in 1830, and he then put the tune to paper and taught other young men to dance it.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Storm Polka
description: Storm Polka is a polska in the key of D from the Scandinavian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Misirlou
description:
A folk melody from the Eastern Mediterranean, documented prior to 1920. The title 'Misirlou' means 'Egyptian Girl,' and the piece is associated with various regional dance and rebetiko styles.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Flop Eared Mule
description:
A G major reel appearing in Southern fiddle collections during the 19th century. It remains a standard in old-time repertoire.

The recording heard here is by Bev Baker and Norman Combs, preserved by the Internet Archive.

title: Nine Pound Hammer
description: A labor and coal-mining song from the Appalachian region, with documented versions in Kentucky, Virginia, and Tennessee from the early 20th century.

title: Johnson Boys
description:
A Southern Appalachian courtship song and fiddle tune appearing in early 20th-century field recordings. It was a common feature of the Round Peak and Blue Ridge traditions.

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)
tags: singable, beginner, courtship, mountain, round peak

title: Way Downtown
description: A blues-inflected Appalachian breakdown with roots in the 1920s–30s string band tradition. Popularized by Gid Tanner and the Skillet Lickers, the tune features a minor-leaning melody within a G major framework.

title: East Tennessee Blues
description:
A blues-influenced breakdown from the East Tennessee fiddle tradition of the early 20th century. Credited to Charlie Bowman (1889-1962), the tune reflects the cross-pollination of Southern breakdown and blues styles. Included in Miles Krassen's 'Appalachian Fiddle' (1973).

The tune is credited (by biographer Bob Cox) to Tennessee fiddler Charlie Bowman (1889-1962), who is said to have composed it in the 1920's.

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: Buffalo Gals
description:
Originally a minstrel song titled 'Lubly Fan' (1844), this tune was adapted by 19th-century itinerant performers under numerous regional titles. at dances and camp meetings, its call-and-response structure transitioned naturally into the fiddle repertoire.

The recording heard here is a 78rpm disc by Pickard Family, digitized by the Internet Archive.

title: Camptown Races
description:
Composed by Stephen Foster in 1850, this tune was quickly adopted into the fiddle tradition. It was performed by Black and white musicians shortly after publication, serving as a popular dance tune due to its driving rhythm.

(Source: Internet Archive)

title: Deep Elem Blues
description:
Associated with the Deep Ellum entertainment district in Dallas, this tune was recorded by the Lone Star Cowboys in 1933 and later by the Grateful Dead in 1970. It sits at the intersection of blues, country, and old-time music.

The recording heard here is by The Bansai Bills, preserved by the Internet Archive.
tags: blues, dallas, string band, grateful dead, singable
audio_source: The Bansai Bills via Internet Archive (2014)

title: Fox Chase
description: A narrative fiddle piece imitating a fox hunt, featuring horn calls and hounds. Associated with the Appalachian tradition and virtuoso fiddlers like Tommy Jarrell, the piece serves as a platform for performance mimicry.

title: Little Maggie
description:
Recorded by the Stanley Brothers in 1946, it connects to older British Isles traditions. Included in Traditional Tune Archive.

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

The recording heard here is by Alan F Brookes, preserved by the Internet Archive.

title: Train 45
description:
A railroad-themed tune from the Round Peak area of Surry County, North Carolina, definitive in the playing of Tommy Jarrell. The number 45 refers to a specific locomotive route.

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

The recording heard here is a 78rpm disc by Sonny Osborn, digitized by the Internet Archive.

title: Stoney Point
description: Named for Stoney Point, North Carolina, this reel is a standard in the Round Peak and Piedmont fiddle traditions. It exemplifies the Southern 'long bow' style.
tags: north carolina, round peak, long bow, session standard

title: Bright Morning Star
description: A modal tune with origins in the Sacred Harp tradition, moving into the fiddle repertoire. The A minor (Dorian) setting provides an archaic sound linked to Anglo-American folk music.

title: Growling Old Man and Grumbling Old Woman
description: A comic 19th-century Southern dance tune depicting an argument between an old couple. Its structure relies on alternating phrases to imitate different character voices.
