title: Jawbone
description:
An antebellum tune referencing the use of a mule's jawbone as a percussion instrument. Cited in Frederick Douglass's narrative, it reflects African American contributions to old-time vocabulary.

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: Railroad Bill
description:
Based on the life of Morris Slater, an outlaw who robbed Alabama trains in the 1890s. The tune was recorded by string bands across the color line in the 1920s–30s.

The recording heard here is by The Homesteaders, preserved by the Internet Archive.
tags: outlaw ballad, african american, alabama, singable, blues

title: Charming Betsy
description:
A flowing Appalachian reel with an Irish-influenced melodic structure, common in the 19th-century mountain South.

(Source: Internet Archive)
audio_source: D.D.Teoli Jr. A.C. via Internet Archive

title: Coal Creek March
description: Memorializing the 1891–92 Coal Creek War in Tennessee, a labor conflict regarding convict mine labor. The tune serves as a piece of regional identity.
tags: march, labor history, tennessee, coal mining, historical

title: Wake Up Susan
description: A late 19th-century breakdown from the Appalachian fiddle tradition. Its driving energy and simple structure made it a staple at Southern dances.

title: Barlow Knife
description: Named for the 19th-century Barlow folding knife, a standard trade item. This reel circulated in the mountain South through the 20th century.

title: Pretty Little Horse
description: An Appalachian lullaby that transitioned into an instrumental fiddle piece. Collected in the 1920s–30s in Virginia and North Carolina.

title: Roving Gambler
description: A gambling ballad from the British broadside tradition, popular in the 1920s–30s. Collected by Cecil Sharp, it was widely recorded by players such as Doc Watson.

title: Ida Red (Canote Version)
description: A version of 'Ida Red' emphasizing the 1920s string band tradition rather than later rock influences. This hypnotic tune influenced Chuck Berry's 'Maybellene' (1955).
tags: driving, A major, chuck berry, string band, 1920s

title: Cindy (Full Version)
description: A widely recorded American courtship song. It appeared in shape-note hymnals and was a staple of the fiddle camp repertoire.
tags: courtship, singable, beginner, jam standard, appalachian

title: Hangman's Reel
alternative_titles: Reel du Pendu, Le Reel du Pendu, Reel of the Hanged Man
description:
A convergence of the French-Canadian 'Le Reel du Pendu' (recorded by Joseph Allard, 1928) and an Appalachian version popularized by Albert Hash (1917–1982). Folk legends suggest the tune was composed by a prisoner to gain freedom.

The Appalachian old-time version was popularized by Albert Hash (1917–1982) of Rugby/Whitetop, Virginia, who learned it from a 1968 recording by Texas fiddler Bill Northcutt. Recorded sources : - County CO-CD-2711, Kirk Sutphin - "Old Roots and New Branches" (1994).

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)
tags: cross-tuning, french-canadian, appalachian, dramatic, albert hash, festival

title: Greasy Coat
description:
A signature tune of Edden Hammons (1876–1955), recorded in 1947. The piece combines European modal scales with African-American rhythmic drive. The title has been variously attributed to a comic poem or an old-time euphemism.

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)
tags: cross-tuning, modal, west virginia, hammons family, dorian, edden hammons

title: Old Buck
alternative_titles: Ol' Buck
description:
One of the most charming creation stories in the old-time repertoire. In the 1940s, Tommy Jarrell (1901–1985) of Round Peak, Surry County, North Carolina, was trying to learn 'Paddy on the Turnpike' from fiddler Rafe Brady, who played it twice for him. About a year later, Jarrell worked up what he believed was his version of it. When he played it for Brady, Brady said: 'Tommy, that ain't Paddy on the Turnpike, that's Old Buck.' Jarrell responded: 'Well, if there's a tune named Old Buck I don't know nothing about it — but that was all that was said, and that's what I called it from then on. So I made a tune I reckon.' The tune belongs to the double-tonic reel family, its two parts playing off each other with a shifting harmonic center. Tommy Jarrell and musical partner Fred Cockerham (1905–1980) became the most chroniclers of Round Peak style, and their recordings were central to the 1970s old-time revival.

Included in *Old Time Herald vol. 3 No. 1* (August 1991). Will I was a trying to learn "Paddy On the Turnpike," Rafe Brady came down here one time and I got him to play it twice for me. I played it for him and he says "Tommy, that ain't 'Paddy on the Turnpike', that's Old Buck'.

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: Honey Babe
alternative_titles: Red Rocking Chair, Ain't Got No Honey Baby Now, Red Apple Juice, Sugar Babe
description: Part of a sprawling song family, 'Honey Babe' features floating verses shared by multiple Southern folk songs. It was a staple of mountain social gatherings and singings.

title: Squirrel Heads and Gravy
description:
The most successful practical joke in old-time music history. Around 1975, Missouri fiddler Chris Germain composed a tune and deliberately passed it off as an ancient Appalachian reel, claiming he'd learned it from an old West Virginia fiddler 'who died shortly after teaching it.' The inspiration came from friends who overheard a child at a music festival ask an elderly fiddler if he knew a tune called 'Squirrel Heads and Gravy' — no such tune existed, but the title was too perfect to waste. The hoax worked: the tune spread through Midwest jams and festivals, was recorded by multiple bands as 'Traditional' — including Bovee and Heil and the Piney Creek Weasels — and developed genuine regional variations in different keys and cross-tunings. Germain's original was in A with AEAE tuning; G major GDad versions followed. Germain eventually confessed, but by then the tune had completed the folk process on its own. It is now, by any measure, a traditional tune.

"Squirrel Heads and Gravey" was composed by fiddler Chris Germain (originally from Ferguson, Missouri, then of Washington D.C.) around the year 1975, apparently as part of a joke. Ironically, the tune has entered tradition and is sometimes listed as a "traditional" melody. The rumor that there is an older tune by the same name only seems to be part of the joke.

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: Reel des Esquimaux
alternative_titles: Reel des Eskimos
description: First recorded in 1939 by French-Canadian fiddler Isidore Soucy. The 'crooked' phrasing of the original is a notable feature in Quebec and Métis traditions.

title: Malheur County Blues
description: Named for the remote Malheur County in eastern Oregon, this tune represents the westward expansion of old-time fiddle culture. It carries a bluesy, modal tonality common in contemplative breakdowns.

title: Turkey in the Straw
alternative_titles: Zip Coon, Natchez Under the Hill
description:
'Turkey in the Straw' began life in 1834 as 'Zip Coon,' a blackface minstrel number published in New York and Baltimore with disputed authorship among performers George Washington Dixon, Bob Farrell, and George Nichols. The character 'Zip Coon' was a caricature of a dandified free Black man — one of minstrelsy's ugliest stock figures. The tune's melody, however, drew from older fiddle and banjo traditions and proved so catchy that it outlived its original context by two centuries. The title 'Turkey in the Straw' emerged in the late 19th century, stripping the minstrel associations and attaching the melody to rural, agricultural imagery. By the early 20th century it was simply a folk tune, recorded by countless string bands and appearing in early country music catalogs. Its pentatonic structure and driving rhythm made it one of the most recognizable American melodies in the world — appearing in ice cream truck jingles, cartoons, and folk festivals with no trace of origin. The minstrel roots are historical fact, not a reason to avoid the tune, but a reason to know its full story.

Included in Francis O'Neill's *Music of Ireland. 1850 Melodies* (1903). Well, I was—where we lived, we lived down on the Williams River, when the—when I saw this thing, and so--. And we always went to bed pretty early, my dad did, and—about eight o’clock we always went to bed—and I laid down and I, didn’t seem like I could go to sleep. And I laid there a while and just directly I heard the click, open come the door, and in walked this skeleton of a man, Lord, I’ve—he was really tall, a-must’ve been six or seven feet tall or looked like that.

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)
tags: beginner, pentatonic, minstrel origins, widely known, driving

title: Pretty Polly
alternative_titles: The Gosport Tragedy, William and Polly
description:
A dark murder ballad descending from the British 'Gosport Tragedy,' documenting Appalachian violence and folk memory. Dock Boggs's 1927 version is the American standard.

It was collected extensively by John Harrington Cox in 'Folk-Songs of the South' (1925) and by Cecil Sharp in the 1910s.
notes: Dock Boggs recorded a banjo version in 1927.

title: Falls of Richmond
description:
A bright D major reel named for Richmond, Virginia, the former capital of the Confederacy and one of the great Southern fiddle cities. The Falls of the James River at Richmond were a significant geographic landmark and transportation chokepoint that shaped the city's industrial history. The tune circulates widely in Appalachian and Southern old-time jam sessions and appears in multiple fiddle collections under variant titles including simply 'Richmond.' Walt Koken, banjoist and co-founder of Highwoods String Band, plays a definitive version in D major with a strong, straight rhythmic drive typical of Southern breakdown style.

Included in David Brody's *Fiddler's Fakebook (The)* (1983). A Aeolian or Dorian ('A'and 'B' parts) & A Major ('C' & 'D' parts). AEae (Brody, Phillips) or ADae tunings (Edden Hammons, Kuntz) {fiddle}. AABCB (Brody): AABBCCDDBB (Kuntz, Phillips, Songer). "Falls of Richmond" has been a popular piece among old-time revival musicians but its original associations apparently were solely with the Hammonds family of West Virginia.

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: Lazy John
description:
A G-major breakdown associated with fiddler Clyde Davenport. Davenport learned the tune from radio broadcasts in the mid-20th century.

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: Last Chance
description: A brisk old-time reel in D with a clean two-part structure common to the Southern Appalachian tradition. Featured on George Jackson's The Old Time 100, Vol. 1.

title: Dry and Dusty
description: One of the most beloved and accessible old-time fiddle tunes in the repertoire. 'Dry and Dusty' has a simple, satisfying melodic arch in G that makes it a favorite at beginner jams. Featured on George Jackson's The Old Time 100, Vol. 1.

title: Policeman
description: A driving Southern Appalachian breakdown in D with a martial, rhythmically propulsive character. Featured on George Jackson's The Old Time 100, Vol. 1.

title: Elk River Blues
description:
A moody, bluesy old-time fiddle tune named for the Elk River in central West Virginia, with a modal feel and spacious phrasing. Featured on George Jackson's The Old Time 100, Vol. 1.

Included in Claire Milliner & Walt Koken's *Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes* (2011). A mountaintop-removal coal mine sits adjacent to the headwaters of Elk River, and the mining process has caused rock overburden to fill the valley at the river's source. Acid runoff has also taken a toll on wildlife and fish in the area. The tune is played slower than a breakdown, at a very brisk walking pace.

Additional notes Source for notated version : - Ernie Carpenter (W.Va.) [Milliner & Koken].

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: Ruffled Drawers
description:
A classic Southern Appalachian reel in D. The tune is associated with lyrical verses collected by John Hartford.

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: Brushy Fork of John's Creek
description: Named after a tributary of Johns Creek in eastern Kentucky, this haunting two-part reel has a distinctly modal Appalachian quality rooted in the Eastern Kentucky fiddle tradition. Featured on George Jackson's The Old Time 100, Vol. 1.

title: Tennessee Breakdown
description:
A Tennessee breakdown in G with a rhythmic structure suitable for square dances. Possibly composed by Dudley Vance.

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: Fall on My Knees
description: A lyrical, expressive waltz-time tune in the old-time tradition with a hymn-like searching quality. Featured on George Jackson's The Old Time 100, Vol. 2.

title: Benton's Dream
description:
A two-part reel in A Mixolydian. Composed by Benton Flippen (1920-2011) of Surry County, North Carolina, in the 1960s. Fiddler Tommy Jarrell reportedly gave the tune its name after hearing Flippen play it. It was Included in Stacy Phillips's Traditional American Fiddle Tunes vol. 1 (1994).

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: Shove That Pig's Foot a Little Farther in the Fire
description: An old-time breakdown in D with one of the most memorable titles in the fiddle canon — raw, earthy, and full of drive. Featured on George Jackson's The Old Time 100, Vol. 2.

title: Josie-O
description: A rhythmically compelling breakdown in G with the momentum and lift characteristic of the best Southern fiddle dance tunes. Featured on George Jackson's The Old Time 100, Vol. 2.

title: Red Prairie Dawn
description: A sweeping waltz-time tune that evokes the open landscape of the American prairie, with gentle arc and sustained melodic lines. Featured on George Jackson's The Old Time 100, Vol. 2.

title: Train on the Island
description: A well-traveled old-time reel found across the Appalachian fiddle tradition, with a clean two-part structure and forward drive. Featured on George Jackson's The Old Time 100, Vol. 2.

title: Dubuque
description: Named for the Iowa city on the Mississippi River, a Midwestern old-time reel with the rolling feel of upper-Mississippi valley fiddle music. Featured on George Jackson's Old Time 100, Vol. 3.

title: Eighth of January
description: A patriotic fiddle tune commemorating Andrew Jackson's victory at the Battle of New Orleans on January 8, 1815. One of the oldest and most known tunes in the American fiddle canon. Also known as 'Battle of New Orleans.' Featured on George Jackson's Old Time 100, Vol. 3.

title: Jack of Diamonds
description: A traditional gambling song and fiddle tune found throughout the Appalachian and Texas fiddle traditions, recorded by many old-time artists. Featured on George Jackson's Old Time 100, Vol. 3.

title: Jeff Sturgeon
description: A breakdown named for Jeff Sturgeon, a fiddler in the Southern Appalachian tradition. Composer-named tunes anchor repertoire to specific regional players and communities. Featured on George Jackson's Old Time 100, Vol. 3.

title: John Brown's Dream
description: A rolling modal reel in A with the haunting quality characteristic of eastern fiddle traditions. Featured on George Jackson's Old Time 100, Vol. 3.

title: Uncle Joe
description:
American reel in G Major. Included in E.F. Adam's Old Time Fiddlers Favorite Barn Dance Tunes (1928). It is considered a derivative of the British Isles’ “Miss McCloud’s Reel.”

(Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)
